## **1 Decision problem, description of the technology and clinical care pathway** 

**Complement 3 glomerulopathy (C3G) is an ultra-rare chronic and progressive kidney disease which is characterised by deposits of complement component 3 (C3) in the glomeruli. C3G is commonly diagnosed at a young age[1-3]** 

- C3G is caused by overactivation of the complement alternative pathway of the immune system,[1, 4, 5] which leads to the deposition of C3 and its cleavage products within the glomeruli of the kidneys, triggering inflammation and glomerular injury.[5, 6] As glomeruli are injured, normal kidney function becomes impaired, with wide-ranging consequences including proteinuria (protein in the urine), haematuria (blood in the urine), renal dysfunction, hypertension (high blood pressure) and fatigue[7-10] 

- C3G is a progressive disease, in which individuals experience continuous symptom worsening alongside irreversible kidney damage, before reaching kidney failure.[5] Patients reaching kidney failure require chronic dialysis or kidney transplantation[11-13] 

- Based on registry data, the current prevalence of C3G in the United Kingdom (UK) is estimated as 0.37 in 50,000, with an estimated 427 people living in England with C3G in 2024.[3, 14, 15] C3G is commonly diagnosed in young people, with the median age at diagnosis reported as 21–23 years old[1, 16, 17] 

**With current treatments, approximately 50% of patients with C3G progress to kidney failure within 10 years of diagnosis,[3, 16, 18, 19] and the rate of C3G recurrence following kidney transplantation is high (55–85%)[5, 19-24]** 

- There are currently no targeted therapies for C3G, and currently used treatments predominantly constitute supportive care with limited evidence in C3G[25] 

- Angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors (ACEis) or angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs) are recommended as initial therapy to reduce proteinuria and manage hypertension.[25] Further treatment options include mycophenolate mofetil (MMF) and/or corticosteroids (CS), or sodium-glucose co-transporter-2 inhibitors (SGLT2is), although clinical trial enrolment is often preferred by UK clinicians.[25-27] The use of eculizumab in the UK is very limited and restricted to highly aggressive cases of post-transplant recurrent C3G[26-28] 

- None of the currently available treatments address the underlying pathophysiology of C3G. Many C3G patients therefore progress to kidney failure and become reliant on chronic dialysis or require a kidney transplant at a young age, with the disease commonly recurring following transplantation[5, 19-24] 

- Disease progression is associated with increasing clinical, humanistic and economic burden, including co-morbidities, reduced quality of life (QoL), costs for the National Health Service (NHS), and productivity losses for people with C3G and their carers. There is therefore an unmet need in C3G for targeted therapies which slow disease progression 

**Iptacopan, a novel, oral proximal complement inhibitor, is expected to be the first targeted treatment for C3G**[29] 

- Iptacopan is a twice daily (b.i.d.) oral complement inhibitor targeting Factor B,[29] and expected to be the first targeted treatment addressing the underlying pathophysiology of C3G and therefore the high unmet need of this ultra-rare, progressive condition 

Company evidence submission for iptacopan for treating C3 glomerulopathy [ID6283] © Novartis (2025). All rights reserved 




<!-- page 13 -->

- It is anticipated that iptacopan will be licensed for the treatment of adult patients with C3G in combination with a renin-angiotensin system (RAS) inhibitor, or in patients who are RAS-inhibitor intolerant, or for whom a RAS inhibitor is contraindicated[30]

This submission covers the full expected marketing authorisation of iptacopan for this indication. The decision problem addressed in this submission is provided in Table 1, which outlines any differences from the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) final scope.[31]

## _**1.3.1 Disease pathophysiology**_ 

Complement 3 glomerulopathy (C3G) is an ultra-rare, complex and progressive chronic kidney disease, which is characterised by deposits of complement component 3 (C3) in the glomeruli.[1, 2] 

The complement system, a crucial part of the innate immune system, consists of more than 50 small proteins.[5] When stimulated, these proteins form a cascade that promotes inflammation and the activity of the innate immune system.[1, 4, 5, 48, 53, 54] The complement system can be activated by three pathways: the classical, lectin and alternative pathways (Figure 1).[5] 

The classical and lectin pathways remain inactive unless triggered; the alternative pathway, however, remains constitutively active at a low level and plays a pivotal role in providing a rapid defence mechanism against a wide range of pathogens and amplifying the complement response.[4, 5, 55, 56]

**Figure 1: The alternative pathway of the complement system** 

**==> picture [452 x 294] intentionally omitted <==**

**Abbreviations:** C3, complement component 3; C5, complement component 5; FB, Factor B; FD, Factor D; FH, Factor H; FI, Factor I; MAC, membrane attack complex **Sources:** Adapted from Bomback et al. 2022,[48] and Keir et al. 2012.[55] 

C3G is a form of primary glomerulonephritis which is caused by acquired and/or genetic abnormalities resulting in overactivation of the complement alternative pathway in blood plasma and in the glomerular microenvironment within the kidney.[1, 4, 5] This leads to the deposition of C3 and its cleavage products within the glomeruli, triggering inflammation and glomerular injury.[5, 6] 

As glomeruli are injured, normal kidney function becomes impaired, with wide-ranging consequences. These can include haematuria (blood in the urine), proteinuria (protein in the urine), oliguria (low urine output), and kidney damage.[5, 57] The kidney damage observed as a result of continued complement activity is progressive and mostly irreversible.[5] 

## _**1.3.2 Epidemiology**_ 

While incidence and prevalence are difficult to ascertain, given the rare nature of C3G and its relatively recent definition as a distinct disease in 2013,[42] C3G is considered an ultra-rare disease. 

Studies reporting C3G incidence are limited. A study from Medjeral-Thomas et al. 2014 arrived at annual incidence estimates of 1 per million population based on data from a single centre in the UK, and 2 per million population based on data from a single centre in Ireland.[16] However, the study methodology – a retrospective, manual review of all reports of kidney biopsies referred to two tertiary, specialist sites – may overestimate the diagnosed incidence in the overall population. 

No studies reporting population-based prevalence estimates for C3G could be identified. The National Organization for Rare Disorders (NORD) website states an estimated prevalence of 

Company evidence submission for iptacopan for treating C3 glomerulopathy [ID6283] © Novartis (2025). All rights reserved 




<!-- page 23 -->

C3G of 2–3 per 1,000,000 people, i.e. 0.1–0.15 per 50,000 people.[58] Based on data from the National Registry of Rare Kidney Diseases (RaDaR), which includes data from 109 renal centres across the UK,[59] Novartis estimates that there are currently approximately 505 prevalent patients with C3G in the UK overall, or 427 patients in England,[a] equating to a prevalence of 0.37 in 50,000.[3, 14, 59, 60] 

C3G predominantly affects young people aged under 40 years. The median age at diagnosis is reported as 21–23 years old, with C3G commonly diagnosed under 18 years of age.[1, 16, 18, 19] In a recent analysis of data from 258 UK patients with C3G in RaDaR,[59] the median age at diagnosis was 22 years (interquartile range [IQR]: 12–45 years), with 44% of patients diagnosed below the age of 18 years.[17] 

## _**1.3.3 Presentation and diagnosis**_ 

Patients with C3G often present with a range of signs and symptoms, including proteinuria, haematuria and varying degrees of renal dysfunction.[5, 57] Other signs and symptoms may include hypertension (high blood pressure), fatigue, oedema (swelling of some areas of the body, including feet, hands and ankles), and oliguria (low urine output).[7-10] Some patients with C3G present with nephrotic syndrome, which is a term used to describe the association of high levels of proteinuria (urine protein-creatinine ratio [UPCR] >300–350 mg/mmol) with peripheral oedema, hypoalbuminemia (serum albumin <25 g/L) and severe hyperlipidaemia (total cholesterol often >10 mmol/L).[61] 

While clinical presentation plays a role in diagnosis, laboratory tests and a kidney biopsy are required for differentiation between various glomerular diseases including other forms of membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis (MPGN) or immunoglobulin A nephropathy (IgAN).[5, 25, ] 42 

Genetic and antibody testing is used to determine whether there is an underlying complement abnormality.[42] For example, low levels of serum C3 combined with normal levels of another complement component, C4, indicate activation of the alternative complement pathway.[42] Urine analysis often shows the presence of red blood cells, white blood cells, and protein.[62] 

Kidney biopsy is required for a definitive diagnosis of C3G.[1] C3G is divided into two subtypes, dense deposit disease (DDD) and complement 3 glomerulonephritis (C3GN), according to kidney biopsy findings at the electron microscopy level.[42] The clinical presentation and prognosis are consistent between subtypes and clinical management remains the same.[5, 18, 19, 43] 

## _**1.3.4 Disease course**_ 

C3G is a progressive disease, in which individuals experience continuous symptom worsening alongside irreversible kidney damage, before reaching kidney failure.[5] C3G carries one of the 

a As of November 2024, RaDaR contained data from overall 1,232 patients with membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis (MPGN).[60] The MPGN cohort in RaDaR comprises patients with C3G as well as patients with immune complex-mediated MPGN (IC-MPGN), although exact diagnosis is not always captured in RaDaR data. In an analysis conducted in 2023, among 287 patients with exact diagnosis recorded, 47% had C3G and 53% had IC-MPGN.[3] Applying this split to the entire cohort (N=1,232) and considering that 157 patients of the overall MPGN cohort in RaDaR had died prior to July 2022,[14] the number of prevalent C3G patients in RaDaR can be estimated as a maximum of 505 patients for the UK overall, or 427 patients for England.[15]

highest risks for irreversible kidney failure of all primary glomerular diseases, with approximately 50% of patients progressing to kidney failure within 10 years of diagnosis.[3, 16, 18, 19] 

## **1.3.4.1 Glomerular filtration rate** 

Kidney function in individuals with C3G is impacted due to damage caused to the glomeruli, impairing their ability to filter blood effectively, leading to a reduced glomerular filtration rate (GFR).[63] The filtration rate is usually monitored via an estimated GFR (eGFR), which is a measure of kidney filtration calculated based on serum creatinine levels, age, sex, and other factors (measured in mL/min/1.73 m[2] to adjust for body surface area).[13] The Chronic Kidney Disease Epidemiology Collaboration (CKD-EPI) eGFR creatinine equation is considered the preferred method of calculating eGFR in adults with glomerular diseases.[25] 

Tracking eGFR, as a marker of kidney damage, provides valuable insights into the progression of C3G, with eGFR levels used to define stages of disease progression (Section 1.3.4.3). An eGFR ≥90 mL/min/1.73 m[2] is considered to represent normal kidney function.[25] In a recent analysis of 109 UK patients with C3G and eGFR data available in RaDaR, the median eGFR at diagnosis was 71 mL/min/1.73 m[2] .[17] A progressive decline in eGFR in C3G patients is associated with poor outcomes.[3, 64] 

## **1.3.4.2 Proteinuria** 

Proteinuria is a key sign of C3G and can be assessed by the level of protein excretion into urine. This can be calculated as urine protein to creatinine ratio (UPCR) or urine albumin to creatinine ratio (UACR), with UPCR generally preferred for glomerular diseases including C3G.[11, 25, 27, 65] Proteinuria may be measured using a first morning void (FMV) sample, when the first urine of the day is collected for a concentrated analysis, or all samples collected over a 24-hour period.[66] 

A UPCR of <50 mg/mmol is considered to be in the normal range for adults, with a higher UPCR associated with worse kidney outcomes.[65, 67, 68] In an analysis of UK patients with C3G and UPCR data available in RaDaR (n=91), median UPCR at diagnosis was 442 mg/mmol (IQR: 140–871 mg/mmol).[17] Overall, 82% of patients had UPCR ≥100 mg/mmol at diagnosis,[17] indicating increased risk of progression to kidney failure;[25] 66% of patients had nephrotic-range proteinuria (UPCR ≥300 mg/mmol) at time of diagnosis.[17] An international cross-sectional study further showed high levels of persistence of proteinuria with currently available treatments, with 62% of 263 patients with C3G having UPCR ≥1 g/day (≥113 mg/mmol) despite receiving treatment.[10] Among 50 patients who had been receiving treatment for C3G for more than two years at the time of the analysis, 44% still had UPCR ≥1 g/day.[10] 

Proteinuria is a key risk factor for progression to kidney failure, as evidenced widely for chronic kidney disease (CKD) more generally, and glomerular diseases including C3G and IgA nephropathy.[3, 17, 25, 64, 67, 69-72] Recent analyses of registry data from patients with C3G in the UK (RaDaR) and Spain found that reduction in proteinuria was significantly associated with a lower risk of kidney failure.[3, 72] 

## **1.3.4.3 Clinical staging** 

CKD is classified into stages, which can be used to define the level of risk and monitor for disease progression in C3G over time. eGFR, as measure of kidney function, provides information on the level of damage in the glomeruli and can be used to categorise CKD into CKD stages 1 (eGFR ≥90 mL/min/1.73 m[2] ; normal kidney function) to 5 (eGFR <15 mL/min/1.73 m[2] ; kidney failure).[11, 13, 73, 74] The international Kidney Disease Improving Global Outcomes (KDIGO)

## **1.3.4.4 Kidney failure and kidney replacement therapy** 

Long-term management of C3G typically involves regular monitoring of kidney function, blood pressure control, and the use of specific medications to reduce proteinuria and inflammation (see Section 1.3.5). However, as these treatments do not target the underlying cause of the disease, patients still progress to kidney failure, with approximately 50% of patients with C3G progressing to kidney failure within 10 years of diagnosis.[3, 16, 18, 19] In a study by Bomback et al. 2018, of 111 patients with C3G in the United States (US), 40% of patients progressed to advanced CKD, kidney failure or death, over a mean follow-up period from diagnosis of 6 years.[18] In a retrospective analysis of C3G patients in the UK and Ireland by Medjeral-Thomas et al. 2014, 29% of 70 patients with adequate follow-up data progressed to kidney failure after a median follow-up of 28 months (IQR: 7–84 months).[16] A case series by Servais et al. 2012 in a French multi-centre study identified that 36.5% of 134 patients with C3G progressed to kidney failure within 10 years of diagnosis.[19] Similarly, a recent analysis of data from UK patients with C3G in

Given the young average age at diagnosis (median age 21–23 years),[1, 16, 17] and short median time to kidney failure, patients with C3G are often reliant on chronic dialysis or require a kidney transplant at a young age. In the prevalent RaDaR cohort of 240 people with C3G and a mean age of 40.6 years (standard deviation [SD]: 19.34), 51% had reached kidney failure at the time of analysis.[17] 

Patients reaching kidney failure require kidney replacement therapy (KRT) in the form of dialysis or kidney transplantation.[11, 12] Dialysis is a mechanical procedure to remove waste products and excess fluid from the blood, and can take two forms, haemodialysis (HD) and peritoneal dialysis (PD).[75-78] HD involves the individual’s blood being transferred in and out of a dialysis machine and is typically performed at dialysis centres, though this can also be performed at home.[77, 79] HD sessions typically occur three times a week, taking approximately four hours per session.[77] PD involves the infusion of dialysis solution into the peritoneal cavity (the space within the abdomen that contains the intestines, the stomach, and the liver) through a catheter, which allows the 

Company evidence submission for iptacopan for treating C3 glomerulopathy [ID6283] © Novartis (2025). All rights reserved 




<!-- page 27 -->

lining of the abdomen to act as a filter to remove waste products and excess fluid from the blood.[77, 78] PD can take the form of continuous ambulatory peritoneal dialysis (CAPD) and automated peritoneal dialysis (APD), and is administered at home.[77] CAPD is repeated approximately four times a day, with each session lasting 30–40 minutes. APD is performed daily for 8–10 hours, usually overnight.[77] 

Once individuals with C3G have progressed to kidney failure, they may receive a kidney transplant if a suitable living or deceased donor kidney is available. Transplants can also be preemptive, providing patients with a transplant prior to the start of dialysis.[80] For patients to be eligible for a transplant, they must be in good general health as there is a risk of significant physical side effects, most notably post-transplant infection or acute rejection.[81, 82] Immunosuppressants are prescribed long-term following kidney transplantation to prevent organ rejection, and are also associated with a number of side effects.[13, 82] 

## **1.3.4.5 Post-transplant recurrence and graft failure** 

As C3G is characterised by overactivation of the complement alternative pathway, which occurs upstream of the kidneys,[5] kidney transplantation does not address the underlying pathophysiology of C3G.[23] Therefore, C3G commonly recurs following kidney transplantation, with recurrence rates reported to be between 55–85%, with a median time to recurrence of 14– 28 months.[5, 19, 20, 22-24, 83] 

As a consequence of disease recurrence, the risk of graft failure in C3G is high, with reported graft failure rates of 50% among patients with disease recurrence, and a median time from transplant to graft failure of 77 months.[24] Following graft failure, patients are required to either return to dialysis or receive another kidney transplant. RaDaR data from patients with C3G indicate a median time to graft failure post-transplant of 6.5 years; among 75 prevalent kidney transplant recipients with C3G, 14 patients (18.7%) had received two or more kidney transplants at the time of analysis.[17] 

## **1.3.4.6 Mortality** 

While data for C3G as an ultra-rare disease are limited, decline in kidney function is widely acknowledged to be associated with an increased risk of complications of kidney disease, including cardiovascular disease and mortality.[47, 70, 84-86] An analysis in 27,285 people from the UK with rare kidney diseases included in RaDaR (including 1,089 people with either C3G or MPGN) estimated a standardised mortality ratio (SMR) of 2.29 (95% CI: 2.09, 2.49) compared to the general population in England and Wales; for people with rare kidney diseases with kidney failure (eGFR ≤15 mL/min/1.73 m[2] or receiving KRT) the SMR was 3.99 (95% CI: 3.55, 4.42).[14] 

The mortality burden of CKD on an individual level is largest in younger patients, with a recent US study estimating that a 20-year-old with CKD loses on average 15.6 life years compared with a 20-year-old without CKD, while a 70-year-old with CKD would on average lose 3.9 life years compared to a similarly aged individual without CKD.[87] While these values are not C3G-specific and mortality in rare kidney diseases may be lower than in CKD overall,[14] these data are pertinent given that individuals with C3G tend to be diagnosed at a young age (median age at diagnosis 21–23 years old) and approximately 50% will progress to kidney failure within 10 years of diagnosis.[1, 19, 88, 89]

## _**1.3.5 Treatment pathway**_ 

Ultimately, maintaining kidney function and preventing kidney failure are the key treatment goals in C3G.[26] However, currently available therapies do not address the underlying pathophysiology of C3G, and predominantly constitute supportive care.[25, 26] 

KDIGO published international clinical practice guidelines in 2021 on the management of glomerular diseases, including C3G.[25] KDIGO highlights that an optimal treatment strategy for C3G has not been established, and that current management recommendations are based on expert opinion, retrospective cohort data and extrapolation from other glomerular diseases, as well-controlled data in C3G were unavailable at time of guideline writing.[25] 

KDIGO recommendations as well as information about the use of various treatments in UK clinical practice, based on insights from two advisory boards held by Novartis with UK clinicians in 2022 (nine advisors)[26] and 2024 (10 advisors),[27] are summarised below in the following sections. An overview of the current treatment pathway for C3G in the UK is presented in Figure 3.

## **1.3.5.1 ACEi/ARB** 

For the treatment of people with C3G, the international KDIGO 2021 guidelines recommend standard supportive measures as for other glomerular diseases.[25] This includes the use of an ACEi or ARB (RAS inhibitors) to a maximally tolerated licensed dose, as initial therapy to reduce proteinuria and manage hypertension.[25] Lifestyle modifications, such as optimal nutrition, weight normalisation, regular exercise, and smoking cessation, should be encouraged alongside use of ACEis/ARBs.[5, 25] 

In clinical advisory boards, UK clinicians confirmed that ACEis/ARBs are commonly used in UK clinical practice, in up to 100% of their patients with C3G.[26, 27] Advisors were aligned that ACEi/ARB treatment was effective in reducing proteinuria and has a favourable safety profile; Company evidence submission for iptacopan for treating C3 glomerulopathy [ID6283] © Novartis (2025). All rights reserved Page 26 of 151 




<!-- page 29 -->

however, they highlighted that ACEis/ARBs do not alter active glomerular inflammation or affect the underlying complement-mediated disease process in C3G, and are thus unable to prevent disease progression.[26] 

In an international cross-sectional study (Adelphi Disease Specific Programme [DSP]), 90.6% (n=29/32) of patients with C3G from the UK were receiving treatment at the time of survey completion by their nephrologists. Of these, 82.8% (n=24/29) received an ACEi or ARB.[90] 

## **1.3.5.2 Immunosuppression with MMF and/or CS** 

The KDIGO 2021 guidelines recommend that C3G patients with moderate to severe disease (proteinuria >1 g/day and haematuria or have had declining kidney function for at least 6 months) should be further treated with MMF plus CS.[25] 

Discussion in an advisory board held by Novartis in 2022 highlighted mixed opinions among UK clinicians about the clinical utility of MMF and CS in C3G, with usage of these treatments (in combination or individually) varying across centres.[26] Advisors emphasised that the evidence for the use of MMF in C3G was limited and that the KDIGO recommendation was based on observational data only, with clinical effectiveness findings varying between studies.[25, 26] Views on the effectiveness of CS were similar, although it was suggested that short-term use could be beneficial in some patients for reducing inflammation.[26] With both MMF and CS, in addition to limited efficacy evidence in C3G, clinicians considered the risk of gastrointestinal side effects and an increased risk of infection with immunosuppression when determining the benefit-risk profile for individual patients.[26, 91] CS are also associated with various other side effects including musculoskeletal effects (osteoporosis and myopathy), weight gain, hypertension and insomnia which can be worsened by increased doses and continued administration.[92] Several UK clinicians reported that they often prefer to enrol patients with C3G in a clinical trial instead of using MMF and/or CS, if a suitable study is available.[26] 

During the 2024 advisory board, clinicians estimated that MMF/CS use in UK clinical practice ranged from 30–70% of patients; while this points to some variation between centres, one advisor also highlighted that estimates may differ depending on whether clinicians considered the proportion of their patients on MMF/CS currently, or at any time during the disease course.[27] In the Adelphi DSP, of the UK patients receiving treatment at the time of survey completion, 41.4% (n=12/29) and 37.9% (n=11/29) were receiving treatment with MMF and CS, respectively.[90] 

## **1.3.5.3 SGLT2 inhibitors** 

Whilst not reflected in the KDIGO 2021 guidelines, following recent licence extensions to patients with CKD, SGLT2is are also increasingly used as part of established clinical management, as supportive background medication alongside ACEis/ARBs.[26, 27] However, no data are available on the efficacy and safety of SGLT2is specifically in patients with C3G, and UK clinicians noted that SGLT2is would not be used in patients who are on immunosuppression, including transplanted patients.[26] 

## **1.3.5.4 Eculizumab** 

The KDIGO 2021 guidelines state that if treatment with MMF plus CS fails, eculizumab should be considered.[25] However, in the UK, funding of eculizumab for C3G is restricted by an NHS England Clinical Commissioning Policy, and its use is highly limited.[26, 28] NHS England commissioning criteria restrict the use of eculizumab to a subset among patients with posttransplant recurrence of C3G, with evidence indicative of highly aggressive disease, for example, 

Company evidence submission for iptacopan for treating C3 glomerulopathy [ID6283] © Novartis (2025). All rights reserved 




<!-- page 30 -->

active glomerulonephritis with cellular crescents on kidney biopsy and a >20% decline in eGFR within the previous three months.[26, 28] Since the policy was established in 2017, up to March 2023, only 7 UK patients with C3G met the criteria and were able to access eculizumab.[36] In the 2024 advisory board, one clinician confirmed that overall still only 8 or 9 patients with C3G had received eculizumab in the UK up to October 2024.[27] 

In addition to access limitations, UK clinicians highlighted that as a terminal complement component 5 (C5) inhibitor, eculizumab does not target the overactivation of the complement alternative pathway which is the root cause of C3G.[26] KDIGO also summarises that the benefits of terminal complement blockade with C5 inhibitors remain unestablished in C3G and reports inconsistent efficacy results from small studies,[25] which was echoed by UK clinicians based on their clinical experience with eculizumab in a small number of patients with post-transplant recurrent C3G.[26, 27] 

## **1.3.5.5 Clinical trial enrolment** 

The KDIGO 2021 guidelines recommend that patients who fail to respond to the outlined treatment approaches should be considered for a clinical trial where available.[25] In UK clinical practice, enrolment in a clinical trial is often considered at an earlier stage, given clinicians’ concerns with currently available immunosuppressants and the fact that none of the current treatment options address the underlying cause of disease by targeting C3G pathogenesis.[5, 7, 25-] 27, 88 

## _**1.3.6 Disease burden and unmet need**_ 

## **1.3.6.1 Clinical burden** 

Symptoms of C3G, such as oedema and fatigue, can have a noticeable impact on daily activities.[7-10, 93, 94] Oedema can be intermittent or severe, affecting the ability of people with C3G to carry out physical tasks, such as standing, walking, and climbing stairs.[7, 94] An international cross-sectional survey among people with C3G and a median eGFR of 50 mL/min/1.73 m[2] (IQR: 32–70 mL/min/1.73m[2] ) using the Functional Assessment of Chronic Illness Therapy-Fatigue (FACIT-Fatigue) questionnaire (n=118) found a severe impact of fatigue on all aspects of patients’ lives, with over three-quarters of participants reporting that they limit social activities (78%) and need to sleep during the day (77%), and almost half of the participants (47%) feeling too tired to eat, due to their fatigue.[95] In an international 2017 forum of people with C3G and carers for people with C3G, including representatives from the UK, one participant stated that “the fatigue is overwhelming”.[7] Fatigue may be further exacerbated in patients with C3G receiving dialysis.[96] Other symptoms impacting QoL include back/side/abdominal pain, appetite loss, oliguria, and sleeping problems.[7, 9, 93] Pain/discomfort (at a level of at least ‘slight’) was reported by 65% in an international study of 118 people with C3G completing the EQ-5D-5L questionnaire.[95] Whilst many people with C3G report a diminished QoL, this is especially true for up to 40% of patients who develop nephrotic syndrome, which is characterised by a high symptom burden and complications associated with increased levels of proteinuria, peripheral oedema, hypoalbuminemia and severe lipidaemia.[19, 97, 98] 

Kidney dysfunction and damage associated with C3G can lead to a number of concomitant conditions and comorbidities including cardiovascular diseases such as hypertension.[99] Hypertension can increase the risk of diseases such as cardiac disease or stroke, and is a major global cause of premature death in CKD.[99] Additionally, acquired partial lipodystrophy (APL) and ocular complications such as retinal drusen (yellow deposits under the retina) can occur in 

Company evidence submission for iptacopan for treating C3 glomerulopathy [ID6283] © Novartis (2025). All rights reserved 




<!-- page 31 -->

people with C3G.[1, 100] People with C3G can also experience periodic episodes of gout, which can lead to joint pain.[7, 57, 93 ] Therefore, people with C3G can experience a range of symptoms that can negatively impact their QoL, highlighting the need for effective treatment. 

There are currently no targeted treatments for C3G which address the underlying cause of disease, with most treatments prescribed off-label for symptomatic relief.[25] The evidence on the efficacy of these treatments in C3G is limited, and some treatments are associated with safety risks and side effects (see Section 1.3.5). With currently available treatments, C3G carries one of the highest risks for irreversible kidney failure of all primary glomerular diseases, with approximately 50% of patients progressing to kidney failure within 10 years of diagnosis, as a result there is a significant unmet need.[3, 16, 18, 19] 

KRT is also associated with significant side effects. Dialysis can be associated with fatigue, hypotension (low blood pressure), itchy skin and muscle cramps.[96] Kidney transplantation is associated with multiple short-term risks including surgical complications, bleeding, posttransplant infection, and acute rejection of the transplanted kidney.[101] The longer-term risks of transplants similarly include infections, organ rejection, and recurrent disease,[81, 101] which is particularly common in C3G (see Section 1.3.4). Kidney transplant recipients may also experience significant side effects (see Section 1.3.5) and risks associated with long-term use of immunosuppressive regimens to prevent graft rejection, such as increased risk of cancer.[81, 101-] 103 

## **1.3.6.2 Humanistic burden** 

In addition to symptoms of C3G, the QoL of people with C3G is particularly impacted by the high level of uncertainty around the risk of progression to kidney failure, as well as the current lack of treatment options, which can lead to anxiety and depression.[7, 93 ] In the aforementioned 2017 C3G international patient forum, one participant stated that “It’s horrible all around. You know it’s going to get worse” and another noted “what’s most difficult is knowing that time is not on my side…without a viable drug treatment, I know that a healthy diet, exercise, and following doctor’s orders will not stop the progression of this disease…This absolutely frightens me…I can only imagine things getting worse”.[7] The impact of the disease on mental health is further aggravated by the ultra-rare nature of C3G, with the lack of information available about the disease and symptoms adding to a feeling of helplessness, isolation, and loneliness.[7, 93 ] One participant of the 2017 patient forum stated “you feel like you’re going through it alone”, with 34% of attendees reporting they felt others did not understand the experience of living with C3G.[7] In a UK patient advisory board conducted by Novartis in 2022, participants described how the uncertainty around future progression of C3G limits the choices they have in life, both on a personal and professional level.[93] In the 2017 C3G patient forum, one participant summarised their feelings as “We were afraid to travel. We were afraid to make plans. We were afraid to do much of anything”.[7] 

Symptoms of the disease, lifestyle and diet restrictions, and dialysis as a very time-consuming treatment, put a burden on daily life for patients and their families and carers.[7, 93, 104 ] Young people with C3G report not being able to attend education regularly, impacting their future career opportunities, and feeling stigmatised among peers from having to follow a strictly controlled diet.[93] Treatment decisions can also contribute to the psychological burden of the disease, with concerns around kidney transplants and the potential for C3G recurrence resulting in patients feeling as though they must “trade in their current condition for another unknown”.[7] 

Company evidence submission for iptacopan for treating C3 glomerulopathy [ID6283] © Novartis (2025). All rights reserved 




<!-- page 32 -->

Overall, QoL in people with C3G is lower than in the general population, with EQ-5D showing impact in particular in the anxiety/depression, pain/discomfort, and usual activities domains.[95] QoL notably decreases in more advanced stages of CKD, as reported by both C3G patients,[8] and CKD patients more broadly, with dialysis associated with the lowest utility values.[105] 

Available carer burden evidence is limited in C3G, although given the substantial symptom burden experienced by patients with C3G (see Section 1.3.6.1), their family and carers may need to provide additional support with daily activities and medical appointments.[7, 90, 106] The impact on family life was explored in the 2017 C3G patient forum, with participants explaining that “[t]he anxiety is spread throughout an entire family”.[7] 

## **1.3.6.3 Economic burden** 

Due to the rarity of the condition, there is limited evidence regarding the economic burden of C3G (see Appendix G). A Kidney Research UK report notes that the key driver of the cost of rare kidney diseases, such as C3G, is the need for dialysis or transplants in patients reaching kidney failure.[106] As discussed in Section 1.3.4, the prognosis for many people with C3G is kidney failure, with 50% of patients progressing to kidney failure within 10 years of diagnosis.[3, 16, 18, 19] Given the early age at diagnosis (median age 21–23 years), rapid disease progression, and high likelihood of post-transplant disease recurrence,[1, 16] patients are likely to require dialysis for several decades, or multiple transplants over a lifetime which increases the economic burden of C3G. In a recent analysis of prevalent C3G patients in RaDaR, 46% of 240 patients were on KRT (15% on dialysis, 31% transplanted).[17] 

While there is limited information regarding direct costs for C3G, CKD more broadly places a high economic burden on the NHS, which increases substantially as the disease progresses. For example, the number of minimum routine monitoring checks recommended by NICE increases with CKD stage.[11] In 2023, the costs of CKD stages 1–5 prior to initiation of KRT were estimated to be £1.95 billion, with 91% estimated to be attributable to CKD stages 3–5.[106] This highlights the importance of preventing or delaying disease progression in chronic kidney diseases such as C3G. 

KRT is a key driver of the high costs associated with CKD, including estimated costs to the NHS in 2023 of £1.05 billion for dialysis, £225 million for dialysis transport costs, and £293 million for transplantations.[106] Most transplant costs are attributable to the procedure itself; however, there are additional costs associated with ongoing care following transplantation and adverse events due to transplantation and organ rejection.[106] Furthermore, whilst patients are waiting for a suitable donor organ, which currently ranges from 2–3 years in the UK, many will require dialysis, leading to further costs to the NHS in the interim.[106] There are also concerns with NHS resource constraints, with dialysis and transplantation services reported to already be operating at maximum capacity.[106] Due to the high rates of disease recurrence and high risk of graft failure in patients with C3G,[5, 19, 20, 22-24, 83] many patients may need to go back onto chronic dialysis or receive a further kidney transplant, which means that costs associated with KRT may be incurred for prolonged periods of time and/or incurred multiple times. With growing numbers of people requiring dialysis, the demand for dialysis  is estimated to require a 400% increase in capacity by 2033, which would place an increased economic burden on the NHS.[106] 

In addition to the direct costs associated with dialysis, some patients rely on NHS-funded transport for in-centre haemodialysis (HD) (3x per week).[106, 107] A UK study from Liu et al. 2015 suggests these costs could be significant, costing the NHS approximately £9,600 per in-centre HD patient per year (value inflated to 2022/23; further details are provided in Section 3.5.2).[108, ]

109 Transport costs funded by the NHS may be expected to increase, given the NHS’ recent universal commitment to supporting patients’ transport for in-centre HD sessions through organised transport or financial reimbursement, as outlined in the national eligibility criteria for non-emergency patient transport services (NEPTS).[110-112] 

## **Indirect costs/productivity losses** 

C3G is also associated with productivity losses for individuals with C3G and their carers. Dialysis was estimated in 2023 to cost the UK economy £372 million due to lost patient and carer productivity (missed work time), and this is expected to increase in the next decade.[106] In an international study using the Work Productivity and Activity Impairment (WPAI) questionnaire, people with C3G reported a mean overall work impairment score of 47.7%, with an impairment at work score of 43.8% and work time missed reported as 17.6%, due to their C3G (where 100% represents being completely prevented from undertaking work).[90] In the international 2017 patient forum of individuals with C3G, 25% of respondents reported that they had missed school or work due to C3G.[7] 

## **1.3.6.4 Unmet need** 

There are currently no approved targeted therapies for C3G. Treatments that are used have limited efficacy in C3G, and around 50% of patients progress to kidney failure within 10 years of diagnosis.[3, 16, 18, 19] Once someone has progressed to kidney failure, they require lifelong dialysis or a kidney transplant.[7, 48] Kidney transplantation is not curative, however, and there is a high rate of C3G recurrence post-transplant (55–85%).[5, 19, 22-24, 83, 113] 

There is therefore a high unmet need in C3G. UK clinicians participating in advisory boards conducted by Novartis described the current unmet need in C3G as “huge” and “enormous” and highlighted the need for novel targeted therapies in C3G.[26, 27] Clinical and patient organisations further attested to this unmet need in their responses to the draft scope consultation of iptacopan for C3G.[104 ] 

## _**1.3.7 Proposed positioning of iptacopan**_ 

In C3G, overactivation of the complement alternative pathway leads to deposition of C3 within the glomeruli, triggering inflammation and glomerular injury.[48] Iptacopan is an oral, first-in-class, proximal complement inhibitor that specifically binds Factor B (Figure 4). This selectively blocks alternative pathway overactivation by inhibiting alternative pathway-related C3 convertase activity, leading to decreased cleavage of C3 and reduced C3 deposition in the kidney.[37] Iptacopan is expected to be the first targeted treatment which addresses the underlying pathophysiology of C3G.

## **1.4 Equality considerations** 

Novartis supports access to treatment for all people with C3G regardless of their age, ethnicity and socioeconomic background. While the currently available iptacopan clinical trial results and expected licensed indication are limited to adults, Novartis is committed to pursuing a licence extension and access to iptacopan for younger people with C3G as soon as the available evidence permits. 

Average wait time for adults in the UK to receive a kidney transplant is currently 2-3 years.[106] However, the 2023–2024 NHS Blood and Transplant annual report on ethnicity differences in organ donation and transplantation and a Kidney Research UK report from 2023 both highlight that there is considerable inequality across ethnic groups with regards to CKD and access to kidney transplants, with individuals of Black and Asian descent more likely to be diagnosed later, progress faster towards kidney failure and face much lengthier wait times for transplants compared with white people.[106, 118] Socio-economic deprivation is also correlated with poor survival outcomes in CKD, with people who are socio-economically deprived experiencing faster rates of disease progression, a higher risk of cardiovascular disease and premature mortality.[106] Socio-economic deprivation is also associated with lengthier wait times for transplants and limited access to living donor transplants, leading to higher rates of long-term kidney failure and mortality.[106] 

People with C3G face an inherent level of health inequalities due to the ultra-rare nature of the disease which leads to significant disparities in healthcare access and outcomes, when compared to more common conditions. Robust evidence generation for new medicines is challenging in ultra-rare diseases, with small patient populations restricting the ability to conduct large-scale clinical trials. Small sample sizes in clinical trials further result in challenges in health technology assessments (HTAs) due to the resulting higher degree of uncertainty in the available evidence. Consequently, this may limit the availability of effective treatment options for people with ultra-rare diseases. Lack of awareness and education about ultra-rare diseases, including among healthcare professionals, further exacerbates health inequalities when compared to more common conditions, due to delays in diagnosis, absence of evidence-based care pathways, and variation in service provision across different parts of the country.[119-121] 

The NICE Prioritisation Board confirmed that iptacopan for C3G meets the Highly Specialised Technologies (HST) routing criteria that relate to rarity of the disease (routing criteria 1 and 2).[122] While the NICE evaluation takes place using the Single Technology Appraisal (STA) route, NICE are asked to apply flexibility in the STA process for iptacopan for C3G to enable timely and equitable access for people with an ultra-rare disease of this nature, when compared to treatments being assessed through the STA process for conditions with a much higher prevalence.

## **2 Clinical effectiveness** 

**The main clinical evidence base for iptacopan as an add-on treatment to standard of care (SoC) in adult patients with C3G is informed by the APPEAR-C3G trial, with supportive evidence from the Phase 2 study and an open-label extension study** 

- APPEAR-C3G (NCT04817618)[32] is an international, multicentre, randomised, doubleblind, parallel group, placebo-controlled Phase 3 study to evaluate the efficacy and safety of iptacopan in patients with native kidney C3G (N=74) 

- The Phase 2 study (NCT03832114)[123] was an international, multicentre, open-label, single-arm, non-randomised study in adults with native kidney or post-transplant recurrent C3G (N=27) 

- The open-label extension study (NCT03955445)[35] is an ongoing non-randomised study in patients receiving iptacopan after completing treatment in APPEAR-C3G or the Phase 2 study 

## **Clinical evidence demonstrated the efficacy of iptacopan in adult patients with C3G** 

- APPEAR-C3G met its primary endpoint with iptacopan treatment resulting in a statistically significant and clinically meaningful reduction in 24h UPCR by 35.1% (95% CI: 13.8%, 51.1%; p=0.0014) following 6 months of treatment with iptacopan compared with placebo on top of optimised background therapy[33] 

- The change in eGFR in APPEAR-C3G supported the treatment effect of iptacopan, with a change from baseline to 6 months of 2.16 mL/min/1.73m[2] (95% CI: −2.75, 7.06; multiplicity-adjusted 1-sided p-value: 0.3241), as measured by the adjusted mean difference of iptacopan versus placebo (secondary endpoint)[33] 

- An exploratory endpoint assessed the change in eGFR slope, comparing the rate of change of eGFR following initiation of iptacopan with patients’ eGFR trajectory prior to iptacopan treatment. Patients included in APPEAR-C3G showed a rapid decline in eGFR prior to starting iptacopan treatment, with an eGFR slope of −7.22 mL/min/1.73 m[2] /year (95% CI: −10.10, −4.35; estimated based on up to 2.5 years of pre-iptacopan data). Treatment with iptacopan (including longer-term follow-up data from the extension study, with up to 2 years treatment duration) led to stabilisation of the eGFR decline, with the oniptacopan slope estimated as −0.29 mL/min/1.73m[2] /year (95% CI: −3.88, 3.31). This equated to a change in annual eGFR slope of 6.94 mL/min/1.73m[2 ] (95% CI: 3.48, 10.39; p=0.0001) compared with pre-iptacopan treatment[124] 

**Iptacopan was well-tolerated; AEs were balanced between the iptacopan and placebo arms during the controlled double-blind period of APPEAR-C3G (controlled safety set)** 

- The safety profile of iptacopan was well characterised in the clinical trials. In APPEARC3G, iptacopan was well tolerated, with the majority of AEs being mild or moderate in severity[33, 125] 

- In the broad safety set, including data from all patients receiving at least one dose of iptacopan 200 mg b.i.d. in the treatment periods of all three studies (N=101), 36 serious adverse events (SAEs) were experienced by 19.8% of patients; approximately half of these were infection-related.[125] Three patients discontinued iptacopan due to AEs (all discontinuations occurred during the ongoing open-label extension study), with all three due to SAEs determined not to be related to iptacopan[125]

## **2.1 Identification and selection of relevant studies** 

A systematic literature review (SLR) was conducted in October–December 2021, and subsequently updated in October 2024, to identify relevant clinical trial evidence on the efficacy and safety of treatments for patients with C3G. The SLR scope was broad, including both randomised and non-randomised clinical trials in patients diagnosed with C3G, and receiving any intervention for C3G (including investigational treatments, best supportive care or placebo). 

Across the original SLR and its update, 33 publications reporting on 15 unique studies were included. Of these, 2 studies included patients with C3G who were treated with iptacopan (in the SLR, categorised as APPEAR-C3G and the Phase 2 trial, with open-label extension study results for patients originating from the Phase 2 trial included as linked publications for the Phase 2 trial). 

Full details of the process and methods used in the SLR, as well as a description of the included studies and results, are provided in Appendix B. 

## **2.2 List of relevant clinical effectiveness evidence** 

As identified by the SLR, the primary source of clinical efficacy evidence for iptacopan in C3G is the Phase 3 trial APPEAR-C3G. Supportive evidence is provided by the Phase 2 trial, and an open-label extension study including patients who completed either the Phase 2 trial or APPEAR-C3G. An overview of these studies is provided in Table 4.[33, 37, 38, 126] The clinical SLR did not identify any other studies for iptacopan in the relevant patient population as defined by the NICE final scope.

## **2.3 Critical appraisal of the relevant clinical effectiveness evidence** 

APPEAR-C3G was quality assessed using the Cochrane Risk of Bias 2 tool, while the single-arm Phase 2 trial was assessed using the Cochrane Risk of Bias In Non-Randomized Studies (ROBINS-I) tool.[128, 129] APPEAR-C3G was determined to be at low risk of bias, while the Phase 2 trial was considered to be associated with a moderate risk of bias. Further details are provided in Appendix B. 

## **2.4 APPEAR-C3G** 

## _**2.4.1 Summary of methodology**_ 

APPEAR-C3G (NCT04817618) is an international, multicentre, randomised, double-blind, parallel group, placebo-controlled Phase 3 study to evaluate the efficacy and safety of iptacopan in patients with native kidney C3G.[32, 33, 48, 126] 

The APPEAR-C3G trial comprised the following three periods (Figure 6):[33] 

- A screening/run-in period lasting up to 90 days 

- A 6-month double-blind treatment period, during which patients received blinded treatment with 200 mg iptacopan or placebo orally b.i.d. (randomisation 1:1) 

- A 6-month open-label treatment period, during which all patients received open-label iptacopan 200 mg orally b.i.d. 

Following completion of study treatment at 12 months, patients were given the option to discontinue iptacopan treatment and enter a 30-day safety follow-up period or continue iptacopan treatment by transitioning to a roll-over open-label extension study (further information on the open-label extension study is provided in Section 2.5.2).[33]

## **2.4.1.1 Patient disposition** 

In APPEAR-C3G, a total of 74 patients were enrolled in the adult cohort, with 38 patients randomised to the iptacopan arm and 36 randomised to the placebo arm. Patient disposition for the double-blind and open-label periods are presented in Table 6. All 74 patients completed the 6-month double-blind period. However, two patients in the iptacopan arm discontinued doubleblind treatment due to patient decision and a technical issue. Both of these patients continued double-blind study visits (without treatment) until the end of the double-blind period, and then transitioned to the open-label period where they attended study visits and received open-label iptacopan.[33] 

Overall, 73 of the 74 patients completed the full 12 months of the study (6 months double-blind period plus 6 months open-label period). One patient originally randomised to the placebo arm discontinued treatment during the open-label period, with the reason recorded as patient decision, was subsequently lost to follow-up and discontinued from the study.[33]

## **2.4.1.2 Baseline demographics and disease characteristics** 

Patient demographics and disease characteristics at baseline are summarised in Table 7. Of the 74 patients enrolled in the study, 47 were male (63.5%) and 27 were female (36.5%). The majority of patients were of White race (68.9%) and from study sites in Europe (55.4%). The mean (SD) age of all patients was 27.9 (10.7) years.[33] 

The 74 patients enrolled in the study represent a C3G population at high risk of disease progression based on a mean (SD) 24h UPCR of 3.40 (2.07) g/g or 384.41 (233.46) g/mol at baseline. A high proportion of patients had nephrotic range proteinuria (24h UPCR ≥3 g/g, 43.2%). Mean (SD) eGFR at baseline was well preserved at 94.1 (31.6) mL/min/1.73m[2] , and systolic and diastolic blood pressures were well controlled.[33] 

The treatment arms were generally balanced; however, there were imbalances between groups in some baseline disease characteristics such as UPCR, eGFR, and C3G subtype (Table 7). Patients randomised to the iptacopan arm had notably higher UPCR and lower eGFR at baseline, compared with those from the placebo arm. Furthermore, there were a greater number of participants with baseline nephrotic range proteinuria (≥3 g/g) in the iptacopan arm (55.3%) than in the placebo arm (30.6%; Table 7).[33]

## **2.4.1.3 Concomitant therapies** 

All participants were required to be on a stable, maximally recommended or tolerated dose of an ACEi/ARB for the 90-day Screening period and during the study. Patients who received a stable dose of MPA, lower-dose CS (prednisolone ≤7.5 mg/day or equivalent) or SGLT2is were eligible for enrolment and continued these treatments on the same dose during the study. Changes in dose of concomitant therapies were allowed if indicated due to an AE or other safety issue.[33 ] 

Overall, 37 participants (97.4%) in the iptacopan arm and 36 participants (100%) in the placebo arm received at least one concomitant medication affecting proteinuria during the double-blind period. The most common concomitant medications received by participants in both arms were RAS inhibitors (iptacopan: 37 participants, 97.4%; placebo: 36 participants, 100%). Therefore, all but one participant, who was intolerant to ACEis/ARBs, received background RAS inhibitor therapy. Additionally, 44.6% of patients received CS and/or MPAs and 5.4% of patients received SGLT2is. A summary of concomitant therapies relevant to C3G is presented in Table 8.[33]

- **APPEAR-C3G Description** 0.025 level 

- • The primary analyses were based on the FAS • At baseline and Month 6, the geometric mean of two 24h UPCR values obtained from two distinct 24h urine collections was used in the analysis as the 24h UPCR measurement for that visit. In case only one 24h UPCR value was available, that value was used as the 24h UPCR measurement for that visit in the analysis 

- • 24h UPCR measurements collected after initiation or intensification of antiproteinuric therapies or KRT were imputed, to reflect a poor response and also to reflect that 24h UPCR levels would deteriorate (increase) had these treatments not been received 

- • Statistical analysis was performed using a mixed model for repeated measures (MMRM) for the log ratio to baseline in UPCR measurements. This model included treatment, time point, CS and/or MPA at randomisation (yes versus no) as fixed effects, treatment*time point as interaction term and log (baseline UPCR) as covariate. The correlations between visits within patients were modelled using an unstructured covariance matrix. The Kenward-Roger adjustment for degrees of freedom was used 

- • If there were intercurrent events occurring in the study, the analysis was carried out in the imputed datasets. Each imputed dataset was analysed using the MMRM and the results were combined using Rubin’s rules 

- • The ratio of geometric means (iptacopan versus placebo) was presented for the 6-month time point together with the two-sided 95% CI and one-sided p-value for the hypothesis test. The study was considered positive if the one-sided p-value for the hypothesis test was <0.025 

- _Handling of intercurrent events_ • Initiation or intensification of antiproteinuric therapies after randomisation: Values after the intake of additional antiproteinuric therapies were set to missing and imputed using the “jump to reference” (J2R) approach[132] for the iptacopan arm and the missing-atrandom (MAR) assumption for the placebo arm (hypothetical strategy) 

- • Initiation of KRT after randomisation: Values after initiation of KRT were imputed using the J2R approach[132] for the iptacopan arm and the MAR assumption for the placebo arm (hypothetical strategy) 

- • Treatment discontinuation for any reason (other than the antiproteinuric therapies or KRT): 24h UPCR measurements after discontinuation of study treatment were collected and used in the analysis (treatment policy strategy) 

- _Handling of missing values not related to intercurrent events_ • The MMRM model used for the primary analysis implicitly imputes missing data under a MAR assumption 

- **Statistical Secondary endpoint analyses of the 6-month double-blind period: analysis of secondary** Analyses were performed based on the FAS.

## _**2.4.3 Clinical effectiveness results**_ 

The APPEAR-C3G trial provides the primary clinical evidence base for iptacopan. During the 6- month double-blind period, patients received either treatment with iptacopan or placebo. Following the double-blind period, all patients randomised to the placebo arm crossed over to open-label iptacopan treatment. All patients were then treated with iptacopan for another 6- month period, up to Month 12 of the study. Following completion of APPEAR-C3G, patients were able to continue treatment with iptacopan as part of an open-label extension study, the details of which are presented separately in Section 2.5.2.[33, 38] 

The following sections present the clinical efficacy data for iptacopan, as assessed in APPEARC3G. 

## **2.4.3.1 Primary efficacy results: proteinuria reduction** 

## _**Primary endpoint (double-blind period): CfB in 24h UPCR up to Month 6**_ 

APPEAR-C3G met its primary endpoint; iptacopan treatment resulted in a statistically significant and clinically meaningful relative reduction in 24h UPCR by 35.1% (95% CI: 13.8%, 51.1%; p=0.0014) following 6 months of treatment compared with placebo (both arms as add-on to background therapy) (Table 10). The adjusted mean ratios to baseline of 24h UPCR at the Day 180 visit using MMRM analysis in the iptacopan arm and the placebo arm were 0.70 (95% CI: 0.57, 0.85) and 1.08 (95% CI: 0.88, 1.31), respectively (i.e. reduction of 24h UPCR from baseline with iptacopan was 30% compared with an increase of 8% with placebo) (Figure 7; Table 10). These results demonstrate that treatment with iptacopan in patients with C3G reduces proteinuria compared with placebo.[33]

## _**Primary endpoint (double-blind period): sensitivity analyses**_ 

Pre-specified sensitivity analyses for the primary endpoint considered alternative imputation approaches following intercurrent events. Intercurrent events were rare, reported in only three patients (7.9%) in the iptacopan arm. The sensitivity analyses, presented in Table 11, are consistent with the primary analysis, confirming robustness to varying assumptions on the handling of intercurrent events. This is expected given that only one intercurrent event (increasing CS dose) required imputation based on the hypothetical strategy. The other two intercurrent events were treatment discontinuations in the iptacopan arm; UPCR measurements after treatment discontinuation were used in the primary analysis as per the treatment policy strategy. Additional post-hoc sensitivity analyses were conducted due to observed imbalances at baseline to assess the impact of adjustment for these baseline covariates (Table 11).[33]

## _**Primary endpoint (open-label period): CfB in 24h UPCR up to Month 12**_ 

Results from the open-label period of APPEAR-C3G demonstrated that in patients initially randomised to iptacopan, the observed reduction in 24h UPCR was sustained up to Month 12 (40% geometric mean reduction from baseline; geometric mean ratio 0.60 [95% CI: 0.45, 0.80]; Table 12).[33] 

Patients initially randomised to the placebo arm who switched to open-label iptacopan at Month 6 had a 27% UPCR reduction from baseline to Month 12 (geometric mean ratio 0.73 [95% CI: 0.58, 0.92]; Table 12). Considering the rise in UPCR between baseline and Month 6 (while on placebo), the reduction in UPCR from Month 6 to Month 12 (on iptacopan) was 31%, which was similar to the reduction observed in the iptacopan arm from baseline to Month 6 (34%) (Table 12). The 24h UPCR reduction up to Month 12 is presented in Figure 9.[33]

## _**Supplementary analyses for primary efficacy results**_ 

A post-hoc analysis evaluated the proportion of patients with nephrotic-range proteinuria, defined as ≥3 g/g (339 g/mol) 24h UPCR. In the iptacopan arm, the proportion of participants with nephrotic range proteinuria decreased from 55.3% at baseline to 31.6% at Month 6 and 36.8% at Month 12 (Figure 10). In the placebo arm, during the double-blind period, the proportion of patients with nephrotic-range proteinuria increased from 30.6% at baseline to 41.7% at Month 6. Following switch to open-label iptacopan at Month 6, the proportion decreased to 27.8% at Month 12 (Figure 10).[33] 

Furthermore, in the iptacopan arm there was an increase in the proportion of patients achieving UPCR <1 g/g (<113 g/mol) at Month 12, from 0% at baseline to 10.5% at Month 6 and 23.7% at Month 12 (Figure 10). In the placebo arm, the proportion with UPCR <1 g/g increased marginally from 2.8% at baseline to 5.6% at Month 6. After switch to iptacopan at Month 6, it increased to 13.9% at Month 12 (Figure 10).[33]

## _**Exploratory endpoint: eGFR slope change analyses**_ 

In addition to the CfB analyses, eGFR data were also analysed to assess the change in annualised eGFR slope with iptacopan treatment compared to patients’ eGFR trajectory prior to iptacopan initiation. 

For this purpose, historical serum creatinine data were collected for the patients enrolling in APPEAR-C3G. Study sites were instructed to provide all available serum creatinine values from the 2 years prior to the screening visit. All data within that period were accepted provided there was a corresponding date of sample collection. Historical eGFR values were derived from serum creatinine measurements using the CKD-EPI formula, consistent with the eGFR calculations for measurements collected during the APPEAR-C3G study.[33] 

For the eGFR slope change analyses, the historical data were combined with all observed instudy eGFR data. Pre-iptacopan eGFR data were defined as measurements before initiation of iptacopan treatment and thus included the historical values (up to 2 years or since C3G diagnosis if less than 2 years) as well as screening/run-in data and placebo arm data from the 6- month double-blind period of APPEAR-C3G. This resulted in participants randomised to placebo contributing up to 2.5 years of eGFR data to the pre-iptacopan slope, while participants randomised to iptacopan contributed up to 2 years of data to the pre-iptacopan slope. Overall, the pre-iptacopan slope was derived from 494 eGFR observations in 74 patients, comprising of 198 historical observations, 146 during the screening/run-in period, and 150 from patients while receiving placebo in the double-blind period.[33] 

The on-iptacopan eGFR slope included data from the double-blind and open-label periods (Day 1 to 360) for patients randomised to the iptacopan arm and data from the open-label period (Day 180 to 360) for patients randomised to the placebo arm, after the patients had switched to iptacopan.[33 ] 

A longitudinal mixed effects model, with a common intercept, a pre-iptacopan slope and a change in the slope following iptacopan treatment was used to model the change in eGFR trajectory. Subject-level intercept and slope were included in the model as random effects. Missing data were handled implicitly through the model. The eGFR slope prior to iptacopan treatment and the change in slope after iptacopan treatment were estimated.[33] 

Company evidence submission for iptacopan for treating C3 glomerulopathy [ID6283] © Novartis (2025). All rights reserved 




<!-- page 61 -->

The mean pre-iptacopan eGFR slope was −7.57 mL/min/1.73 m[2] /year (95% CI: −10.57, −4.56) in the full study population. Initiation of iptacopan led to stabilisation of eGFR, with eGFR slope for iptacopan estimated as 1.44 mL/min/1.73m[2] /year (95% CI: −2.18, 5.06), which equated to a change in eGFR slope of 9.01 mL/min/1.73m[2] /year (95% CI: 5.43, 12.60; p <0.0001) compared to the pre-iptacopan eGFR decline (Figure 14).[33] A longer-term eGFR slope analysis in the APPEAR-C3G population, including data from the open-label extension study, is presented in Section 2.5.2 and utilised in the economic model (Section 3.3.2).[33]

## **2.4.3.3 Secondary efficacy results: composite renal endpoint** 

## _**Secondary endpoint: composite renal endpoint at Month 6**_ 

Results from APPEAR-C3G demonstrated a statistically significant improvement in the proportion of participants achieving the composite endpoint of stable eGFR (≤15% decrease) and ≥50% reduction in UPCR at Month 6 in patients treated with iptacopan versus placebo (multiplicity adjusted 1-sided p=0.0166). The marginal proportion of participants (95% CI) who achieved the composite renal endpoint at Month 6 was 29.0% (14.9%, 43.1%) in the iptacopan arm and 5.7% (−1.9%, 13.4%) in the placebo arm (Figure 16).[33]

## **2.4.3.4 Secondary efficacy results: C3G histologic total activity score** 

## _**Secondary endpoint: CfB in C3G histologic total activity score at Month 6**_ 

No significant differences were observed in the histologic total activity score from kidney biopsies after 6 months of iptacopan treatment in comparison with placebo. ## **2.4.3.5 Secondary efficacy results: FACIT-Fatigue total score** 

## _**Secondary endpoint: CfB in FACIT-Fatigue at Month 6**_ 

Mean (SD) FACIT-Fatigue scores at baseline were near the general population norm for both treatment arms: 42.4 (10.08) in the iptacopan arm and 41.9 (8.91) in the placebo arm. Participants taking iptacopan did not show an improvement in FACIT-Fatigue. The adjusted mean difference of CfB in the FACIT-Fatigue total score in the iptacopan arm versus placebo arm was −2.60 (95% CI: −6.03, 0.84; multiplicity-adjusted 1-sided p-value: 0.9310) after 6 months of treatment (Table 19).[33 ]

## **2.4.3.7 Exploratory efficacy results: effect of iptacopan on complement biomarkers** 

## _**Exploratory endpoint: circulating biomarker levels at Month 6 and Month 12**_ 

Inhibition of the complement alternative pathway by iptacopan at Month 6 and Month 12 was validated via circulating biomarker levels, including serum C3, alternative pathway activity, plasma Bb, plasma sC5b-9 and urinary sC5b-9/creatinine. In patients with C3G, altered levels of complement biomarkers are indicative of alternative pathway dysregulation. This can include: 

- Decreased serum C3 

- Overactivity of alternative pathway activity, observed via Wieslab assay 

- Increased plasma Bb 

- Increased plasma sC5b-9 

- Increased urinary sC5b-9 creatinine 

With iptacopan treatment, there was a rapid rise in serum C3 levels, which was sustained throughout the study, while the C3 concentration in the placebo arm remained unchanged. In addition, decreases were observed with iptacopan in alternative pathway activity, plasma Bb, plasma sC5b-9 and urinary sC5b-9 (Table 21). Circulating biomarker levels were measured up to Month 12, to demonstrate the change in inhibition of the complement pathway following initiation of iptacopan treatment in the placebo-iptacopan switch arm. A sustained increase of serum C3 in the iptacopan arm was observed for the entire 12 months treatment period, as well as a rapid rise in placebo arm patients after switching to iptacopan at Day 180, mirroring the effect seen in the iptacopan arm in the double-blind period.[33]

## **2.5 Supportive clinical efficacy results** 

Supportive evidence for the clinical efficacy of iptacopan for the treatment of patients with C3G is provided by the Phase 2 study (Section 2.5.1) and the open-label extension study (Section 2.5.2).[34, 38] The Phase 2 study included patients with post-transplant recurrence of C3G and is therefore summarised in the submission to provide data on this cohort, as APPEAR-C3G only included native kidney patients.[34] The open-label extension study is included to provide data on the long-term clinical efficacy and safety of iptacopan in C3G, as it represents the longest followup period in the clinical trial programme for iptacopan in C3G.[38]

## _**2.5.1 Phase 2 study**_ 

## **2.5.1.1 Summary of methodology** 

The Phase 2 study (NCT03832114) was an international, multicentre, open-label, single-arm, non-randomised study in adults with biopsy-confirmed C3G. The study included two cohorts of patients, one with native kidney C3G (native kidney cohort; Cohort A) and one with C3G recurrence following kidney transplantation (post-transplant recurrent cohort; Cohort B). All patients received iptacopan twice daily for 12 weeks. A total of 27 patients were enrolled and completed the study: 16 in the native kidney cohort and 11 in the post-transplant recurrent cohort.[37] 

A summary of the methodology of the Phase 2 study is provided in Table 22.

## **2.5.1.2 Trial design** 

The Phase 2 study included a screening period comprised of run-in (≤60 days) and a 30-day baseline period. Patients then entered treatment period 1, lasting 12 weeks, with dose escalation of iptacopan up to 200 mg b.i.d. (Figure 17). At Week 12, kidney biopsies were collected; these were optional for the native kidney cohort and mandatory for the post-transplant recurrent cohort.[34] 

Following 12 weeks of treatment in the Phase 2 study, patients could roll over to the extension study (NCT03955445) if treatment continuation was found to be beneficial by the investigator. If continuation of treatment was not deemed beneficial by the investigator, study medication was titrated down to 25 mg once daily for 7 days, followed by 10 mg once daily for a further 7 days. The patient then continued in the follow-up period (12 weeks) until the end-of-study visit.[34]

## _**Patient disposition**_ 

A total of 27 patients (16 patients in the native kidney cohort and 11 patients in the posttransplant recurrent cohort) were enrolled and treated with iptacopan. All 27 patients (100%) completed the 12-week study and there were no discontinuations.[37] 

Twenty-six patients (96.3%) rolled over into the open-label extension study (NCT03955445) to continue long-term iptacopan treatment. One patient in the post-transplant recurrent cohort did not roll over and completed the tapering down and the follow-up period.[37]

## **2.5.1.3 Statistical analysis and definition of study groups** 

Sample size calculation was performed assuming that 15 patients in the native kidney cohort and 12 in the post-transplant recurrent cohort would provide 93% power for demonstration of true treatment reduction in log-transformed UPCR of 40% (SD 0.6) in the native kidney cohort, and 94% power for demonstration of true treatment reduction in C3 deposit score of 2 (SD 2) in the post-transplant recurrent cohort, respectively, for statistical significance at a 1-sided 10% significance level accounting for a drop-out rate of 20% in the native kidney cohort and 17% in the post-transplant recurrent cohort.[37] 

The log ratio of Week 12 to baseline in UPCR (primary endpoint in native kidney cohort) was analysed using an MMRM model. Change in C3 deposit score from baseline to Week 12 (primary endpoint in post-transplant recurrent cohort) was analysed using the Wilcoxon signed rank test to compare the median difference (80% CI).[37]

## **2.5.1.4 Clinical effectiveness results** 

## _**Native kidney cohort, primary endpoint: UPCR reduction at Week 12**_ 

In the native kidney cohort, treatment with iptacopan resulted in a 45% reduction in 24h UPCR from baseline (geometric mean: 401.9 g/mol) to Day 84 (geometric mean: 220.1 g/mol), with an adjusted geometric mean ratio of 0.55 (80% CI: 0.46, 0.65; 2-sided p=0.0003; see Figure 18).[37]

## **2.5.2.2 Clinical effectiveness results for open-label extension study** 

The presentation of clinical effectiveness results from the open-label extension study in this section focuses on long-term data for UPCR and eGFR as the most clinically relevant outcomes. Further results are presented in Appendix J.3.5.[27] 

## _**CfB in FMV UPCR – extension study data for patients originating from the Phase 2 study**_ 

In patients originating from the Phase 2 study native kidney cohort with a geometric mean FMV UPCR of 2.66 g/g at baseline, a reduction in FMV UPCR with iptacopan treatment was observed early and sustained up to Day 1,164 (Figure 21). FMV UPCR reduction at Day 1,164 amounted to 40%.[38]

## _**Change in eGFR slope analysis – extension study data for patients originating from the Phase 2 study**_ 

In the native kidney cohort, historical eGFR data were available for 13 of 16 patients, with a median of 4 historical eGFR values (range 1–10). All 16 patients had on-iptacopan eGFR data. The pre-iptacopan annualised eGFR slope was −13.43 mL/min/1.73m[2] /year (95% CI: −20.36, −6.51). The annualised eGFR slope upon initiation of iptacopan was estimated as −2.08 mL/min/1.73m[2] /year (95% CI: −11.34, 7.18), representing a change in the eGFR trajectory of 11.35 mL/min/1.73m[2] /year in annualised eGFR compared to the pre-iptacopan period (95% CI: 3.30, 19.41; p=0.0089; Figure 23).[38]

## _**Change in eGFR slope analysis – extension study data for patients originating from APPEAR-C3G**_ 

Methods for the eGFR slope analysis in the APPEAR-C3G population are described in Section 2.4.3.2 (‘Exploratory endpoint: eGFR slope change analyses’). The eGFR slope analysis in patients originating from APPEAR-C3G including data from the extension study was informed by 74 patients contributing data for the calculation of the pre-iptacopan slope as well as the oniptacopan slope. The pre-iptacopan slope was estimated based on 494 eGFR measurements, while 564 eGFR measurements were available for estimation of the on-iptacopan slope. Among the 74 patients included in the analysis, 73 (98.6%) had completed 12 months of iptacopan treatment and 36 (48.6%) had completed 18 months of iptacopan treatment at the time of analysis.[124]

The mean pre-iptacopan eGFR slope was −7.22 mL/min/1.73 m[2] /year (95% CI: −10.10, −4.35). This equated to a change in annual eGFR slope of 6.94 mL/min/1.73m[2 ] (95% CI: 3.48, 10.39; p=0.0001) compared with preiptacopan treatment (Figure 25).[124]

## **2.6 Subsequent treatments used in the relevant studies** 

Information on subsequent treatments for patients discontinuing iptacopan was not systematically collected in the clinical trials. In the economic model, patients who discontinued iptacopan were assumed to receive SoC alone (see Section 3.3.3). 

## **2.7 Subgroup analysis** 

This submission covers the full population of the planned marketing authorisation in C3G. 

The pre-specified subgroup analyses conducted for the primary endpoint of APPEAR-C3G are presented in Section 2.4.3. This includes a subgroup analysis for people with C3GN and DDD; however, interpretability of results is limited by the small sample size and imbalance between groups (DDD patients in iptacopan arm n=9, placebo arm n=1).[33] 

Company evidence submission for iptacopan for treating C3 glomerulopathy [ID6283] © Novartis (2025). All rights reserved 




<!-- page 80 -->

Whilst a distinction between C3GN and DDD is made based on kidney tissue biopsy findings,[133] the clinical presentation, disease course, and management of these C3G subtypes are generally considered to be consistent.[5, 18, 19, 43] Consequently, the clinical and cost-effectiveness of iptacopan are not expected to differ between people with C3GN and DDD.[40] Similarly, CFHR5 nephropathy is a subtype of C3GN, caused by a genetic mutation endemic to people of Cypriot origin,[44, 45] and clinical and cost-effectiveness of iptacopan are not expected to differ from other people with C3G. 

Evidence for the clinical efficacy of iptacopan in patients with post-transplant recurrence of C3G is presented in Section 2.5.1 (12-week data from Phase 2 study)[34] and Section 2.5.2 (longerterm data from extension study).[38] 

Economic modelling is based on iptacopan trial data from patients with native kidney C3G, based on APPEAR-C3G.[33] For patients with post-transplant recurrence, the sample size of the Phase 2 clinical trial cohort (N=11) did not permit a robust economic analysis.[34] However, given that the underlying disease mechanism is the same in native kidney and post-transplant recurrent C3G, UK clinicians advised that iptacopan data in native kidney patients are considered transferable to transplanted patients.[27, 40] Furthermore, the approach to model only a native kidney population aligns with that taken in previous NICE appraisals in other chronic kidney diseases, with the NICE recommendations for these treatments not excluding transplanted patients even where transplanted patients were excluded from the clinical trials. Further details are provided in Table 12 of Appendix E. 

## **2.8 Meta-analysis** 

In order to leverage all available data, including for a scenario analysis used in the economic model (Section 3.3.2), an exploratory analysis pooling data across trials was conducted for the eGFR slope outcome. Results of this analysis are presented below in Section 2.8.1. 

In addition, iptacopan safety data were summarised across trials (broad safety set) and are presented in Section 2.10. 

## _**2.8.1 Pooled eGFR slope analysis**_ 

An exploratory analysis pooled eGFR data across APPEAR-C3G, the Phase 2 trial (native kidney cohort) and the open-label extension study. This analysis maximises data availability for the estimation of eGFR slope in terms of sample size and length of follow-up. Overall, 90 patients with native kidney C3G contributed data to the pre-iptacopan slope as well as the on-iptacopan slope, with a total of 596 eGFR measurements informing the pre-iptacopan and 828 informing the on-iptacopan slope, respectively. Among the 90 patients, 72 (80.0%) were on iptacopan for at least 12 months at the time of analysis, and 38 patients (42.2%) were on iptacopan for at least 18 months.[124] 

Across the pooled data, the mean pre-iptacopan eGFR slope was −8.32 mL/min/1.73 m[2] /year (95% CI: −10.89, −5.74). Treatment with iptacopan led to stabilisation of eGFR decline, with the on-iptacopan slope estimated as −0.70 mL/min/1.73 m[2] /year (95% CI: −3.77, 2.36); consequently, the change in annualised eGFR slope following initiation of iptacopan treatment versus pre-iptacopan treatment was 7.62 mL/min/1.73 m[2 ] (95% CI: 4.62, 10.62; p<0.0001; Figure 26).[124 ]
