## **2.9 Indirect and mixed treatment comparisons** 

The APPEAR-C3G trial and the historical eGFR analyses presented in previous sections are considered to provide a robust source of SoC data in C3G. Background medications received by the patient population in APPEAR-C3G were considered reflective of UK clinical practice by clinicians.[27] Therefore, data from APPEAR-C3G (including historical data) were deemed suitable to inform the comparison of iptacopan with established clinical management (SoC comparator) in the economic model. 

Comparative data versus eculizumab were not available from the iptacopan clinical trial programme in C3G. Whilst eculizumab is considered of limited relevance as a comparator for this submission (for reasons described in Table 1), the feasibility of an indirect treatment comparison (ITC) was assessed for completeness. The clinical trials SLR (Appendix B) identified three trials which assessed eculizumab for C3G. However, none of the three studies reported eGFR results, the outcome of interest for the economic model (see Section 3.3.2.1). In addition, sample sizes were small, ranging from 4–6 patients across each of the three trials. None of the studies were conducted in the UK, and thus did not reflect the patient population who is eligible to receive eculizumab under the NHS England commissioning policy criteria.[28] Overall, an ITC was not considered feasible. Further details of the ITC feasibility assessment are described in Appendix B.1.7.

## **2.10 Adverse reactions** 

The safety data presented in this section cover the placebo-controlled period of the APPEARC3G trial, as well as all available safety data pooled across APPEAR-C3G, the Phase 2 study, and the ongoing open-label extension study for iptacopan in C3G. Two safety sets are presented below: 

- The **controlled safety set (N=74)** includes data from the 6-month double-blind placebocontrolled period of APPEAR-C3G from all adult patients who received at least one dose of iptacopan 200 mg b.i.d. (N=38) or placebo (N=36)[125] 

- The **broad safety set (N=101)** includes data from all adult patients who received at least one dose of iptacopan 200 mg b.i.d. in the treatment period of any of the three iptacopan studies in C3G (Phase 2, APPEAR-C3G, and the ongoing open-label extension study), up to the data cut-off date of 6[th] May 2024[125] 

## _**2.10.1 Summary of adverse events**_ 

In the controlled safety set, AEs were overall balanced between the iptacopan and placebo arms. The number of patients with treatment-emergent adverse events (TEAEs) reported during the 6- month double-blind period was comparable between the iptacopan (30/38, 78.9%) and placebo (24/36, 66.7%) arms. Iptacopan was well tolerated with the majority of AEs being mild to moderate in severity. A low number of serious adverse events (SAEs) was reported and there were no deaths. Iptacopan was well tolerated with the majority of AEs being mild to moderate in severity. No patients discontinued treatment due to AEs.[125] 

In the broad safety set, with 189.8 patient-years (PYs) of iptacopan 200 mg b.i.d. exposure overall, the proportion of patients who had at least one TEAE was 85.1% (86/101). There was no evidence of increased risk of TEAEs with longer exposure. The exposure-adjusted occurrence rate (defined as the number of AE episodes/100 PYs of exposure) was 266.5 episodes/100 PYs in the broad safety set, which was lower than that in the iptacopan group of the controlled safety set (431.8 episodes/100 PYs). One death was reported (not suspected to be related to iptacopan), and three patients discontinued iptacopan due to AEs.[125]

Most treatment-related SAEs were infections, all of which were resolved or resolving at the time of data read-out.[125]

## _**2.10.4 Deaths**_ 

One death occurred across the three C3G studies, during the open-label extension study. The cause of death was presumed to be cardiac arrhythmia that the investigator did not consider to be related to iptacopan.[125] 

## _**2.10.5 Treatment discontinuations due to adverse events**_ 

No treatment discontinuations due to TEAEs were reported in the controlled safety set. In the broad safety set, three patients discontinued iptacopan treatment due to TEAEs during the ongoing open-label extension study. All three cases were due to SAEs not related to iptacopan treatment, as determined by the investigator.[125]

In the controlled safety set, TEAEs leading to study treatment interruption were reported in 10.5% and 11.1% of patients in the iptacopan and placebo groups, respectively. The most frequently reported TEAE leading to interruption of iptacopan treatment was COVID-19 (reported in four patients, 10.5%).[125] 

In the broad safety set, TEAEs leading to study treatment interruption were reported in 10.9% of patients. In addition, one patient had a temporary dose reduction due to non-serious tonsillar hypertrophy.[125] 

## _**2.10.6 Adverse events of special interest**_ 

The AEs of special interest for iptacopan were determined based on its mechanism of action, pre-clinical safety studies and clinical studies, and include infections caused by encapsulated bacteria, testicular effects, thyroid changes, malignancy, hypersensitivity, and decreased platelets.[125] 

In the controlled safety set, three patients in the iptacopan group and one patient in the placebo group were reported to have infections caused by encapsulated bacteria. Additionally, one patient in the placebo group experienced a non-serious TEAE of blood thyroid stimulating hormone increased.[125] 

In the broad safety set, 10 patients (including the three described above in the controlled safety set) were reported to have infections caused by encapsulated bacteria. Most patients had infections that were non-serious and not considered to be related to iptacopan treatment. All infections resolved and patients either continued iptacopan treatment or resumed after resolution of the infection. Additionally, eight patients reported AEs recorded as hypersensitivity, but these were not considered related to iptacopan treatment.[125] 

No AEs of special interest related to testicular effect, malignancy or decreased platelet count were reported in either safety population. A summary of AEs of special interest is presented in Table 30.[125]

## **2.11  Ongoing studies** 

As detailed in Section 2.5.2, the long-term clinical efficacy and safety of iptacopan in C3G are being examined in the open-label extension study (NCT03955445), which is ongoing and expected to complete in 2033.[35] The APPEAR-C3G study (NCT04817618) is ongoing for the adolescent C3G cohort (aged 12 to below 18 years of age), with an expected completion date in 2026,[32] and anticipated to subsequently inform a regulatory submission for an extension of the licensed indication. 

## **2.12  Interpretation of clinical effectiveness and safety evidence** 

## _**Trial design and generalisability to UK clinical practice**_ 

APPEAR-C3G is the first placebo-controlled clinical trial in C3G. The double-blind, placebocontrolled methodology during the randomised treatment period represents a major strength of the study, in a disease area where prospective and controlled evidence for current SoC is lacking.[25-27, 33, 104] Iptacopan was directly compared with placebo whilst also allowing use of concomitant medications such as ACEis/ARBs, MMF, CS or SGLT2i (at a stable dose), reflecting the current UK SoC for C3G.[27, 33] APPEAR-C3G therefore provides methodologically robust, relevant and meaningful comparative data for the clinical effectiveness and safety of iptacopan for the treatment of adults with C3G.[27, 33] 

The sample size of APPEAR-C3G (N=74) was reflective of the ultra-rare nature of C3G, which may have contributed to some imbalances in baseline characteristics between the randomised treatment groups.[33] Patients in the iptacopan arm had notably higher proteinuria at baseline and exhibited a steeper pre-trial eGFR decline than the placebo arm, suggesting a more severe disease phenotype.[27, 33] Comparisons between groups may therefore underestimate the efficacy of iptacopan.[27] 

The placebo-controlled period of APPEAR-C3G was limited to 6 months for ethical reasons, with patients randomised to placebo subsequently switching to open-label iptacopan for the remainder of the 12-month study.[33] Proteinuria, a well-recognised risk factor for progression to kidney failure,[3, 17, 25, 64, 67, 69-72] decreased rapidly with iptacopan treatment, with a statistically significant reduction in UPCR demonstrated in comparison with placebo at 6 months.[33] Iptacopan arm data at 6 months further suggested a stabilisation in eGFR (CfB of +1.30 mL/min/1.73m[2] ; 95% CI: −2.14, 4.73), whereas placebo arm data was suggestive of further decline (CfB −0.86; 95% CI: −4.36, 2.64);[33] clinicians suggested that the 6-month duration of the double-blind treatment period may have been too short to show a statistically significant effect in the comparison between groups.[27] Longer-term data from the extension study – whilst lacking a placebo control arm – suggest stabilisation of kidney function with continued iptacopan treatment;[124] in comparison, with current SoC approximately 50% of patients progress to kidney failure within 10 years of diagnosis.[3, 16, 18, 19] 

UK nephrologists and complement specialists consulted in a Novartis UK advisory board in November 2024 (N=10) considered data from APPEAR-C3G generalisable to UK clinical practice.[27] The clinicians confirmed that clinical characteristics at baseline and historical eGFR decline were reflective of the UK C3G population and patients who advisors considered would be expected to benefit from iptacopan treatment in clinical practice.[27] Most advisors agreed that it was reasonable to focus on patients with elevated proteinuria (UPCR ≥1 g/g or ≥113 mg/mmol) despite use of a maximally tolerated dose of an ACEi or ARB, consistent with the APPEAR-C3G inclusion criteria.[27] The proportion of patients in APPEAR-C3G on background medication of Company evidence submission for iptacopan for treating C3 glomerulopathy [ID6283] © Novartis (2025). All rights reserved Page 87 of 151 




<!-- page 90 -->

MMF and/or CS (44.6%) was considered in line with current UK experience, reflecting the absence of targeted treatment options; however, clinicians emphasised the importance of being able to use iptacopan ahead of MMF/CS in clinical practice, given the limited evidence for efficacy of these treatments in C3G.[25-27] 

Advisors further highlighted that generalisability of the trial data to UK clinical practice was also supported by the UK being well-represented within the iptacopan C3G studies. In APPEAR-C3G, 12.2% of patients (9/74) were from the UK and the majority of patients were from study sites in Europe. Similarly, 29.6% of patients (8/27) enrolled in the Phase 2 study were from the UK.[27] 

Given the high rate of post-transplant recurrence of C3G, exclusion of transplanted patients from the APPEAR-C3G study is a limitation of the evidence base. However, data on the efficacy and safety of iptacopan in patients with post-transplant recurrent C3G are available from the iptacopan Phase 2 study.[37] In addition, given that the underlying disease mechanism is the same in native kidney and post-transplant recurrent C3G, UK clinicians advised that iptacopan data in native kidney patients are considered transferable to transplanted patients.[27, 40] Due to the small sample size in the Phase 2 post-transplant cohort, the lack of a comparator arm in the single-arm trial, and no suitable evidence identified for an ITC, a robust economic analysis in post-transplant patients was not considered feasible. However, the approach to model only a native kidney population aligns with that taken in previous NICE appraisals in various other chronic kidney diseases, without this leading to exclusion of transplanted patients from the NICE recommendation (see Appendix E, Table 12). 

## _**Clinical effectiveness of iptacopan**_ 

APPEAR-C3G met its primary efficacy endpoint, with a statistically significant and clinically meaningful reduction in 24h UPCR by 35.1% (95% CI: 13.8%, 51.1%; p=0.0014) compared with placebo on top of optimised background therapy at the end of the 6-month double-blind period.[33] The benefit of iptacopan on proteinuria was further substantiated by a decrease in the proportion of patients with nephrotic-range proteinuria (UPCR ≥3 g/g), as well as an increase in the proportion of patients achieving UPCR <1 g/g.[33] Improvements in UPCR were sustained over the open-label period of APPEAR-C3G and in the extension study with data up to 2 years.[33, 124] UK experts at the advisory board considered the UPCR reduction with iptacopan as clinically meaningful and strong evidence of its efficacy in C3G; achieving a UPCR <1 g/g, as observed for some patients in the iptacopan arm of the trial (baseline: 0%; Month 6: 10.5%; Month 12: 23.7%),[33] was seen as particularly encouraging, although advisors highlighted that any proteinuria reduction is beneficial.[27] 

Proteinuria results were supported by the effect of iptacopan on eGFR, as key measure of kidney function. The CfB to 6 months in eGFR (secondary endpoint), as measured by the adjusted mean difference of iptacopan versus placebo, was 2.16 mL/min/1.73m[2] (95% CI: −2.75, 7.06; multiplicity-adjusted 1-sided p-value: 0.3241).[33] While statistical significance was not met, clinical experts suggested that this was as expected after only 6 months of follow up.[27] Given the ultrarare nature of C3G, the trial population was small and therefore less powered to detect smaller changes in eGFR that would be expected after a short follow-up period.[27] eGFR slope analyses based on longer follow-up were considered more robust and meaningful by advisors.[27] Collection of historical data from APPEAR-C3G participants enabled a comprehensive comparison with patients’ longer-term pre-trial eGFR trajectory, providing further context to the change in eGFR decline following initiation of iptacopan treatment. Prior to initiation of iptacopan treatment, patients included in APPEAR-C3G had a rapid decline in eGFR of −7.22 mL/min/1.73 m[2] /year (95% CI: −10.10, −4.35; estimated based on up to 2.5 years of pre-iptacopan data).[124] With a Company evidence submission for iptacopan for treating C3 glomerulopathy [ID6283] 

© Novartis (2025). All rights reserved 




<!-- page 91 -->

mean baseline eGFR of 94.1 mL/min/1.73 m[2] and no change in treatment, this would be expected to result in kidney failure within approximately 11 years, consistent with observed C3G real-world data including from the UK (RaDaR).[3, 16-19, 27] Treatment with iptacopan led to stabilisation of the eGFR decline, with the on-iptacopan slope estimated as −0.29 mL/min/1.73m[2] /year (95% CI: −3.88, 3.31; analysis including extension study data with up to 2 years iptacopan treatment duration). This equated to a change in annual eGFR slope of 6.94 mL/min/1.73m[2 ] (95% CI: 3.48, 10.39; p=0.0001) compared with pre-iptacopan treatment, suggesting that iptacopan is able to slow the progression of C3G in a meaningful way.[27, 124] An additional analysis pooling data from APPEAR-C3G and the native kidney cohort of the Phase 2 study, with up to 4.7 years of iptacopan treatment duration, further confirmed this conclusion (see Section 2.8.1). 

UK clinicians agreed that both UPCR and eGFR were clinically relevant outcome measures.[27] Increasing evidence supports the link between reduction in proteinuria and both preservation of eGFR and reduced risk of kidney failure.[72, 134] This includes evidence from UK patients with C3G in RaDaR, where reductions in UPCR and a decrease in eGFR decline were both associated with a lower risk of kidney failure,[3] suggesting that the efficacy of iptacopan demonstrated in APPEAR-C3G can lead to improved clinical outcomes for people with C3G. By reducing the risk of kidney failure, iptacopan is expected to reduce the need for dialysis and transplant, which is anticipated to translate into positive impacts on the quality of life of people living with C3G,[7, 93] as well as alleviate NHS capacity constraints for dialysis and transplants.[106] 

In addition to being the first treatment with placebo-controlled trial evidence in C3G, iptacopan is further differentiated from currently used treatments by its targeted mode of action as a proximal complement inhibitor.[27] While current SoC does not address the underlying pathophysiology of C3G and predominantly constitutes supportive care, iptacopan demonstrated rapid and sustained effects on multiple biomarkers for complement alternative pathway dysregulation.[33] In conjunction with benefits seen in clinical outcomes, this further supports iptacopan as a diseasemodifying treatment of C3G.[27, 33] 

## _**Safety of iptacopan**_ 

The safety of oral iptacopan 200 mg b.i.d. in patients with C3G has been well characterised in the iptacopan C3G clinical trial programme, with overall 189.8 patient-years of exposure.[125] Iptacopan was well tolerated with the majority of AEs being mild or moderate in severity, and no evidence of increased risk of TEAEs with longer exposure. Observed SAEs suspected to be related to iptacopan were consistent with the known risks of complement inhibitors, which may predispose patients to serious infections with encapsulated bacteria.[125] Vaccination prior to treatment start is required as part of the iptacopan label, to reduce the risk of serious infections,[30, 49] and experience and guidance in managing the risks of complement inhibitors are available from the use of iptacopan and other complement inhibitors in PNH as well as the use of C5 inhibitors in atypical haemolytic uraemic syndrome (aHUS).[133]

## **3 Cost effectiveness** 

## **Modelling approach and structure** 

- A _de novo_ economic analysis was developed for this submission to evaluate the costeffectiveness of iptacopan in addition to SoC versus SoC alone for adults with C3G 

- The model is a Markov cohort model with health states for CKD stages 1, 2, 3a, 3b, 4, 5 (pre-KRT), dialysis, post-transplant, and death, with a cycle length of 3 months and a lifetime horizon 

- Progression through CKD stages over time is modelled based on eGFR slope data 

- The analysis was conducted in accordance with the NICE reference case[39] 

## **Model inputs** 

- Patient baseline characteristics in the model were based on data from APPEAR-C3G[33] 

• Transition probabilities for progression through CKD stages were estimated for SoC and iptacopan from eGFR slope analyses using pre-iptacopan and on-iptacopan data, respectively, from patients enrolled in APPEAR-C3G including longer-term follow-up data from the extension study[124] 

- Model inputs relating to KRT (dialysis, transplant, graft failure) were primarily informed by RaDaR data from UK patients with C3G[17] 

• Utility values for CKD stages 1–4 were mapped from EQ-5D-5L collected in APPEARC3G,[33] derived with a mixed effects linear regression model. Utility values for CKD stage 5 (pre-KRT) and KRT were informed by literature,[135, 136] as used in previous NICE appraisals • Costs included treatment acquisition, disease monitoring, and transplant/dialysis costs, as well as AE management and vaccination/antibiotic costs for patients treated with iptacopan • Iptacopan treatment discontinuation and AE rates were sourced from the broad safety set of the pooled iptacopan trials in C3G, leveraging all available data[125] **Cost-effectiveness results** • At the PAS price, the results of the deterministic base-case economic analysis show iptacopan + SoC is associated with 1.74 incremental quality-adjusted life years (QALYs) at an incremental cost of ********** versus SoC alone. The resulting incremental costeffectiveness ratio (ICER) versus SoC is ********** per QALY gained • Results from the probabilistic sensitivity analysis (PSA) were consistent with the deterministic base-case results. ## **3.1 Published cost-effectiveness studies** 

To identify published cost-effectiveness studies for interventions in C3G, an SLR was conducted in September 2020, and subsequently updated in October 2024. Despite keeping the scope of the SLR broad and searching a wide range of sources, no studies meeting the inclusion criteria were identified. Full details of the methodology of the economic evaluations SLR, including the search strategy and the study selection process, are presented in Appendix E. 

Given the lack of published cost-effectiveness studies in C3G, an additional targeted literature review (TLR) was undertaken of NICE technology appraisals in chronic kidney diseases with final guidance published in the last 10 years, in order to support economic model development and inform potential sources for input values. The TLR methodology is described in Appendix E. The TLR identified 13 NICE appraisals meeting the inclusion criteria, with key features of the economic analyses summarised in Table 31. The majority of appraisals identified deployed a Markov model, while two appraisals used patient-level simulations (TA599 and TA358)[137, 138] and one used a microsimulation (TA942).[139] Cycle length ranged from four weeks to one year.[137-140] Health states varied, with some appraisals defining health states primarily in terms of CKD stage[137-139, 141-145] while others focused on other features of the respective disease.[140, 145-149] Appraisals which modelled CKD progression commonly utilised eGFR data from the clinical trial,[138, 139, 141, 143, 144, 146] while some appraisals relied on literature or clinical expert opinion.[137, 142, ] 145

## **3.2 Economic analysis** 

Given the absence of published economic evaluations and previous NICE appraisals in C3G, a _de novo_ economic analysis relevant to the decision problem for this evaluation was developed to evaluate the cost-effectiveness of iptacopan in addition to SoC versus SoC alone. The economic model was developed with input from UK clinical and health economic experts,[27, 40] and built in Microsoft Excel[®] . 

## _**3.2.1 Patient population**_ 

The population addressed in this submission and in the economic analysis is adults with C3G, consistent with the population detailed in the NICE final scope. In line with the design of the clinical trials, the model considers patients with continued risk of disease progression on a maximally tolerated licensed dose of an ACEi or ARB. The baseline characteristics for individuals entering the model are summarised in Section 3.3.1. 

Economic modelling is based on iptacopan trial data from patients with native kidney C3G as included in the APPEAR-C3G study. For patients with post-transplant recurrence, the sample size of the respective cohort of the Phase 2 trial (N=11) did not permit a robust economic analysis. However, given that the underlying disease mechanism is the same in native kidney and post-transplant recurrent C3G, UK clinicians advised that iptacopan data in native kidney patients are considered transferable to transplanted patients.[27, 40] Furthermore, the approach to model only a native kidney population aligns with that taken in previous NICE appraisals in other chronic kidney diseases, with the NICE recommendations for these treatments not excluding transplanted patients even where transplanted patients were excluded from the clinical trials. Further details are provided in Appendix E, Table 12. 

## _**3.2.2 Model structure**_ 

A _de novo_ health-state transition model was developed, using a Markov approach, modelling the progression of CKD to kidney failure and KRT. 

The model has a lifetime time horizon (up to age 100 years), in line with the NICE reference case.[39] A cycle length of 3 months was considered to provide sufficient detail to capture the impact on costs and QALYs as patients progressed through the model. 

The model contains nine mutually exclusive health states – six health states representing CKD stages 1–5, two KRT health states (dialysis and post-transplant), and death as an absorbing state. The model structure is illustrated in Figure 27. At the start of the model, patients with C3G are distributed across CKD stages 1–4, and over the time horizon sequentially progress through subsequent (worse) CKD stages based on their decline in eGFR. To limit technical complexity, the model does not allow for backwards transitions to less severe CKD stages, however, the impact of this simplification is considered limited since sustained improvements to less severe CKD stages are not expected to occur in clinical practice with current SoC. 

Once a patient’s eGFR reaches the KRT threshold (defined as eGFR ≤7.6 mL/min/1.73 m[2] in the base case; see Section 3.3.2.2), they either receive a pre-emptive transplant and are assigned to the ‘Post-transplant’ health state or initiate chronic dialysis and are assigned to the ‘Dialysis’ health state. Patients on dialysis have a per-cycle probability of receiving a transplant in each cycle, while transplanted patients have a per-cycle probability of experiencing graft failure in each cycle, requiring a return to dialysis. The model allows for multiple transplants with multiple 

Company evidence submission for iptacopan for treating C3 glomerulopathy [ID6283] © Novartis (2025). All rights reserved 




<!-- page 99 -->

instances of graft failure over the time horizon, reflecting a common cycle of transplant and dialysis as experienced by patients with C3G.[17, 27, 104] 

Patients can transition directly to the death state from any other health state.

**Abbreviations:** CKD: chronic kidney disease. KRT: kidney replacement therapy. 

The model health states are consistent with two previous recent appraisals in IgAN (TA937)[141 ] and CKD (TA775)[144] and were confirmed by UK clinicians to be relevant and key determinants of quality of life and costs in C3G.[27] Given that CKD stages are defined by eGFR, use of eGFR trial data was considered the most direct approach to modelling disease progression,[40] which is in alignment with the approach taken in several previous appraisals in other chronic kidney diseases (Table 31). While the primary endpoint of APPEAR-C3G was reduction in proteinuria (UPCR), use of this endpoint for economic modelling would have required relying on a surrogacy relationship with clinical outcomes, which is not yet robustly established in quantitative terms for complement inhibitors as a new, disease-modifying class of treatments for C3G.[40 ] Therefore, use of eGFR was preferred for economic modelling, with the approach described in further detail in Section 3.3.2.

## _**3.2.3 Intervention technology and comparators**_ 

The intervention is modelled as iptacopan + SoC, in line with the APPEAR-C3G trial[33] and the proposed positioning of iptacopan in the C3G treatment pathway (Figure 5). Iptacopan is modelled as 200 mg oral capsules which are taken twice daily. 

In line with the final scope of this appraisal, the comparator is SoC alone, which may include ACEi, ARB, CS, MMF, and SGLT2i (see Section 1.3.5), reflecting the current SoC for people with C3G in the UK as confirmed by UK clinical experts.[26, 27] The exact treatment regimens modelled as components of the SoC basket, along with the proportion of patients receiving each component, are detailed in Section 3.5.1.

## **3.3 Clinical parameters and variables** 

## _**3.3.1 Patient characteristics**_ 

In the base case, patient characteristics were taken from the APPEAR-C3G population, in line with the source of eGFR slope data used for modelling disease progression (Section 3.3.2). A scenario analysis using eGFR slope data pooled across trials included patient characteristics from the pooled trial population. The impact of utilising baseline characteristics from a UK realworld cohort with C3G was explored in an additional scenario analysis, using patient characteristics from RaDaR.[17] RaDaR cohort characteristics at time of diagnosis rather than at latest follow-up were used based on clinical experts’ advice, since characteristics at latest followup represent a prevalent population whose C3G has progressed in the absence of effective treatments; clinicians advised that these would be less reflective of future expected clinical practice where iptacopan is anticipated to be initiated earlier in the disease course.[27]

## _**3.3.2 Transition probabilities**_ 

## **3.3.2.1 Modelling disease progression using eGFR slope** 

Disease progression was modelled based on eGFR data from the iptacopan clinical trials in C3G. Whilst several previous appraisals had used trial eGFR data to generate transition probabilities from observed transitions between CKD stages (Table 31), this was not deemed feasible in this case due to the small sample size and the low number of patients in more advanced CKD stages at baseline (Table 33). Therefore, transition through CKD stages was modelled based on eGFR slope. 

eGFR slope options for the SoC arm were discussed as potential model inputs with 10 UK clinicians in an advisory board conducted by Novartis in November 2024 (Table 34).[27] Advisors were aligned that the eGFR slope generated from the 6-month placebo arm data of APPEARC3G (Option 1) was inconsistent with published literature and their clinical experience with current SoC in C3G.[27, 33] While published analyses based on real-world data, including RaDaR,[3] Company evidence submission for iptacopan for treating C3 glomerulopathy [ID6283] 

© Novartis (2025). All rights reserved 




<!-- page 103 -->

estimate a median time from diagnosis to kidney failure of approximately 10 years, extrapolation of the placebo arm data of APPEAR-C3G would overestimate kidney survival by a factor of about 2.3−2.6 (time to kidney failure [eGFR <15 mL/min/1.73m[2] ] with annual eGFR decline of −3.079: 25.7 years, if calculated from baseline eGFR of 94.1 mL/min/1.73m[2] without consideration of mortality; model-predicted: 22.8 years).[33] This was not considered plausible by advisors, and they explained that 6 months of data from 36 patients were likely insufficient to robustly estimate eGFR slope.[27] On the other hand, time to kidney failure predictions for the SoC arm of approximately 10−11 years, generated from eGFR slopes based on 2.5 years of pre-iptacopan data from patients enrolling in iptacopan clinical trials in C3G (Table 34, Options 2 and 3), were considered to be in line with registry data and clinical experience.[27, 40, 124] 

Since predictions based on placebo arm data lacked clinical validity,[27, 40] pre-iptacopan data were therefore used to model disease progression in the SoC arm and compared with oniptacopan data. Based on advice from clinical and health economics experts, eGFR slopes from the APPEAR-C3G population were selected as base case (N=74; Table 34, Option 2).[33, 40] eGFR slopes from a pooled analysis of the APPEAR-C3G and Phase 2 (native kidney cohort) populations (N=90; Option 3) were explored in a scenario analysis.[124] An additional scenario analysis was conducted using data from the 6-month double-blind period of APPEAR-C3G only (Option 1);[33] however, results should be interpreted with caution due to the lack of clinical validity of the predictions for SoC.[27, 40]

The average change in eGFR in a 1-year period was represented by eGFR slope (rate of eGFR decline), for both SoC (based on the pre-iptacopan period) and iptacopan. The eGFR slopes for SoC and iptacopan, respectively, were used to model progression from one CKD stage to the next, generating transition probabilities. The time to move between states was defined as the time taken for eGFR to decline from the midpoint of the current CKD stage to the midpoint of the following stage. This approach assumes a uniform distribution of patients across a CKD stage and was used in the base case following validation with clinical and health economics experts.[40] The clinical expert noted, however, that the use of the midpoint would not be appropriate for transitions to KRT, as this would model that patients commence KRT only at an eGFR of 3.8 mL/min/1.73m[2] (midpoint between KRT threshold [7.6 mL/min/1.73m[2] ] and 0).[40] Therefore, to better reflect UK clinical practice, transitions to KRT were modelled to take place at the KRT threshold instead (7.6 mL/min/1.73m[2] ). A scenario analysis was conducted to test the impact of using the upper eGFR bound to calculate transition probabilities for all transitions (between CKD stages and to KRT). 

The probability of progression in each 3-month cycle was calculated as per the following formula:

mL/min/1.73m[2] and thus has no upper bound, the mean eGFR value of patients in CKD stage 1 at baseline in APPEAR-C3G was used as the midpoint instead (116.9 mL/min/1.73m[2] ). 

While the rate of eGFR decline may vary over the course of disease, the sample size of the iptacopan trials in C3G did not permit estimation of CKD stage-dependent eGFR decline rates. As such, a simplifying assumption that speed of progression is independent of CKD stage and constant over the course of disease was applied.

## **3.3.2.2 Modelling of kidney replacement therapy (KRT)** 

Once individuals reach kidney failure, they require KRT in the form of dialysis or a kidney transplant. In the economic model, patients were assumed to start KRT at an eGFR value of 7.6 mL/min/1.73 m[2] . The NICE guideline for renal replacement therapy (NG107) recommends starting dialysis at an eGFR of around 5 to 7 mL/min/1.73 m[2] if the person has no symptoms, or earlier if symptoms require it.[12] The UK Renal Registry, which collects and reports data annually on approximately 70,000 people receiving KRT in the UK, reports that dialysis was on average started at an eGFR value of approximately 7 mL/min/1.73 m[2] , while pre-emptive (without first receiving dialysis) transplants took place at an eGFR of approximately 10 mL/min/1.73 m[2] .[153] This was in line with estimates from clinicians in the C3G advisory board.[27] For the economic model base case, the threshold to start KRT was set at 7.6 mL/min/1.73 m[2] , derived as a weighted average of the above values, accounting for 18.4% of UK patients with C3G receiving a pre-emptive transplant as their first KRT modality, based on RaDaR data.[17] This was confirmed to be a reasonable assumption by a UK clinical expert.[40] A scenario analysis set the KRT threshold value to 10 mL/min/1.73 m[2] , representing the average eGFR value at receipt of a preemptive transplant.[153] 

In the base case, upon reaching an eGFR value of 7.6 mL/min/1.73 m[2] , 18.4% of patients are modelled to receive a pre-emptive transplant (based on RaDaR data), while the remaining 81.6% of patients start dialysis.[17] Given the young average age at kidney failure, UK clinicians advised that all patients with C3G would be expected to commence KRT, with no patients receiving conservative management instead.[27] 

Adelphi DSP survey data from the EU4 and the UK indicated that among 107 people with C3G in need of a transplant, 18 (16.8%) were considered ineligible to receive a transplant.[154] This was accounted for in the analysis, by patients ineligible for a transplant remaining in the dialysis health state until death. In addition, it was assumed that patients aged ≥80 years would not receive a transplant in the base case (in line with NICE TA942 in CKD);[139] the impact of setting no upper age limit was explored in a scenario analysis. For patients on dialysis who are eligible for a transplant, an 8.7% probability of receiving a transplant in each 3-month cycle was incorporated in the model, derived from a RaDaR analysis in patients with C3G estimating a median time from start of dialysis to receipt of transplant (excluding pre-emptive transplants) of 1.9 years.[17] 

People that received a transplant are modelled to be at risk of graft failure. Using RaDaR data from patients with C3G indicating a median time to graft failure post-transplant of 6.5 years, a per cycle probability of graft failure of 2.6% was included in the model.[17] Upon graft failure, patients return to the dialysis health state but are tracked separately from non-transplanted dialysis patients in the model, in order to allow for continued consideration of post-transplant immunosuppression costs (Section 3.5.2). Following graft failure, it was assumed that a proportion of patients were no longer eligible for transplantation; in the base case, this was assumed to be same as the proportion that were ineligible for a first transplant (16.8%). In the base case, this results in people in the SoC arm receiving on average 1.9 transplants over their lifetime, which a UK clinical expert considered plausible.[40] However, UK clinicians also provided feedback that the proportion of patients ineligible for a first transplant may be lower and the proportion ineligible for a subsequent transplant may be higher, given that with increasing age, they may develop more comorbidities and become more sensitised.[27, 40] Therefore, a scenario analysis assumed that 6.8% were ineligible for a first and 26.8% for a subsequent transplant (reflecting base case value +/- 10%, respectively).

## _**3.3.3 Treatment discontinuation and subsequent therapy**_ 

## **3.3.3.1 Discontinuation prior to kidney failure** 

The iptacopan discontinuation rate among patients who have not reached kidney failure was based on all-cause treatment discontinuation of iptacopan in the pooled APPEAR-C3G, Phase 2 and extension studies (broad safety set).[125] Overall, there were 13 permanent discontinuations from iptacopan across the pooled cohort, in a total of 189.8 patient-years of exposure. Information on reasons for discontinuation is provided in Table 37. When deriving the discontinuation rate for use in the economic model, one discontinuation due to death was excluded from the calculation, to avoid double-counting of deaths in the model.[40] This resulted in a rate of discontinuation of 0.063 per year, with a per cycle probability of discontinuation of 1.57%. 

SoC treatments were assumed not to be discontinued prior to kidney failure.

## **3.3.3.2 Discontinuation following kidney failure** 

Based on input received from UK clinicians,[27] the base case assumed that patients would discontinue iptacopan treatment at the point of commencing KRT. The same discontinuation assumption was applied for all components of the SoC basket except for ACEi/ARB, since UK clinicians were aligned that these would usually be continued while on KRT, due to their blood pressure-lowering effects.[26, 27] A scenario analysis assumed that all treatments, except for ACEi/ARB, were discontinued once patients reached CKD stage 5 (eGFR <15 mL/min/1.73m[2] ). 

## **3.3.3.3 Subsequent therapy following iptacopan discontinuation** 

Within the model, patients that discontinue iptacopan subsequently receive SoC alone, with the eGFR slope of the SoC arm applied from the point of iptacopan discontinuation onwards. No residual treatment effect of iptacopan was modelled following discontinuation, based on clinical advice.[40] 

## _**3.3.4 Adverse events**_ 

In the double-blind, placebo-controlled period of APPEAR-C3G, no single severe TEAE occurred in more than one patient in either the iptacopan or the placebo arm.[33] 

To ensure the impact of AEs associated with iptacopan which would be likely to affect QALYs and costs was still captured in the model, serious AEs (SAEs) suspected to be related to iptacopan were included. Data from the broad safety set (pooled trial populations) were used for maximum sample size and follow-up duration (N=101; 189.8 patient-years). Due to the absence of a placebo control arm following the 6-month double-blind period of APPEAR-C3G, only SAEs suspected to be related to iptacopan were included, rather than all SAEs.[125] 

In the pooled population, there were 4 patients who experienced overall 9 SAEs suspected to be related to iptacopan (Table 38). However, in 2 patients, several SAEs occurred concurrently and were linked to each other.[40, 125] Therefore, based on clinical advice, the incidence of SAEs suspected to be related to iptacopan for use in the economic model was calculated based on overall 5 SAE episodes (Table 38).[40] In 189.8 patient years, this corresponded to a 0.66% probability of SAEs per 3-month model cycle. A scenario analysis tested the impact of assuming 9 SAEs in 189.8 patient years, corresponding to a 1.18% probability of SAEs per 3-month model cycle. 

Almost all SAEs suspected to be related to iptacopan were infections with encapsulated bacteria (an AE of special interest for iptacopan; Section 2.10.6) leading to pneumonia or consequences thereof such as sepsis,[40, 125] and considered accordingly in the economic analysis for AE disutilities (Section 3.4.4) and costs (Section 3.5.3).[40]

## _**3.3.5 Mortality**_ 

As described in Section 1.3.4, the impact of C3G on life expectancy is not well reported. Therefore, data to capture excess mortality associated with CKD in the model were sourced from a broader population. Hazard ratios (HRs) as a function of CKD stage were combined with data on mortality for the general population (as a function of age and sex) to estimate the absolute mortality risk in the model, using 2021–2023 general population life tables for England and Wales.[155] 

A study by Wong et al. 2024 reported mortality ratios, standardised to the general population of England and Wales, for patients in RaDaR with and without kidney failure, respectively (Table 39).[14] While not C3G-specific, this recent analysis was based on a total of 27,285 people from the UK with rare kidney diseases, including 1,089 people with either C3G or MPGN,[14] and recommended by clinical experts for use in the economic model.[27] 

A scenario analysis used HRs from a US longitudinal study including 1,120,295 adults who had ≥1 outpatient measure of creatinine (Go et al. 2004) for pre-transplant mortality,[84] and a study of people with Type 1 diabetes and a functioning kidney transplant in the Finnish Kidney Transplant Registry (N=2,543; Ortiz et al. 2019) for post-transplant mortality.[156]

## **3.4 Measurement and valuation of health effects** 

## _**3.4.1 Health-related quality-of-life data from clinical trials**_ 

EQ-5D-5L data were collected in APPEAR-C3G at baseline, Day 14, 30, 90, 180, 210, 270, and 360.[33] Overall, 74 patients contributed 484 EQ-5D measurements which could be used to generate utility values. Since the majority of people participating in APPEAR-C3G were in an early stage of disease, no EQ-5D data were available from the trial for CKD stage 5 (pre-KRT) and for patients receiving KRT; utility values for these health states were therefore sourced from the literature (see Section 3.4.3). The EQ-5D-5L data collected in APPEAR-C3G were mapped to EQ-5D-3L (see Section 3.4.2). Table 40 presents the mapped health state utility values. The mean utility value for CKD stage 1 was deemed implausible as it was lower than the values for CKD stages 2 and 3.

In addition to generating mean utility values based on observed data, a mixed effects linear model for repeated measures was fit to all utility values obtained at baseline and all other visits where patients completed the EQ-5D questionnaire. Consistent with the mean values by CKD stage, the model found that utility values were higher in CKD stage 2 versus stage 1, though this was not statistically significant. 

An alternative model specification pooled CKD stages 1 and 2, which resulted in a plausible pattern of utility values by CKD stage. ## _**3.4.2 Mapping**_ 

EQ-5D-5L data collected in APPEAR-C3G were mapped to EQ-5D-3L using the HernándezAlava mapping algorithm recommended by NICE.[157] 

## _**3.4.3 Health-related quality-of-life studies**_ 

To identify published health-related quality of life (HRQoL) studies in C3G, an SLR was conducted in January 2021, and subsequently updated in November 2024. Two multinational studies were identified which provided utility values for patients with C3G based on EQ-5D-5L. One of these studies was a randomised controlled clinical trial which reported utility values at baseline and at 26 weeks for the intervention and comparator arms, but did not provide values for the model health states.[158] The other study reported utility values based on EQ-5D-5L collected from patients with C3G (n=100) as part of the Adelphi DSP and mapped using a US tariff.[8] While this study provided utilities for CKD stages 1–4/5, these were not considered clinically plausible,[40] since CKD stage 1 patients had the worst HRQoL after patients with CKD stage 4/5 (utility values for CKD stage 1: 0.67; 2: 0.77; 3a: 0.80; 3b: 0.70; 4/5: 0.58).[8] Therefore, utility values from both studies were deemed unsuitable for use in the model. Full details of the methodology and results of the HRQoL SLR are presented in Appendix F. 

While utility values for CKD stages 1–4 could be informed by APPEAR-C3G trial data (Section 3.4.1), utility values from the literature were still required for CKD stage 5 (pre-KRT), dialysis, and transplant. Therefore, in addition to the SLR for C3G-specific utilities which did not identify any suitable values, NICE technology appraisals in chronic kidney diseases with final guidance published in the last 10 years were reviewed in a TLR. The sources for utility values which informed the NICE Committee’s decision making in these appraisals are summarised in Table 42, with further details provided in Appendix F. 

Out of the 13 previous NICE appraisals in chronic kidney diseases identified in the TLR, only two appraisals (TA877 finerenone for CKD in type 2 diabetes;[143] TA775 dapagliflozin for CKD)[144] utilised utility values generated from trial data for CKD stages 1–5 (pre-KRT); all other utility values used in previous appraisals were informed by literature. A publication from Jesky et al. 2016[135] was a commonly used source for utility values for CKD stages 1–5 (pre-KRT). Utility values for dialysis and transplant were most commonly informed by a publication from Lee et al. 2005[136] (7 appraisals), with a few appraisals using utilities from Liem et al. 2008[159] (2 appraisals) or Li et al. 2017[160] (2 appraisals; Table 42). Further details on these studies are provided in Section 3.4.4.

## _**3.4.4 Health-related quality-of-life data used in the cost-effectiveness analysis**_ 

## **3.4.4.1 Health state utility values** 

Utility values generated from APPEAR-C3G trial data or identified in the TLR were reviewed with UK clinical and health economic experts with regards to their suitability for use in the economic model.[40] For CKD stages 1–4, utility values based on EQ-5D-5L collected in patients with C3G in the APPEAR-C3G trial (baseline mean age 27.9 years) were preferred for the base-case 

Company evidence submission for iptacopan for treating C3 glomerulopathy [ID6283] © Novartis (2025). All rights reserved 




<!-- page 114 -->

analysis, utilising values estimated with the regression model pooling CKD stages 1 and 2.[40] Jesky et al. 2016,[135] a UK study which collected EQ-5D-3L data from 745 patients with CKD of any aetiology and a median age of 64 years, was considered appropriate to inform the utility value for CKD stage 5 (pre-KRT), for which no data were available from APPEAR-C3G.[40] A scenario analysis explored the impact of using utility values from Jesky et al. 2016 for CKD stages 1–5 (pre-KRT).[135] 

To inform dialysis and post-transplant utilities in the economic model, experts considered the values published by Lee et al. 2005,[136] which were used in 7 previous NICE appraisals, as most appropriate.[40] Lee et al. 2005, a UK study, estimated utility values for different KRT modalities from EQ-5D-3L collected in 416 patients (mean age 55.5 years in women, 58.2 years in men),[136] using a UK tariff;[165] utility values for haemodialysis (HD), peritoneal dialysis (PD), and posttransplant were reported as 0.44, 0.53, and 0.71, respectively.[136] For the dialysis utility in the economic model, a weighted average was calculated according to the proportion of patients receiving each type of dialysis, sourced from a RaDaR analysis in patients with C3G (HD: 85.3%; PD: 14.7% [APD: 11.8%, CAPD: 2.9%])[17] . 

Utility values from Liem et al. 2008[159] and Li et al. 2017[160] were also discussed with clinical and health economics experts but not considered suitable for use in the model.[40] The methodology of Liem et al. 2008[159] was considered to introduce uncertainty, since it is a meta-analysis of EQ-5Dbased utility values reported across multiple international studies which did not consistently provide information on the value sets used; experts therefore preferred using Lee et al. 2005, given that it was a UK study.[40] In addition, the small difference in the utility values of HD (0.56) and PD (0.58) reported by Liem et al. 2008[159] may underestimate the negative HRQoL impact of 3x weekly in-centre HD compared to at-home PD.[40] 

Utility values from Li et al. 2017[160] were not considered suitable for use in the economic model by the experts for several reasons.[40] The publication reported a utility value for people on the transplant waiting list (0.77), rather than people on dialysis, and the clinical expert highlighted that people on the transplant waiting list tend to be healthier than people on long-term dialysis.[40] This value was therefore not seen as representative of the HRQoL of people receiving chronic dialysis. Furthermore, the study used the preliminary value set for England to generate utility values from EQ-5D-5L,[166] which NICE advises against utilising.[167] Therefore, based on expert advice,[40] utility values from Li et al. 2017 were not used in the analysis. 

All health state utility values utilised in the base case and scenario analysis are summarised in Table 43. 

Age adjustments were applied in the model to adjust for differences between the source population’s age for literature-based utility values and the baseline age of the modelled population, as well as capture declining HRQoL as the population ages over the model time horizon. Reported utility values were divided by the corresponding general population utility from Hernández-Alava et al. 2022 (age- and sex-matched on the source publication study cohort)[157] to derive a multiplier. This multiplier was then applied in the model to the general population utility of the modelled population, with the general population utility decreasing over time as the population ages.[157] Where utility values were above the relevant general population value, the multiplier used in the model was capped at 1. The approach for age adjustments was validated with a UK health economist,[40] and age adjustments are shown in Table 43.

## **3.4.4.2 AE disutilities** 

As described in Section 3.3.4, SAEs suspected to be related to iptacopan were included in the model. Given that most of these were infections, a disutility associated with infections was included in the model. The disutility was taken from a study by Oppong et al. 2013,[168] which was identified through a published SLR on the impact of acute pneumococcal disease on health state utility values.[169] Oppong et al. 2013 collected EQ-5D-3L from patients in England with cough and lower respiratory tract infections in a longitudinal manner and generated utility values using the UK tariff.[168] The difference in utility between acute presentation (baseline) and recovery (week 4) was reported as 0.156, which was used in the model as disutility for infections.[168] The duration for the disutility was assumed as 32.1 days, in line with the mean duration of SAEs suspected to be related to iptacopan in the broad safety set trial data.[125] 

## **3.4.4.3 Cardiovascular event disutilities** 

As noted above, CV events were modelled as part of a scenario analysis, with the associated disutilities presented in Appendix K. 

## **3.5 Cost and healthcare resource use identification, measurement and valuation** 

The base-case economic analysis considers the following cost categories: 

- Drug acquisition costs 

- Healthcare resource use costs (including disease monitoring, transplant, and dialysis costs) 

- Vaccination and antibiotic costs 

- AE management costs 

- End of life costs 

Where costs were not available from established sources within the NHS, such as the National Schedule of NHS Costs 2023/2024[151] or PSSRU Unit Costs of Health and Social Care 2023,[108] costs were derived from relevant literature. All relevant costs were inflated to the 2022/2023 fiscal year using the NHSCII Pay and Price Index, pending the release of an updated PSSRU unit cost manual.[108] 

Cost and healthcare resource use (HCRU) studies in C3G were searched for in an SLR conducted in February 2021 and subsequently updated in October 2024. The cost and HCRU SLR identified 6 publications presenting data on HCRU in C3G, however no relevant evidence for use in this submission was identified within these publications. Further details are provided in Appendix G. 

Since no relevant information on HCRU in C3G was identified in the SLR, an additional TLR was undertaken of NICE technology appraisals in chronic kidney diseases with final guidance published in the last 10 years. The sources for health state costs which informed the NICE Committee’s decision making in these appraisals are summarised in Table 44, with further details provided in Appendix G. The costs in these appraisals were derived from a number of sources, including NHS reference costs, NICE guidelines and a number of publications in CKD.

As discussed in Section 1.3.5, SoC for patients with C3G can include ACEis/ARBs, MMF, CS, and SGLT2is. In the base case, the proportion of patients receiving each component of SoC was sourced from participant characteristics at baseline in APPEAR-C3G, and was assumed equal in the iptacopan and comparator arms.[33] While the proportion of patients in APPEAR-C3G on ACEi/ARB and CS and/or MMF was considered broadly reflective of UK clinical practice, clinical experts advised that the use of SGLT2i had become more common compared with the 5.4% of patients receiving SGLT2i as part of their background medication in the APPEAR-C3G study.[27] Therefore, a scenario analysis assumed the proportion of patients on SGLT2i as 50% (of note, this only impacts costs and not outcomes in the model).

## _**3.5.2 Health-state unit costs and resource use**_ 

## _**Disease monitoring costs and healthcare resource use**_ 

Since no relevant literature could be identified, the outpatient resource use by patients with C3G was informed by a survey of UK clinicians participating in a Novartis advisory board conducted in November 2024.[27] Advisors were asked to provide information on the average number of routine monitoring visits per year for adult patients with C3G by CKD stage, as well as information regarding which tests they routinely conduct during monitoring visits, based on their current clinical practice. Overall 9 of the 10 advisory board participants completed the survey, with several advisors highlighting that monitoring frequency would also depend on a patient’s level of proteinuria, rather than CKD stage alone.[27] The mean number of visits by CKD stage (Table 47) was calculated across all responses received and considered reasonable by a clinical expert.[40] 

At each monitoring visit, a range of monitoring tests was costed, based on input received in above-mentioned survey and subsequent discussion during the advisory board.[27] These are presented in Table 48 including unit costs and the per visit testing frequency. Unit costs were sourced from the NHS reference costs or PSSRU unit costs.[108, 151 ] 

A scenario analysis based disease monitoring frequency on the NICE guideline Chronic kidney disease: assessment and management (NG203), which provides recommendations on the minimum monitoring frequency for CKD (Table 47).[11]

Several previous NICE appraisals (TA937,[141] TA775)[144] utilised a publication from Kent et al. 2015 to inform healthcare resource use.[170] Kent et al. 2015 estimated annual hospital costs, including hospital admissions and outpatient/day-case attendances, as part of a randomised trial in 7,246 people (mean age 63 years) with impaired kidney function in Europe, North America, and Australasia.[170] The study was considered as a potential alternative to modelling health state costs based on advisory board survey inputs. However, while Kent et al. 2015 included both inpatient and out-patient hospital care, the estimated costs (inflated to 2022/23 prices; Table 49) were too low to cover the costs of routine monitoring visits as advised specifically for patients with C3G by UK clinicians (Table 47 and Table 48), from CKD stage 3a onwards (for example, CKD stage 3a: 3 nephrologist visits at £206.69 each = £620.07, compared with £555.48 based on Kent et al.). Therefore, a UK clinician advised that it was preferable to utilise the advisory board survey inputs for the model base case.[40] The impact of using CKD stage costs based on Kent et al. 2015 was explored in a scenario analysis; in this analysis, disease monitoring resource use was set to zero, to prevent double counting of costs.

## _**Transplant and dialysis costs**_ 

Dialysis and kidney transplant costs are presented in Table 50. The one-time cost of kidney transplant was based on 2023/2024 NHS reference costs, following a calculation approach used in previous NICE appraisals (TA775, TA942).[139, 144, 151] The proportion of patients receiving living or deceased donor transplants, respectively, was sourced from RaDaR data in patients with C3G.[17] Following transplantation, annual costs for immunosuppression medication to prevent graft rejection were applied, based on an NHS Blood and Transplant fact sheet used in multiple previous appraisals (TA775, TA890, TA942),[139, 140, 144, 171] and it was assumed that these costs would continue to be incurred following graft failure. 

The cost of dialysis was calculated using NHS reference costs, with HD assumed to be repeated three times per week and continuous ambulatory peritoneal dialysis (CAPD) and automated peritoneal dialysis (APD) assumed to be carried out daily.[77, 78, 151] The proportions of patients receiving each type of dialysis was informed by RaDaR data in patients with C3G.[17] 

Additionally, transport costs contribute to the resource use in CKD with patients receiving incentre HD required to travel three times per week to receive treatment. An estimate for associated transportation costs was sourced from Liu et al. 2015,[109] a study estimating costs of HD from a UK payer perspective, as used in previous appraisals (TA937,[141] TA809[147] ). Liu et al. derived a weighted transport cost estimate per in-centre HD session, accounting for multiple modes of transport with usage informed by a National Kidney Care Audit Patient Transport Survey.[109] After inflating the published value to 2022/23 costs,[108, 109] transport costs of £63.40 was applied for all in-centre HD sessions in the model. Based on total activity reported in the 2023/2024 NHS reference costs, it was assumed that 96.8% of all HD patients would receive incentre HD (96.8% hospital or satellite HD; 3.2% home HD).[151]

## _**3.5.3 Miscellaneous unit costs and resource use**_ 

## **Vaccination and antibiotic costs** 

The use of complement inhibitors may predispose patients to serious infections with encapsulated bacteria. Based on the SmPC, patients treated with iptacopan must therefore be vaccinated against _N. meningitidis_ and _S. pneumoniae_ , while vaccination against _H. influenzae_ type B is recommended.[30] In line with advice from UK nephrologists and existing UK guidelines for the prevention of meningococcal disease in adults receiving C5 inhibitors for aHUS, all patients treated with iptacopan within the model were assumed to receive vaccinations for _N. meningitidis_ and _S. pneumoniae_ every 5 years (modelled as 0.2 per year), and one vaccination for _H. influenzae type B_ at the start of iptacopan treatment;[27, 133] this is consistent with the assumptions in the previous NICE appraisal of iptacopan for PNH (TA1000).[52] Vaccination costs were sourced from the BNF.[51] 

Additionally, the cost of prophylactic antibiotics (penicillin, 250 mg b.i.d.) was also included for all patients treated with iptacopan, based on clinical expert advice and in line with standard UK practice for C5 inhibitors in aHUS.[27, 40, 133] Vaccination and antibiotic resource use and costs associated with iptacopan are summarised in Table 51.

As described in Section 3.3.4, SAEs suspected to be related to iptacopan were included in the model. ## _**End-of-life costs**_ 

The model included end-of-life costs, in the form of hospital costs for terminal care in the 30 days prior to death. These costs were taken from Kerr et al. 2017,[174] which reported on end-of-life care in CKD in England, and inflated to 2022/2023.[108] This approach aligned to that in TA937.[141] A one-off cost of £3,952.43 was therefore applied to patients entering the ‘Death’ state.

As noted in Section 3.3.6, CV events were modelled as part of a scenario analysis, with the costs associated presented in Appendix K.

## **3.7 Uncertainty** 

The NICE Prioritisation Board confirmed that iptacopan for C3G meets the Highly Specialised Technologies (HST) routing criteria that relate to rarity of the disease (routing criteria 1 and 2).[122] While the NICE evaluation takes place using the STA route, it is therefore vital that the challenges associated with an appraisal in a very rare condition, such as small sample sizes in clinical trials, and any resulting uncertainty are considered when evaluating the evidence. 

Iptacopan is the first treatment to be appraised in C3G. Consequently, no HTA precedents exist. C3G-specific data sources to inform the model are scarce and where available, usually limited to smaller sample sizes. This may in turn give rise to uncertainty around mean parameter values. Where appropriate data were available, the model inputs were based on C3G-specific data, from the iptacopan clinical trial programme in C3G or the C3G cohort of RaDaR. To ensure model inputs were clinically appropriate, clinical input from UK experts in C3G was sought to validate all key parameters (as detailed in Section 3.13). 

C3G is an ultra-rare disease and generating comparative efficacy data can be challenging as the number of patients included in clinical trials is typically small. While the methods applied to generate comparative efficacy data for this submission are in line with best practice, the ultrarare nature of the disease leads to uncertainty in the estimates. 

Novartis asks the NICE Committee to consider the strength of the data presented in light of the rarity of the condition. Flexibility in NICE’s STA process is therefore expected to be relevant in this appraisal.

## **3.10 Exploring uncertainty** 

As detailed in Section 3.7, model parameters were associated with uncertainty as would be expected in an ultra-rare disease. In order to assess the impact of parameter uncertainty on the economic model results, both probabilistic and deterministic sensitivity analyses were conducted, the results of which are presented in Sections 3.10.1 and 3.10.2, respectively. In addition, key assumptions in the model were explored in several scenario analyses, the results of which are presented in Section 3.10.3. 

## _**3.10.1 Probabilistic sensitivity analysis**_ 

Probabilistic sensitivity analysis (PSA) was conducted to assess the impact of uncertainty around parameter values on the results of the model base case. Where data were available, probability distributions were assigned to parameters, to characterise uncertainty associated with the precision of the mean values, based on the nature of each parameter. Where empirical probability distributions were not available, the standard error was assumed to take a value equal to 10% of that of the mean. The base-case ICER stabilised from approximately ~150 iterations onwards (see Figure 28 for the probabilistic ICER convergence plot), therefore 1000 iterations were considered sufficient without incurring a significant run-time. 

The probabilistic base-case results expressed in terms of incremental costs, incremental LYGs, incremental QALYs and ICERs are presented in Table 58 and the probabilistic INHB at WTP thresholds of £20,000 and £30,000 are presented in Table 59. The probabilistic ICER of iptacopan and SoC versus SoC is ********** per QALY gained, falling within *% of the deterministic ICER, indicating that cost-effectiveness results were consistent. 

The cost-effectiveness plane and acceptability curves are presented in Figure 29 and Figure 30, respectively.

## _**3.10.2 Deterministic sensitivity analysis**_ 

To further assess the robustness of the base-case model results, deterministic sensitivity analyses (DSA) were conducted by varying one model input at a time to assess which parameters had the largest impact on the ICER. Some parameters that do not have any uncertainty associated with the input value were excluded from the DSA. 

Details on the parameters and ranges tested in the DSA are provided in Appendix L. 

For clinical and utility parameters, 95% CI were used, which were sourced from published data, where available, and calculated where data were not available. For other parameters, the variation was assumed to be a set percentage of the mean (±20%); upper and lower values were either calculated directly by adding or subtracting the respective percentage (for the cost inputs), or by using this to further calculate appropriate variations (in the case for the lognormal variation of the mortality HRs). 

Results of the DSA show that the most influential parameter on the base-case ICER is the iptacopan treatment effect, with APPEAR-C3G utilities the next most influential parameters (Figure 31).

## **3.11 Subgroup analysis** 

As described in Section 1.1, this submission covers the full expected marketing authorisation for iptacopan in C3G. 

Economic modelling has been based on iptacopan trial data from patients with native kidney C3G, based on the Phase 3 APPEAR-C3G study. For patients with post-transplant recurrence, the sample size of the Phase 2 clinical trial cohort (N=11) did not permit a robust economic analysis. However, given that the underlying disease mechanism is the same in native kidney and post-transplant recurrent C3G, UK clinicians advised that iptacopan data in native kidney patients are considered transferable to transplanted patients.[27, 40] Furthermore, the approach to model only a native kidney population aligns with that taken in previous NICE appraisals in other chronic kidney diseases, with the NICE recommendations for these treatments not excluding transplanted patients even where transplanted patients were excluded from the clinical trials (Appendix E, Table 12). 

Whilst a distinction between C3GN and DDD is made based on kidney tissue biopsy findings,[133] the clinical presentation, disease course, and management of these C3G subtypes are generally considered to be consistent.[5, 18, 19, 43] Similarly, CFHR5 nephropathy is a subtype of C3GN, caused by a genetic mutation endemic to people of Cypriot origin.[44, 45] Consequently, the clinical and cost-effectiveness of iptacopan are not expected to differ between people with C3GN (including CFHR5 nephropathy) and people with DDD.[40] Economic analyses for subgroups are therefore not presented in this submission. 

## **3.12 Benefits not captured in the QALY calculation** 

The economic analysis has attempted to include all the potential benefits related to iptacopan within the QALY calculation. There are, however, several potential benefits of treatment with iptacopan which are not captured within the assessment. 

As discussed in Section 1.3.6, C3G has a large impact on patient and carer quality of life, with the impact of the symptoms themselves, their effects on a person’s ability to participate and complete daily activities, and the uncertainty surrounding disease progression and lack of treatment options impacting mental health.[7, 93] This was also highlighted by several UK patient organisations during the draft scope consultation of iptacopan for C3G.[104] The disease impacts may not be fully captured in standard generic HRQoL measures such as EQ-5D, and the clinical benefit of iptacopan should therefore be considered in this context. 

C3G also impacts on patients’ and carers’ time and productivity. People receiving dialysis require multiple sessions per week, with each session taking multiple hours.[77] Individuals with C3G, as well as their carers, may therefore have to reduce hours at work or in education as a result of their disease.[7, 93] A patient organisation described in their response to the draft scope consultation how affected individuals have to “fit a life around dialysis treatment”, with in-centre dialysis “tak[ing] out three days a week of normal life”, once transport time, waiting time, and the four-hour treatment duration are taken into account.[104] Young patients have reported not being able to attend education regularly, impacting their future career opportunities.[93] These impacts are likely insufficiently captured in the QALY calculation. Iptacopan, by delaying kidney failure and the need for KRT, may therefore be able to provide additional benefits not captured in the economic analysis. 

Company evidence submission for iptacopan for treating C3 glomerulopathy [ID6283] © Novartis (2025). All rights reserved 




<!-- page 142 -->

The expected reduced need for KRT with iptacopan has the potential to provide further benefits to people with kidney diseases more broadly and the NHS. As noted in Section 1.3.6, the current wait time for kidney transplants in the UK is 2–3 years.[106] By reducing the number of people requiring a transplant due to their C3G, the availability of iptacopan may be able to reduce the number of patients on waiting lists and speed up access for other patients in need of a kidney transplant. A report from Kidney Research UK in 2023 also highlighted capacity constraints for dialysis in the UK, estimating that capacity would need to grow by 400% by 2033 to meet increasing demand.[106] Iptacopan, by delaying the time to kidney failure, may be able to reduce the increase in the demand for dialysis. These effects are not captured in the QALY calculation. 

Finally, the availability of iptacopan has the potential to reduce health inequalities in the NHS. As highlighted in Section 1.4, there is considerable inequality across ethnic groups with regards to access to kidney transplants, with individuals of Black and Asian descent more likely to face much lengthier wait times.[106, 118] Equitable access for all ethnicities to iptacopan, with its potential to reduce the need for transplants, would address this inequality for people with C3G. 

## **3.13 Validation** 

## _**3.13.1 Validation of cost-effectiveness analysis**_ 

## _**Clinical and health economist validation**_ 

Novartis UK held two advisory boards with nine (April 2022) and ten (November 2024) UK clinicians with experience in treating patients with C3G in NHS clinical practice; insights from both advisory boards informed this submission.[26, 27] Advisors provided their views on the current SoC and treatment landscape for C3G, level of unmet need, and iptacopan trial data, as well as clinical input for modelling disease progression and disease management before and after kidney failure. 

Additionally, calls with two individual UK clinicians were conducted to clarify individual points of uncertainty relating to the submission, and model validation was undertaken in a joint call with one clinical and one external health economics expert from the UK.[40] Model validation covered selection of the base case for modelling disease progression and treatment effect, health state utility values, health state costs, and AEs, as well as validation of clinical outputs of the draft economic model. 

The modelling approach, inputs and assumptions presented in this submission took into account the feedback received by clinical and health economics experts, as detailed throughout Section 3. 

## _**Internal technical validation**_ 

Once the model was completed, in alignment with best practice, an independent team of health economists who were not involved in programming the model performed a full technical quality control check which was conducted by completing two checklists, based on the published TECHVER checklist:[175] 

- **Quality control checklist** , which involved checking through every cell of the model to ensure that all formulae are correct, that macros have been coded correctly, that everything is referenced correctly, that there are no spelling or grammar mistakes, and that the formatting is consistent 

Company evidence submission for iptacopan for treating C3 glomerulopathy [ID6283] © Novartis (2025). All rights reserved 




<!-- page 143 -->

- **Internal validation checklist** , which involved setting up different scenarios to check that the model responds in the appropriate manner; for example, when all utility values are set to 1, the LYs should equal the QALYs. The model is pushed to the extremes to test whether it reacts to extreme values in an expected way 

Together these checklists provided quality control and internal validation of the model through a documented review process. In addition, an independent analyst performed a full input quality check, checking all model inputs against their original source.

## _**3.14.2 Strengths and limitations**_ 

The model was developed in line with the NICE reference case.[39] The selected model structure, which includes health states for CKD stages and KRT, was aligned with several prior appraisals in other chronic kidney diseases which also used eGFR data to model disease progression (see Table 31). The modelling approach and key inputs were discussed with UK clinicians with expertise and experience in treating C3G in NHS clinical practice, and their input in two advisory boards and other validation meetings (see Section 3.13.1) guided the selection of the base case inputs and confirmed the validity of the approaches.[26, 27, 40] 

While C3G is an ultra-rare disease with associated evidence generation challenges, key model inputs were informed by evidence from the population of interest. Efficacy and safety inputs came from the clinical trial programme for iptacopan in C3G. The use of iptacopan within APPEAR-C3G matches its intended indication, and therefore the data incorporated into the model can be expected to align to clinical practice.[33] 

Clinical experts confirmed that model predictions for the SoC arm in the base case (such as time to kidney failure) aligned well to current real-world evidence from RaDaR, a UK-specific source of C3G patient data and therefore of high relevance to the modelled population.[17, 27, 40] 

Although some model inputs had to be taken from the broader CKD literature, utility values for health states prior to kidney failure could be sourced from APPEAR-C3G. Model inputs relating to KRT, including dialysis, transplant, and graft failure, were mostly informed by analyses of the C3G cohort in RaDaR, which provides UK-specific longitudinal data from the population of interest for this appraisal.[17, 59] RaDaR, the largest rare kidney disease registry in the world,[14] is considered the most clinically relevant data source outside of the clinical trial programme, and the use of UK-specific data in the model, despite the ultra-rare nature of C3G and relative lack of data worldwide, strengthen the validity of the model results. 

Company evidence submission for iptacopan for treating C3 glomerulopathy [ID6283] © Novartis (2025). All rights reserved 




<!-- page 144 -->

The economic analysis had some limitations. As discussed in Section 3.7, C3G is an ultra-rare disease and iptacopan is the first targeted treatment, and as such, data sources and precedents to inform the model are limited. Where relevant, information from previous NICE appraisals in other chronic kidney diseases was utilised to inform this submission. NICE are asked to apply flexibility in the STA process to enable timely and equitable access for people with a rare disease of this nature, when compared to products being assessed through the STA process for conditions with a much higher prevalence. 

Due to ethical reasons, the placebo-controlled period of APPEAR-C3G was limited to six months.[33] Placebo arm data from APPEAR-C3G are therefore limited to a relatively short period, and predictions of time to kidney failure based on the placebo arm data were deemed clinically implausible by UK clinicians.[27, 40] The model therefore does not use data from the placebocontrolled period of the trial in the base case. However, the comparison of on-iptacopan versus pre-iptacopan, which was modelled instead, allowed for the use of data from a greater number of patients and a longer treatment period; eGFR slopes used in the base case were generated from 74 patients with up to 2.5 years of pre-iptacopan and up to 2 years of on-iptacopan data.[124] As noted above, the pre-iptacopan data from this analysis align well with data from RaDaR, and clinical validity was further supported by UK clinical experts.[27, 40] 

Economic modelling in this submission is based on data from patients with native kidney disease, in line with previous appraisals in various other chronic kidney diseases which did not model post-transplant cohorts. For patients with post-transplant recurrence of C3G, the sample size of the Phase 2 clinical trial cohort and absence of a comparator arm did not permit a robust economic analysis. However, the results from the Phase 2 and extension studies support the clinical effectiveness of iptacopan in patients with post-transplant recurrence, and clinical advisors confirmed they expected iptacopan to be effective in patients with post-transplant recurrence.[27, 34, 38] Therefore, though not directly modelled, it is expected that the benefits demonstrated by the economic model would translate into this cohort with high unmet need. 

## _**3.14.3 Conclusions on cost-effectiveness**_ 

The results of the base case cost-effectiveness analysis indicate that iptacopan plus SoC was associated with 1.74 QALYs versus SoC alone. ****** *** **** ** ************** *** ***** ** ***** *** ****************** ********** ******** **** ** ***** ********* ** *** ** *** *** ** * ************** ****** ******* ** ******** **** *** ******* *** ****************************************************************** ******** 

Given the current absence of effective disease-modifying treatment options for C3G, there remains a critical unmet need for targeted therapies in this population. Individuals with C3G, carers, patient organisation representatives and clinicians have expressed a need for improved treatment options, given that current treatment with SoC does not prevent disease progression to kidney failure.[26, 27, 93, 104] Iptacopan is therefore expected to provide a vital treatment option for people with C3G.
