## **2.2 Exploring uncertainty** 

## _**2.2.1 Probabilistic sensitivity analysis**_ 

Probabilistic sensitivity analysis (PSA) was conducted to assess the impact of uncertainty around parameter values on the results of the model base case. Where data were available, probability distributions were assigned to parameters, to characterise uncertainty associated with the precision of the mean values, based on the nature of each parameter. Where empirical probability distributions were not available, the standard error was assumed to take a value equal to 10% of that of the mean. The PSA was run with 1000 iterations, with the probabilistic ICER convergence plot shown in Figure 1. 

The probabilistic base-case results expressed in terms of incremental costs, incremental LYGs, incremental QALYs and ICERs are presented in Table 4 and the probabilistic INHB at WTP thresholds of £20,000 and £30,000 are presented in Table 5. The probabilistic ICER of iptacopan and SoC versus SoC ************************************************* is ************** per QALY gained, falling within *********** % of the deterministic ICER. 

Please note that errors in relation to the PSA identified by the EAG in their review of the company’s economic model (as described in the EAG report), as well as one further PSA error subsequently identified by the company, were corrected prior to running these analyses. The implemented corrections are described in the company factual accuracy check comments document as submitted to NICE on 11[th] June 2025, ‘Section 5: Company modelling inaccuracies’. 

The discrepancy between the deterministic and probabilistic base-case ICERs was investigated and found to be connected to structural capabilities of the model which prevent positive eGFR slopes, due to the clinical implausibility of eGFR increasing continuously over the lifetime horizon. The iptacopan eGFR slope (cell I11, Clinical data tab) is calculated from the SoC eGFR slope and the iptacopan treatment effect. In this calculation, the iptacopan eGFR slope is capped at a maximum value of 0, i.e. not allowing positive eGFR slope values. When both the SoC eGFR slope and iptacopan treatment effect are varied, for all simulations which would result in a positive iptacopan eGFR slope, the iptacopan eGFR slope is thus capped at 0. For these simulations, the ICER is approximately ****** % below the deterministic value. For simulations where capping is not applicable and the iptacopan eGFR slope is a more negative value than the deterministic value, there is a significant impact on the ICER, due to its sensitivity to the iptacopan eGFR slope. As a result, in the calculation of the average cumulative ICER across many simulations, the large ICERs due to the uncapped eGFR slope values dominate vs the smaller ICERs from the capped eGFR slope values. 

The cost-effectiveness plane and acceptability curves are presented in Figure 2 and Figure 3, respectively.

## _**2.2.2 Deterministic sensitivity analysis**_ 

To further assess the robustness of the base-case model results, deterministic sensitivity analyses (DSA) were conducted by varying one model input at a time to assess which parameters had the largest impact on the ICER. Some parameters that do not have any uncertainty associated with the input value were excluded from the DSA. 

For clinical and utility parameters, 95% CI were used, which were sourced from published data, where available, and calculated where data were not available. For other parameters, the variation was assumed to be a set percentage of the mean (±20%); upper and lower values were either calculated directly by adding or subtracting the respective percentage (for the cost inputs), or by using this to further calculate appropriate variations. 

Results of the DSA show that the most influential parameter on the base-case ICER ********** **************************************** is the iptacopan treatment effect, with inputs relating to graft failure the next most influential parameters (Figure 4).

Given the current absence of effective disease-modifying treatment options for C3G, there remains a critical unmet need for targeted therapies in this ultra-rare disease. Individuals with C3G, carers, patient organisation representatives and clinicians have expressed a need for improved treatment options, given that current treatment with SoC does not prevent disease progression to kidney failure.[1-4] Iptacopan is therefore expected to provide a vital treatment option for people with C3G.

## **SECTION 2: Current landscape** 

## **2a) The condition – clinical presentation and impact** 

Please provide a few sentences to describe the condition that is being assessed by NICE and the number of people who are currently living with this condition in England. 

Please outline in general terms how the condition affects the quality of life of patients and their families/caregivers. Please highlight any mortality/morbidity data relating to the condition if available. If the company is making a case for the impact of the treatment on carers this should be clearly stated and explained. 

## **What is C3G?** 

C3G is a very rare kidney disease that is chronic (lifelong) and progresses (worsens) over time. The disease commonly affects young people. The average age at diagnosis is 21– 23 years old.[2-4] 

C3G severely damages the kidneys,[5] which can cause many different problems. As C3G gets worse over time, the kidneys may stop working (‘kidney failure’), meaning they can no longer remove waste and extra water from the blood. 

Summary of information for patients for iptacopan for treating C3 glomerulopathy [ID6283] © Novartis (2025). All rights reserved Page 3 of 23 




<!-- page 174 -->

## **What causes C3G?** 

C3G is caused by a part of the _immune system,_ called the _complement system_ , working incorrectly. The complement system helps to fight bacteria and viruses.[6] However, in C3G, the complement system is too active because of a person’s genes or problems that develop during a person’s life.[6] 

Due to the complement system not working correctly, a specific protein called _complement component 3 (C3)_ is broken down into small pieces (fragments).[6] These fragments of C3 become lodged in the kidney, causing inflammation (an immune system response) and damage to the kidney’s filtering units ( _glomeruli_ ).[6] Damaged glomeruli are not able to filter the blood very well, and waste products build up in the blood causing more kidney damage.[6] 

## **How many people have C3G?** 

C3G is a very rare disease. Therefore, it is difficult to determine the exact number of people with C3G. It is estimated that there are approximately 427 people in England living with C3G.[5, 7-9] 

## **What are the signs and symptoms of C3G?** 

Individuals with C3G can have a variety of signs and symptoms. These include too much protein in the urine ( _proteinuria_ ), blood in the urine (haematuria), high blood pressure (hypertension), tiredness (fatigue), and swelling of the hands, feet and ankles (oedema). These can cause foamy urine, less urine production, headaches, and joint pain.[10, 11] 

## **How does C3G progress over time?** 

As C3G gets more severe, symptoms get worse, and complications increase. This can include worsening fatigue, and the development of high blood pressure and cardiovascular disease (conditions affecting the heart or blood vessels).[2, 12, 13] Approximately half of individuals with C3G have kidney failure within 10 years of diagnosis.[3, 5, 14, 15] People who have kidney failure will require _kidney replacement therapy_ . There are two options:[16] 

- _Kidney transplant_ – a healthy kidney from a donor is placed into the body using surgery, to take over the function of the kidneys which stopped working 

- _Dialysis_ – a treatment, often with a machine, that removes waste and excess fluid from the blood when the kidneys are not functioning 

Kidney transplants do not address the cause of C3G so the disease can return following a transplant of a new kidney.[17] If the disease returns and the transplanted kidney stops working (graft failure), the person will need to receive another transplant or go back to receiving dialysis. 

## **How is C3G progression measured?** 

_Proteinuria_ is when there is too much protein in the urine. This indicates that the kidneys are not working properly. In C3G, the amount of protein in the urine can be used to assess 

Summary of information for patients for iptacopan for treating C3 glomerulopathy [ID6283] © Novartis (2025). All rights reserved Page 4 of 23 




<!-- page 175 -->

how well the kidneys are functioning by measuring the _urine protein-to-creatinine ratio (UPCR)._ UPCR is a test that compares the amount of protein and a waste product called _creatinine_ in a urine sample. In people with no kidney disease, the kidneys filter blood effectively, without letting significant amounts of protein pass into the urine. In people with C3G, UPCR levels are increased, which is a sign of worse kidney function.[5, 18-21] 

The _estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR)_ measures how well the kidneys are filtering waste from the blood. eGFR is measured using a blood test. In people with C3G, eGFR levels are lower than normal, which is a sign of worse kidney function.[5, 21, 22] 

To categorise how well people’s kidneys are working and measure whether a person’s C3G is getting worse, a system called Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD) staging is used.[19] There are 6 stages (CKD stage 1, 2, 3a, 3b, 4 and 5) based on eGFR levels, with Stage 1 being the mildest and Stage 5 indicating kidney failure.[19] 

## **Impact of C3G on quality of life** 

The wide-ranging symptoms of C3G can have a negative impact on a person’s quality of life. This can include: 

- Swelling of hands, feet and ankles can cause difficulties with standing, walking and climbing stairs.[23, 24] 

- Severe fatigue can limit social activities and cause individuals to need to sleep during the day and feel too tired to eat.[25] 

- Episodes of gout (severe pain and joint swelling) may limit physical activities.[11, 23] 

The symptoms of C3G, restrictions to lifestyle and diet, and kidney replacement therapies all impact the quality of life of individuals with C3G (see **Section 2d** for more information). People with C3G face uncertainty around disease progression and the lack of available treatment options, which can impact their mental health and lead to anxiety and depression.[23, 26] C3G is a very rare disease, with limited information available and this can also cause feelings of helplessness, isolation and loneliness.[23, 26] 

C3G can impact the ability of people to attend education and work regularly, potentially limiting their future career opportunities.[26] C3G also impacts the families and carers of people with C3G. Carers may be required to support with day-to-day activities and attending medical appointments. This can impact the carer’s ability to work or study (productivity), adding an economic burden. 

As mentioned, approximately half of people with C3G progress to kidney failure within 10 years of diagnosis and then require kidney replacement therapies.[3, 5, 14, 15] Kidney replacement therapies can also have negative impacts on people with C3G. People with C3G have to wait on average 2–3 years for a suitable donor organ and may require dialysis whilst they wait.[27] Transplants are associated with multiple risks including the risk of surgery, infections, kidney rejection (where the body sees the transplanted kidney as a threat and attacks it) and graft failure (where the transplanted kidney stops working).[28] To prevent kidney rejection, medicines called _immunosuppressants_ are used to stop the immune system from attacking the transplanted kidney. These medicines are also associated with _side effects_ , including increased risk of infections, high blood pressure, 

Summary of information for patients for iptacopan for treating C3 glomerulopathy [ID6283] © Novartis (2025). All rights reserved Page 5 of 23 




<!-- page 176 -->

weight gain, difficulty sleeping, and gastrointestinal side effects, which can all impact quality of life, as well as an increased risk of cancer associated with long-term use.[29] 

Dialysis treatment is repeated for the rest of a person’s life or until the person receives a kidney transplant. There are two types of dialysis. One is carried out at a clinic three times a week to filter the blood through a machine and takes four hours per session.[30] Alternatively, dialysis can be done at home but this usually needs to be repeated every day.[30] Therefore, dialysis requires people with C3G to take time out of work, education or social activities, which reduces quality of life.[23, 26] People who have dialysis can experience side effects of fatigue, low blood pressure, itchy skin, joint pain and muscle cramps.[31] 

## **2b) Diagnosis of the condition (in relation to the medicine being evaluated)** 

Please briefly explain how the condition is currently diagnosed and how this impacts patients. Are there any additional diagnostic tests required with the new treatment? 

People with C3G go to the doctor when they have symptoms such as blood in the urine, foamy urine (a sign of too much protein in the urine), fatigue, or swelling in the hands and feet.[6] If a doctor suspects that someone has a kidney disease like C3G, they will test the person’s blood and urine to measure how well the kidneys are working. 

To diagnose C3G, a kidney biopsy is needed. The kidney biopsy involves inserting a needle through the skin that lies over the kidney to remove a small piece of tissue from the kidney, which is then looked at with special microscopes to check for signs of C3G.[32] 

## **2c) Current treatment options:** 

The purpose of this section is to set the scene on how the condition is currently managed: 

- What is the treatment pathway for this condition and where in this pathway the medicine is likely to be used? Please use diagrams to accompany text where possible. Please give emphasis to the specific setting and condition being considered by NICE in this review. For example, by referencing current treatment guidelines. It may be relevant to show the treatments people may have before and after the treatment under consideration in this SIP. 

- • Please also consider: 

   - if there are multiple treatment options, and data suggest that some are more commonly used than others in the setting and condition being considered in this SIP, please report these data. 

   - are there any drug–drug interactions and/or contraindications that commonly cause challenges for patient populations? If so, please explain what these are. 

There are currently no treatments that directly target the cause of C3G.[19] The current treatment options (referred to as standard of care) are used for many different diseases and aim to slow down the process of kidney damage and manage symptoms. Standard of care can include the following treatments:[6, 19 ] 

- Angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors (ACEi) and angiotensin receptor blockers (ARB) – these are used to reduce protein in the urine and to lower blood pressure. ACEi/ARB are examples of a type of treatment called RAS inhibitors. 

Summary of information for patients for iptacopan for treating C3 glomerulopathy [ID6283] © Novartis (2025). All rights reserved Page 6 of 23 




<!-- page 177 -->

- Corticosteroids (CS) and/or mycophenolate mofetil (MMF) – these are examples of immunosuppressants and are used to reduce inflammation. 

- Sodium-glucose co-transporter 2 inhibitors (SGLT2i) – these are used to lower blood pressure in the kidneys. 

- Eculizumab – this targets a part of the complement system. Only a very limited number of people whose C3G has returned after a kidney transplant and meet a list of criteria can receive this treatment in the UK. 

- _Clinical trial_ enrolment – individuals whose disease continues to worsen with standard of care treatments are often considered for a clinical trial where a new medication is tested, if available. 

How the currently available treatments are used is shown in **Figure 1.** 

**Figure 1** also shows when iptacopan could be used, if it is recommended by NICE. Adults with C3G are expected to receive iptacopan if treatment with an ACEi or ARB alone is not sufficient to reduce the risk of disease progression. Iptacopan would be given in addition to an ACEi or ARB, unless the person is unable to receive ACEi/ARB. Iptacopan may also be given to individuals who are receiving MMF, CS or SGLT2i.

## **2d) Patient-based evidence (PBE) about living with the condition** 

## **Context:** 

- **Patient-based evidence (PBE)** is when patients input into scientific research, specifically to provide experiences of their symptoms, needs, perceptions, quality of life issues or experiences of the medicine they are currently taking. PBE might also include carer burden and outputs from patient preference studies, when conducted in order to show what 

Summary of information for patients for iptacopan for treating C3 glomerulopathy [ID6283] © Novartis (2025). All rights reserved Page 7 of 23 




<!-- page 178 -->

matters most to patients and carers and where their greatest needs are. Such research can inform the selection of patient-relevant endpoints in clinical trials. 

In this section, please provide a summary of any PBE that has been collected or published to demonstrate what is understood about **patient needs and disease experiences** . Please include the methods used for collecting this evidence. Any such evidence included in the SIP should be formally referenced wherever possible and references included. 

As discussed in **Section 2a** , C3G can have a negative impact on a person’s quality of life. The symptoms of C3G and, after kidney failure, the requirement for dialysis can make it difficult to carry out daily activities, socialise, exercise and work. 

A survey of people with C3G was conducted using a questionnaire called the Functional Assessment of Chronic Illness Therapy-Fatigue (FACIT-Fatigue). This questionnaire measures how fatigue affects people’s daily activities and their overall quality of life.[33] The questionnaire found that 78% of people with C3G limit their social activities due to fatigue, 77% need to sleep during the day and 47% feel too tired to eat.[33] In a 2018 forum for people with C3G and their carers (conducted by the National Kidney Foundation in the United States), people with C3G expressed that “the fatigue is overwhelming”, impacting all aspects of their lives.[23] 

C3G can also have an impact on a person’s mental health.[23] People with C3G discussed feeling scared and lonely, with their future unknown. Some people with C3G noted:[23] 

- “What’s most difficult is knowing that time is not on my side…without a viable drug treatment, I know that a healthy diet, exercise, and following doctor’s orders will not stop the progression of this disease…This absolutely frightens me…I can only imagine things getting worse” 

- “You feel like you’re going through it alone” 

As mentioned in **Section 2a** , people with C3G often feel helpless and isolated as there is not much information available on this rare disease. They can also experience anxiety and depression as they worry about their symptoms and disease progression.[23, 26] 

As mentioned in **Section 2a** , approximately half of people with C3G progress to kidney failure within 10 years of diagnosis.[3, 5, 14, 15] Kidney replacement therapies can increase the disease burden for people with C3G. Dialysis is a very time-consuming treatment which puts a burden on the daily life of people with C3G and their carers. A UK patient organisation reported how individuals with C3G have to “fit a life around dialysis treatment”, with in-centre dialysis “tak[ing] out three days a week of normal life”, once transport time, waiting time, and the four-hour dialysis duration are taken into account.[34] Young people with C3G have reported not being able to attend education regularly, which can impact their social lives and future careers.[23, 26] 

The burden of C3G is increased for some individuals due to the pressure of making treatment decisions, specifically when it comes to the choice of receiving a transplant, knowing that C3G can return in the transplanted kidney. People with C3G expressed feeling that they must “trade in their current conditions for another unknown.”[23] This burden increases with continued disease progression.

**SECTION 3: The treatment** 

## **3a) How does the new treatment work?** 

What are the important features of this treatment? 

Please outline as clearly as possible important details that you consider relevant to patients relating to the mechanism of action and how the medicine interacts with the body 

Where possible, please describe how you feel the medicine is innovative or novel, and how this might be important to patients and their communities. 

If there are relevant documents which have been produced to support your regulatory submission such as a summary of product characteristics or patient information leaflet, please provide a link to these. 

As mentioned in **Section 2a** , C3G is caused by the incorrect functioning of a part of the immune system called the complement system. Iptacopan is a treatment which directly targets the cause of C3G in the complement system. Iptacopan reduces the amount of C3 in the kidneys, slowing down kidney damage.[33, 35]

As mentioned in **Section 1b** , iptacopan is expected to be used in combination with a RAS inhibitor _,_ or without a RAS inhibitor in adults who are unable to receive a RAS inhibitor. People who take iptacopan may also continue to take other treatments such as SGLT2i, CS, MMF.

How and where is the treatment given or taken? Please include the dose, how often the treatment should be given/taken, and how long the treatment should be given/taken for. 

How will this administration method or dosing potentially affect patients and caregivers? How does this differ to existing treatments? 

Iptacopan is taken twice daily as a 200 mg capsule that is swallowed.[36] Iptacopan has no special storage conditions, so it does not need to be kept in the fridge.[36] C3G is a chronic disease and treatment may be lifelong.

## **3e) Efficacy** 

Efficacy is the measure of how well a treatment works in treating a specific condition. 

In this section, please summarise all data that demonstrate how effective the treatment is compared with current treatments at treating the condition outlined in section 2a. Are any of the outcomes more important to patients than others and why? Are there any limitations to the data which may affect how to interpret the results? Please do not include academic or commercial in confidence information but where necessary reference the section of the company submission where this can be found. 

The APPEAR-C3G trial described in **Section 3d** above studied the efficacy (how well a treatment works) and safety (side effects) of iptacopan as a treatment for C3G. This was compared with placebo.[37] The efficacy of iptacopan was assessed by measuring the change in UPCR and change in eGFR in people treated with iptacopan or placebo (described in **Section 2a** ). 

After six months of treatment in the APPEAR-C3G trial, individuals taking iptacopan had _clinically meaningful_ and _statistically significantly_ lower UPCR levels, compared to those taking placebo.[33, 40] Individuals taking iptacopan for six months in the APPEAR-C3G trial also had an improvement in eGFR while patients taking placebo had a decline, suggesting that with iptacopan the disease worsens at a slower speed. However, this result was not statistically significant and is therefore uncertain. Data from participants who received iptacopan for 12 months (in the APPEAR-C3G trial) or longer (in the extension study) show that the effects of iptacopan are maintained with longer-term treatment. 

More results on the efficacy of iptacopan can be found in **Section 2 of the company submission** .

## **3f) Quality of life impact of the medicine and patient preference information** 

What is the clinical evidence for a potential impact of this medicine on the quality of life of patients and their families/caregivers? What quality of life instrument was used? If the EuroQol-5D (EQ-5D) was used does it sufficiently capture quality of life for this condition? Are there other disease specific quality of life measures that should also be considered as supplementary information? 

Please outline in plain language any quality of life related data such as **patient reported outcomes (PROs).** 

Please include any **patient preference information (PPI)** relating to the drug profile, for instance research to understand willingness to accept the risk of side effects given the added benefit of treatment. Please include all references as required. 

The ‘EQ-5D’ is a questionnaire that is recommended by NICE for measuring a person’s quality of life. As the EQ-5D is a general tool used for all diseases, it does not always capture the specific challenges associated with a disease. In the APPEAR-C3G trial, people with C3G were asked to answer questions about their quality of life **,** using EQ5D.[33, 40] Further information about the EQ-5D data is provided in **Section 3i** . 

The ‘FACIT-Fatigue’ is a questionnaire to understand how fatigue affects daily activities and the overall quality of life of individuals.[41] Fatigue is a common symptom for people with C3G.[42] However, the participants of the APPEAR-C3G study did not have more fatigue than people without C3G. This was likely because most individuals were in an early stage of disease. In APPEAR-C3G, FACIT-Fatigue was measured before and during the trial. There was no statistically significant change in FACIT-Fatigue scores for individuals treated with iptacopan.[33, 40] 

## **3g) Safety of the medicine and side effects** 

When NICE appraises a treatment, it will pay close attention to the balance of the benefits of the treatment in relation to its potential risks and any side effects. Therefore, please outline the main side effects (as opposed to a complete list) of this treatment and include details of a benefit/risk assessment where possible. This will support patient reviewers to consider the potential overall benefits and side effects that the medicine can offer. 

Based on available data, please outline the most common side effects, how frequently they happen compared with standard treatment, how they could potentially be managed and how many people had treatment adjustments or stopped treatment. Where it will add value or context for patient readers, please include references to the Summary of Product Characteristics from regulatory agencies etc. 

Every medicine has the potential to result in side effects, and the same medicine can produce different reactions in different people. Across the three trials, iptacopan was generally well _tolerated_ (participants were able to put up with the side effects of their treatment) and most side effects were mild or moderate. 

The most common side effect occurring in people treated with iptacopan across all three trials was COVID-19, which occurred in 29.7% of people. The trials were conducted during the COVID-19 pandemic. This likely contributed to the high number of people with COVID19. The other most common side effects were nasopharyngitis (13.9%; the common cold), increased levels of a protein called creatine phosphokinase in the blood (10.9%), headache (8.9%), cough (7.9%), anaemia (5.9%; fewer red blood cells than normal) and upper respiratory tract infections (5.9%; infections affecting the nose, throat, and airways). 

Summary of information for patients for iptacopan for treating C3 glomerulopathy [ID6283] © Novartis (2025). All rights reserved Page 12 of 23 




<!-- page 183 -->

19.8% of people treated with iptacopan experienced serious side effects. The most common serious side effects were infections. There were 3 individuals who stopped taking iptacopan due to serious side effects during the extension study. But these side effects were considered not related to iptacopan by the participants’ doctors. There was one death across the three studies, which the participant’s doctor did not consider to be caused by iptacopan. 

Because of the way iptacopan works on the immune system, there is an increased risk of infections. To reduce the risk of serious infections, people are required to have several vaccinations before starting iptacopan.[36] 

## **3h) Summary of key benefits of treatment for patients** 

Issues to consider in your response: 

- Please outline what you feel are the key benefits of the treatment for patients, caregivers and their communities when compared with current treatments. 

- Please include benefits related to the mode of action, effectiveness, safety and mode of administration 

There is a high unmet need in C3G, with no treatments available that directly target the disease. With current treatments, approximately half of the people with C3G need dialysis or a kidney transplant within 10 years after diagnosis. 

Iptacopan is expected to be the first treatment that targets the cause of C3G. In the main clinical trial, iptacopan reduced proteinuria more than placebo. Clinical trial data also suggest that with iptacopan, the disease may progress at a slower speed. Therefore, iptacopan is expected to improve symptoms and quality of life, and fewer people with C3G may need dialysis or a kidney transplant in the future. Treatment with iptacopan was also well tolerated in the clinical trials. 

Iptacopan is a capsule which can be swallowed at home twice a day.

## **3i) Value and economic considerations** 

## **Introduction for patients:** 

Health services want to get the most value from their budget and therefore need to decide whether a new treatment provides good value compared with other treatments. To do this they consider the costs of treating patients and how patients’ health will improve, from feeling better and/or living longer, compared with the treatments already in use. The drug manufacturer provides this information, often presented using a health economic model. 

In completing your input to the NICE appraisal process for the medicine, you may wish to reflect on: 

- The extent to which you agree/disagree with the value arguments presented below (e.g., whether you feel these are the relevant health outcomes, addressing the unmet needs and issues faced by patients; were any improvements that would be important to you missed out, not tested or not proven?) 

- If you feel the benefits or side effects of the medicine, including how and when it is given or taken, would have positive or negative financial implications for patients or their families (e.g., travel costs, time-off work)? 

- How the condition, taking the new treatment compared with current treatments affects your quality of life. 

The pharmaceutical company used a health economic model to compare the costs and benefits of iptacopan with the costs and benefits of the currently used treatments for C3G (standard of care). The health economic model will help NICE decide if the NHS should pay for iptacopan as a treatment for C3G. 

## **How the economic model reflects C3G** 

A picture of the economic model is shown below ( **Figure 2** ). To model the worsening of C3G over the duration of a person’s life, the disease course was split into different stages, known as ‘health states.’ The model uses CKD stages 1–5 (described in **Section 2a** ) to define these health states, and also includes health states for dialysis, kidney transplant and death. 

At the start of the model, people with C3G are in CKD stages 1–4. Over time, if their disease worsens, they move to worse CKD stages. People whose kidneys have stopped working are then modelled to receive dialysis or a transplant. The model also takes into account that C3G can return in some people who have received a transplant. If the transplanted kidney stops working (graft failure), the model considers that this person will then need dialysis or another transplant. 

Summary of information for patients for iptacopan for treating C3 glomerulopathy [ID6283] © Novartis (2025). All rights reserved Page 14 of 23 




<!-- page 185 -->

## **Figure 2: Economic model** 

**==> picture [229 x 332] intentionally omitted <==**

**Abbreviations:** CKD, chronic kidney disease; KRT, kidney replacement therapy. 

The different health states of the economic model are associated with different costs, such as costs of visiting a doctor, costs of dialysis or a transplant, and medication costs. The different health states are also associated with different health outcomes. For example, people receiving dialysis may have a worse quality of life and a shorter life expectancy than people in earlier CKD stages.[7, 43] All costs and health outcomes that occur over a person’s lifetime are included in the calculations of the economic model. 

## **Modelling the effectiveness and safety of iptacopan** 

All calculations in the model are done twice: 

- once for a hypothetical group of adults with C3G who receive current standard of care, and 

- once for a hypothetical group of adults with C3G who receive iptacopan. 

Based on the results from the APPEAR-C3G trial (see **Section 3e** ), people treated with iptacopan may experience a slower disease progression (less eGFR decline) than people treated with standard of care. Therefore, people in the model who are treated with iptacopan are less likely to move to worse CKD stages, and fewer people in this group need dialysis or a transplant. 

Summary of information for patients for iptacopan for treating C3 glomerulopathy [ID6283] © Novartis (2025). All rights reserved Page 15 of 23 




<!-- page 186 -->

The economic model also uses data from the clinical trials on the number of people who had serious side effects with iptacopan, and the number of people who stopped iptacopan treatment (e.g. due to side effects or no longer wanting to take it). 

## **Modelling other important data in C3G** 

Some information was not available from the clinical trials and had to be taken from other sources. This includes information on how many people receive a transplant or different types of dialysis, and how quickly a transplanted kidney can stop working (graft failure). This information was provided by the National Registry of Rare Kidney Diseases (RaDaR), which collects data from people with C3G who live in the UK and have agreed that their information is included in this database.[9] 

No information was available on the risk of death in people with C3G. Instead, data was used from a broader group of people with various rare kidney diseases.[7] 

## **Modelling how much iptacopan improves quality of life** 

Participants of the APPEAR-C3G trial completed the EQ-5D questionnaire (described in **Section 3f** ) which provided information on their quality of life. The responses to this questionnaire were used to calculate quality of life scores ( _utility values_ ) which were used in the economic model. Since APPEAR-C3G did not include people in CKD stage 5 or who were on dialysis or transplanted, information for these groups was taken from published studies which reported quality of life in people with other chronic kidney diseases.[44, 45] These utility values show that people in earlier CKD stages have better quality of life than people in later CKD stages or on dialysis. 

With people receiving iptacopan staying in earlier CKD stages for longer, the group of people receiving iptacopan in the economic model therefore have overall better quality of life than the group of people receiving standard of care. 

## **Modelling how NHS costs differ with iptacopan** 

Various NHS costs were included in the economic model, including: 

- The cost of iptacopan 

- The cost of standard of care medications 

- The cost of people with C3G seeing their doctor 

- The cost of regular urine and blood tests 

- The cost of kidney transplants and dialysis, including the cost of transport to and from dialysis centres 

- The costs of treating the side effects of iptacopan treatment 

- The cost of vaccinations that people must receive before starting iptacopan (see **Section 3g** ) 

In the economic model, the hypothetical group of people receiving iptacopan has lower costs for dialysis and transplants. However, the medication costs for the iptacopan group are higher because of the additional cost of iptacopan. 

Summary of information for patients for iptacopan for treating C3 glomerulopathy [ID6283] © Novartis (2025). All rights reserved Page 16 of 23 




<!-- page 187 -->

## **The results of the economic model** 

The economic model calculates the average total costs and average total health outcomes for a hypothetical group of adults with C3G receiving current standard of care, and for a hypothetical group of adults with C3G receiving iptacopan. The total costs and total health outcomes of these two groups are then compared to calculate the differences. When doing these calculations, health outcomes are expressed using a measure called qualityadjusted life years (QALYs), which considers how long people live and their quality of life. 

Based on the calculations of the pharmaceutical company, treatment with iptacopan is associated with more costs and more health benefits (more QALYs) than current standard of care. This means that whilst iptacopan costs more on average to the NHS, those people treated with iptacopan are expected to have improved quality of life and may live longer than people treated with current standard of care. 

NICE will need to decide whether this expected improvement in quality and length of life is worth the additional costs. 

## **Uncertainty** 

This is the first time that NICE assesses a treatment for C3G. Therefore, there is no experience with economic models for C3G. 

All economic models are associated with some uncertainty because their development involves using data from many different sources and making assumptions. The pharmaceutical company has tried to reduce this uncertainty by getting advice from UK clinicians who have a lot of experience in treating people with C3G in the NHS. Where possible, data sources used are from the UK and provide information on people with C3G specifically. 

Because C3G is a very rare disease, it is more difficult to do clinical trials. Therefore, the number of people in the iptacopan clinical trials was smaller than it tends to be for more common diseases. The pharmaceutical company asks the NICE Committee to take into account that C3G is a very rare disease, when they assess iptacopan as a potential treatment for C3G. 

## **3j) Innovation** 

NICE considers how innovative a new treatment is when making its recommendations. 

If the company considers the new treatment to be innovative please explain how it represents a ‘step change’ in treatment and/ or effectiveness compared with current treatments. Are there any QALY benefits that have not been captured in the economic model that also need to be considered (see section 3f) 

With currently used treatments, about half of the people with C3G need dialysis or a kidney transplant within 10 years of diagnosis. Iptacopan is expected to be the first treatment which directly targets the cause of C3G. Therefore, the pharmaceutical 

Summary of information for patients for iptacopan for treating C3 glomerulopathy [ID6283] © Novartis (2025). All rights reserved Page 17 of 23 




<!-- page 188 -->

company considers that iptacopan is an innovative treatment which may provide significant additional benefit for people with C3G, compared with current treatments. 

Because of the way calculations are done in economic models, it is possible that not all benefits of iptacopan have been included (‘benefits not captured in the QALY’). The EQ5D questionnaire may not capture the full impact of C3G on the quality of life of individuals with C3G and their families and carers, including the feelings of helplessness, isolation and loneliness.[23, 26] 

In addition, the economic model does not consider the impact of dialysis on the time and productivity of people with C3G and their carers, who may have to reduce their hours at work or in education.[23, 46] By fewer people requiring dialysis with iptacopan, the burden would be reduced for individuals with C3G and their carers, but also for the NHS. 

By fewer people with C3G requiring a kidney transplant with iptacopan, the NHS transplant waiting list could become shorter and people with other kidney diseases who need a transplant may be able to get this more quickly. These additional benefits of iptacopan are not captured in the economic model results. However, the pharmaceutical company asks NICE to take these factors into consideration when assessing iptacopan. 

## **3k) Equalities** 

Are there any potential equality issues that should be taken into account when considering this condition and this treatment? Please explain if you think any groups of people with this condition are particularly disadvantaged. 

Equality legislation includes people of a particular age, disability, gender reassignment, marriage and civil partnership, pregnancy and maternity, race, religion or belief, sex, and sexual orientation or people with any other shared characteristics 

More information on how NICE deals with equalities issues can be found in the NICE equality scheme 

Find more general information about the Equality Act and equalities issues here 

At the moment, clinical trial results for iptacopan in C3G are only available for adults. Therefore, the expected marketing authorisation and this NICE assessment will only cover adults with C3G. However, the pharmaceutical company aims to make iptacopan available also to younger people with C3G as soon as possible. 

Research in the UK has identified that there is inequality across ethnic groups in the treatment of kidney disease. Individuals of Black and Asian descent are more likely to have kidney failure faster and wait longer for transplants than White people.[27, 47] Iptacopan reduces disease progression and therefore the need for dialysis or a transplant and so has the potential to address this inequality.

## **Section A : Clarification on effectiveness data** 

## _**Literature searches**_ 

**A 1.** There appear to have been transcription errors in some of the Cochrane Library search strategies. 

Please resubmit the following lines of the Cochrane Library search strategies: 

- Appendix B; Table 4: #9 

- Appendix F; Table 4: #9, #21, #35, #46 

- Appendix G; Table 4: #51 

We apologise for transcription errors in the Cochrane Library search strategies as originally presented. The correct search strategy tables are provided below, with updated parts underlined and highlighted in green. In the Appendix F table, please note that a row was originally missed and has now been included as row 21, with the numbering of rows 22–35 (formerly 21–34) updated, hence highlighted green. The former row 35 was a transcription error and not part of the search strategy, so has now been removed. We confirm that these were transcription errors only, and the number of final hits as presented in the originally submitted tables is correct.

**A 2.** Please confirm that Embase was searched via the Embase.com interface, rather than 

on Ovid, as stated in Appendix E; Tables 1 and 3 and Appendix F; Tables 1 and 2. 

The references to Ovid in Appendix E (Tables 1 and 3) and Appendix F (Tables 1 and 2) were included in error. We apologise for this inaccuracy and can confirm that Embase was searched via the Embase.com interface. 

## _**Decision problem**_ 

**A 3.  Priority question. In Table 1 of the company submission (CS), the company stated that eculizumab is considered of limited relevance as a comparator because in UK clinical practice its use is uncommon, with the NHS England commissioning policy restricting use to a small subgroup among patients with post-transplant recurrence, and its use is limited to patients with highly aggressive recurrent disease. Please include eculizumab as a comparator in clinical effectiveness analyses and a cost effectiveness analysis for the appropriate subgroup as used in UK clinical practice, or exclude this subgroup from the decision problem.** 

There is no head-to-head data for iptacopan versus eculizumab in C3G, and, as further explained in the response to clarification question A11, an indirect treatment comparison is deemed infeasible. It was therefore not possible to include eculizumab as a comparator within the cost-effectiveness model. 

The use of eculizumab for C3G in UK clinical practice is restricted by an NHS England commissioning policy to a subset of patients with highly aggressive post-transplant recurrence of C3G.[1] Amongst others, the NHS England criteria require evidence of a significant decline of transplant function (>20% decline in eGFR) within the previous three months before eculizumab can be initiated.[1] Treatment with iptacopan, on the other hand, can be started as soon as recurrence is diagnosed via biopsy of the transplanted kidney, before the onset of clinical signs such as eGFR decline; this is in line with the available clinical trial evidence from the iptacopan Phase 2 study (see CS Section 2.5.1) and the draft SmPC (section 4.2).[2, 3] Given that transplanted patients are monitored closely, C3G recurrence is usually diagnosed early, and UK clinicians advised that they would want to start iptacopan as soon as possible after histological diagnosis of recurrence.[4, 5] This places iptacopan potentially at a much earlier point in the treatment pathway than eculizumab, which requires evidence of significant eGFR decline posttransplant before it can be initiated.[4, 5] This further reduces the relevance of eculizumab as a comparator for iptacopan. 

In potential rare cases where disease recurrence is diagnosed late, clinical signs including significant eGFR decline are already present and the NHS England eculizumab criteria would be met, iptacopan would likely still be preferred over eculizumab given its (anticipated) licence in C3G, targeted mode of action, and availability of clinical trial data demonstrating efficacy in C3G.[4, 5] Therefore, this subgroup should not be excluded from the decision problem. However, as highlighted in the CS, over the past seven years on average only 1 C3G patient per year has received eculizumab, and the role of eculizumab in C3G is expected to decrease further if iptacopan can be used earlier in the disease course.[4, 6] Consequently, Novartis considers the inability to provide a cost-effectiveness analysis versus eculizumab as a minor limitation of this submission, given that clinical scenarios where iptacopan and eculizumab would be considered 


Clarification questions 



<!-- page 208 -->

at the same point in the treatment pathway will be extremely rare (far lower than 1 patient per year). 

## _**Systematic review**_ 

## **A 4.** Data extraction was conducted by one reviewer and then checked by a second. Please 

confirm how disagreements were resolved? 

Any discrepancies in data extraction were discussed between the two reviewers. If consensus could not be reached, a third independent reviewer was consulted to make a final decision. 

**A 5.** Quality assessments were conducted by one reviewer and then checked by a second. Please confirm how disagreements were resolved. 

Any discrepancies in quality assessment were discussed between the two reviewers. If consensus could not be reached, a third independent reviewer was consulted to make a final decision. 

## _**Clinical effectiveness evidence**_ 

**A 6.  Priority question: Based on Figure 12 of CS (eGFR CfB up to Month 12 by treatment group; page 56 of CS) and Figure 13 of CS (eGFR CfB up to Month 12, adjusted for baseline UPCR; page 57 of CS), there was a big increase in change from baseline of eGFR at day-14 for the iptacopan arm of the APPEAR-C3G trial. Please** 

## **provide an explanation for this big increase in change from baseline of eGFR at day14 for the iptacopan arm of the APPEAR-C3G trial.** 

C3G patients experience overactivation of the complement alternative pathway which leads to deposition of complement component 3 (C3) within the glomeruli, triggering inflammation.[7] Two UK clinicians consulted on a call to obtain clinical expert input for Novartis’ response to the EAG’s clarification questions assumed that the numerical increase in eGFR at Day 14 following iptacopan initiation is due to the rapid resolution of the intense inflammation in the kidney of C3G patients through alternative pathway inhibition.[8] Biomarker results from APPEAR-C3G demonstrated the rapid inhibition of the alternative pathway by iptacopan, with serum C3 levels increasing from baseline to Day 14 by 249% and urine soluble C5b-9 decreasing from baseline to Day 30 by 92.1%.[9] 

The increase in eGFR on Day 14 of iptacopan treatment was transient and short-term, with the Day 30 mean eGFR value on a similar level as subsequent measurements, as visible from Figures 12 and 13 in the CS. A sensitivity analysis on eGFR slope which excluded Day 14 measurements from the analysis confirmed that the short-term, temporary increase in mean eGFR at the start of iptacopan treatment did not impact longer-term eGFR slope estimates (Table 4).

## **A 7.  Priority question: In Figure 14 of CS (eGFR slope change with iptacopan treatment; page 59 of CS), eGFR slope change with iptacopan treatment (post-LNP023 treatment) of the APPEAR-C3G trial was based on the overall data of double-blind period and open-label period of APPEAR-C3G trial. Please provide a separate analysis for the double-blind period of the APPEAR-C3G trial as well as a separate analysis for the open-label period of the APPEAR-C3G trial.** 

An eGFR slope change analysis for the 6-month double-blind period of the APPEAR-C3G trial, split by treatment arms, is presented in Figure 15 and Table 16 of the CS. These results are replicated below in Table 5, alongside eGFR slope estimates (generated in a separate model) for the 6-month open-label treatment period, where all patients received open-label iptacopan. 

As visible in Table 5, patients allocated to the iptacopan arm had a steeper mean eGFR decline pre-randomisation than patients allocated to the placebo arm, consistent with baseline characteristics suggesting a more severe disease phenotype in the iptacopan arm than in the placebo arm (CS Table 7),[4, 9] which may impact comparability between arms.[4]

However, given that UK clinicians advised that a time frame of 6 months may be too short to robustly estimate changes in eGFR,[4] these estimates by treatment period (each based on 6 months of data) should be interpreted with caution, with eGFR slope analyses based on longer follow-up considered more robust and meaningful by clinical advisors.[4, 8]

## **A 8.  Priority question: Based on Table 7 of CS (APPEAR-C3G baseline demographics and disease characteristics; page 42-44 of CS), there were imbalances in relevant baseline characteristics between the intervention arm and control arm of the APPEAR-C3G trial. Please discuss the impact of these imbalances in relevant baseline characteristics between the two arms on the results being derived from the APPEAR-C3G trial.** 

As noted in the CS, there were imbalances between the APPEAR-C3G treatment arms for some baseline disease characteristics; patients randomised to the iptacopan arm had notably higher UPCR and lower eGFR at baseline, compared with those from the placebo arm. Furthermore, there were a greater number of participants with baseline nephrotic range proteinuria (≥3 g/g) in the iptacopan arm than in the placebo arm.[4, 9] The baseline imbalances suggest a more severe disease phenotype in the participants in the iptacopan arm. This was also noted by UK clinicians participating in an advisory board, and they suggested that due to this, comparisons between iptacopan and placebo groups may therefore underestimate the iptacopan treatment effect.[4] 

Due to these imbalances, several post-hoc sensitivity analyses were conducted. Pages 50–51 of the CS (Table 11) present post-hoc sensitivity analyses for the primary endpoint, change from baseline (CfB) in UPCR; these results are replicated below in Table 6.[9] The results of these posthoc sensitivity analyses were consistent with the results of the primary analysis, suggesting that these baseline imbalances did not impact the UPCR endpoint.[9]

**A 10.** Please describe the generalisability of the trial populations to the relevant clinical populations in England and Wales and provide evidence to support the description of the clinical characteristics of the relevant population in England and Wales. 

In a discussion in a UK advisory board, clinical experts were aligned that the inclusion criteria of the APPEAR-C3G and Phase 2 trials were valid, and that the trial populations were reflective of patients with C3G seen in UK clinical practice. For example, the advisors agreed that the concomitant medications (including ACEi/ARBs) in APPEAR-C3G were appropriate and representative of management of C3G patients within UK clinical practice, and that C3G patients generally present with UPCR levels well above 1 g/g (≥113 mg/mmol).[4] The trial generalisability to the C3G population in England and Wales was further supported by the fact that several UK study sites had participated in the trials.[4] 

A comparison of patient characteristics in APPEAR-C3G[9] and the C3G population of RaDaR[12] is shown in Table 9. RaDaR reports characteristics at time of diagnosis, as well as at latest followup (for prevalent patients at the time of the analysis). Median age at diagnosis was similar in APPEAR-C3G and the RaDaR cohort. Age at latest follow-up was higher in the prevalent RaDaR cohort than in APPEAR-C3G patients at baseline. The lower percentage of females in APPEARC3G (36.5%) compared to RaDaR (47%) was noted by UK clinicians as a common finding in clinical trials, especially in young age groups where pregnancy is a concern.[4] 

With regards to clinical characteristics, RaDaR patients were, on average, diagnosed with higher UPCR and a lower eGFR, indicating more advanced disease at time of diagnosis, than patients enrolled in APPEAR-C3G. Baseline mean UPCR of APPEAR-C3G participants was higher (3.40 g/g) compared to the prevalent RaDaR cohort (1.73 g/g). This is expected given that APPEARC3G focused on a population at higher risk of disease progression, with baseline UPCR ≥1 g/g despite treatment with a maximally tolerated dose of ACEi/ARB.[9] UK clinicians confirmed that the APPEAR-C3G UPCR inclusion criterion was reflective of a population who they would intend to use iptacopan in.[4] Higher mean eGFR at baseline in APPEAR-C3G patients (94.12 

mL/min/1.73m[2] ) than in the prevalent RaDaR cohort (67 mL/min/1.73m[2] ) may partially be related to the higher eGFR at diagnosis compared to UK clinical practice, but is also influenced by the APPEAR-C3G eGFR inclusion criterion of ≥30 mL/min/1.73m[2] at screening.[9] UK clinicians advised that they would generally want to start iptacopan treatment as soon as possible after C3G diagnosis, to preserve kidney function at the highest possible level, although people with more advanced disease would also be expected to derive benefit from iptacopan.[4] 

Overall, UK clinicians confirmed that the patients included in APPEAR-C3G and the Phase 2 study (patients with post-transplant recurrence) reflected patients who they considered would benefit from iptacopan in UK clinical practice and considered the trial data generalisable.[4]

## _**Indirect treatment comparison (ITC)**_ 

**A 11. Priority question: The company stated that ITC analysis for the comparison of iptacopan vs. eculizumab was not feasible because the outcome (eGFR) used in the economic model was not reported in the eculizumab trials. Therefore, please conduct ITC analyses based on other outcomes (e.g. proteinuria) that were reported in the eculizumab trials for the subgroup of patients who have previously had a kidney transplant and who have highly aggressive C3G recurrence, by using the posttransplant recurrent cohort of the Phase 2 trial of iptacopan.** 

The ITC versus eculizumab was not deemed feasible for a number of reasons, as noted in Section 2.9 of the CS with further details provided in Section B.1.7 of Appendix B. These reasons included the small sample sizes of the identified eculizumab trials (4–6 patients each) as well as 


Clarification questions 



<!-- page 216 -->

the limited generalisability of the eculizumab trial populations to how eculizumab is used in UK clinical practice. 

The clinical trials SLR identified three trials which assessed eculizumab for C3G. Two single-arm, single-centre trials from the US and Turkey included 6 C3G patients treated with eculizumab each,[13-15] while the third single-arm trial from Italy included overall 10 patients, 4 of which had C3G and were treated with eculizumab.[16] 

None of the studies reported inclusion criteria that were similar to the NHS England Clinical Commissioning Policy, which restricts use of eculizumab in the UK to a subset of patients with post-transplant recurrence of C3G and meeting very specific criteria indicative of highly aggressive disease; this includes evidence of active glomerulonephritis with cellular crescents on kidney biopsy and a >20% decline in eGFR within the previous three months.[1] Therefore, findings from the three international studies identified in the SLR may not be generalisable to eculizumab use in UK clinical practice. 

With regards to outcomes, none of the three studies reported eGFR data (the outcome of interest for economic modelling) for patients with C3G treated with eculizumab. An ITC of proteinuria outcomes was not considered meaningful due to marked differences in the eculizumab trial populations and the patients included in the post-transplant recurrent cohort of the iptacopan Phase 2 trial. The three eculizumab trials enrolled patients with proteinuria >3.5 g/day, ≥3 g/day, and >1 g/day, respectively (see Appendix B, Table 11). In contrast, elevated proteinuria was not an inclusion criterion for the post-transplant cohort in the iptacopan Phase 2 trial; accordingly, the enrolled patients’ proteinuria levels were predominantly normal at baseline, with a geo-mean of 0.28 g/day.[2] Therefore, an ITC of proteinuria reduction outcomes was considered not to provide meaningful results. 

An ITC of iptacopan versus eculizumab was overall not considered feasible, however, as outlined in the response to clarification question A3, given the very limited role of eculizumab in UK clinical practice, Novartis considers this a minor limitation of this submission. 

## _**Adverse events**_ 

**A 12.** The CS stated that approximately half of the serious adverse events (SAEs) were infection-related. Please provide a detailed breakdown of the types and severity of infections observed (e.g., bacterial, viral or fungal). Please also clarify any of these infections related to encapsulated bacteria (e.g., Neisseria meningitidis, Streptococcus pneumoniae). 

Most infections were non-serious and assessed by the investigator as not related to iptacopan. All infections resolved, with patients either continuing study treatment or resuming it after resolution. Importantly, no cases of meningococcal infection were reported.[17] 

In the broad safety set, ten patients experienced a total of 17 infection-related SAEs whilst on iptacopan.[17] The types of infections reported across the C3G studies are shown in Table 10. 

Six of the below SAEs were related to encapsulated bacteria, occurring in a total of four patients. In all cases these were caused by streptococcal infections, with one patient experiencing _Streptococcus gallolyticus_ infection (intervertebral discitis), and all others experiencing _Streptococcus pneumoniae_ infections. The severity of these SAEs was moderate for two patients and severe for two patients.

**A 13.** The CS stated that three patients discontinued iptacopan due to AEs (all in the openlabel extension study), with SAEs determined not to be related to iptacopan. Please clarify the nature of these SAEs and the rationale for concluding that they were unrelated to iptacopan. 

Causality of the three SAEs that led to discontinuation of iptacopan was assessed by the investigator, and these were classified as unrelated to iptacopan. The details regarding the three patients who discontinued iptacopan due to SAEs in the open-label extension study are presented below.[17] 

- One patient discontinued iptacopan due to an SAE of renal impairment 

- One patient discontinued iptacopan due to an SAE of C3G (post-transplant recurrent patient with C3G progression confirmed in kidney biopsy) 

- One patient discontinued iptacopan due to an SAE of acute kidney injury from immune complex glomerulonephritis (post-transplant recurrent patient with several confounding 


Clarification questions 



<!-- page 218 -->

events leading to eGFR decline, none of which were suspected to be related to iptacopan by the investigator; the investigator suspected postinfectious, crescentic glomerulonephritis on top of not yet remitted C3G as the cause of the acute kidney injury) 

**A 14.** The CS stated that one death was caused by cardiac arrhythmia but did not consider it to be related to iptacopan. Please clarify the details. Additionally, please also clarify any cardiovascular events reported, given the potential link between complement inhibition and thrombosis. 

There was one death across the three iptacopan C3G studies, with the cause of death presumed to be cardiac arrythmia that was not considered to be related to iptacopan by the study Investigator.[17] A 24-year-old patient, originally in the Phase 2 Study, was found unresponsive and declared dead on Day 501. Post-mortem examination revealed no obvious cause of death.[17] The evidence pointing to cardiac arrhythmia included arteriolar-nephrosclerosis, a clinical history of C3G, hypertension, focal myocardial scar, and a clinical history of hypocalcaemia.[17] The patient had pre-existing conditions including anxiety, palpitations, and hyperparathyroidism. Possible confounders for the event included concomitant medications of methylphenidate (potential adverse drug reactions [ADRs] of tachycardia and arrhythmia), venlafaxine (potential ADRs of tachycardia and arrhythmia) as well as trazodone (warning for QT prolongation).[17] 

The cardiovascular events reported in the broad safety set in the iptacopan clinical trials in C3G are presented in Table 11, though none of these were deemed to be related to iptacopan by the Investigator. Additionally, across the clinical studies included in the marketing authorisation application for iptacopan in its first indication (paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria [PNH]), no clinically meaningful abnormalities in cardiac safety-related assessments were observed.[17]

Thrombosis was not an AESI in the iptacopan clinical trials in C3G, and no AEs of thrombosis were reported in patients receiving iptacopan (1 patient in the placebo arm had mild thrombosis during the double-blind period of APPEAR-C3G).[9]

## _**Patient population**_ 

**B 1.  Priority question. CS Table 33 provides an overview of baseline patient characteristics from APPEAR-C3G (used in CS base-case), pooled APPEAR-C3G and Phase 2 native kidney cohort (Cohort A) and RaDaR (registry data from patients with C3G in the UK). The RaDaR study indicated that the baseline patient characteristics in the APPEAR-C3G potentially do not accurately reflect UK clinical practice as the proportion of females in APPEAR-C3G is lower and the clinical characteristics (e.g. mean EGFR and CKD stage) do seem to reflect a healthier population in APPEARC3G.** 

- a) Please justify the use of the APPEAR-C3G patient characteristics in the CS basecase. 

The base-case economic model used patient characteristics from APPEAR-C3G to be aligned with the source of clinical efficacy data used in the cost-effectiveness model. 

A scenario analysis was conducted with patient characteristics from RaDaR,[12] using characteristics at time of diagnosis based on clinical experts’ advice, since these were considered more reflective of future expected clinical practice where iptacopan would be initiated early in the disease course.[4] This scenario resulted in a *****% change in the ICER compared to the base case (full results are presented in Table 60 of the CS). 

- b) Please elaborate on the generalisability of both the baseline risks and the relative effectiveness derived from APPEAR-C3G (e.g. as presented in CS Tables 34 and 

   - 35) to UK clinical practice. 

UK clinicians confirmed that the patients included in APPEAR-C3G reflected patients who they considered would benefit from iptacopan in UK clinical practice and considered the trial data generalisable.[4] Further information is provided in the response to clarification question A10. 

- c) According to CS Table 7 (APPEAR-C3G baseline demographics and disease characteristics), there are significant imbalances between the two APPEAR-C3G arms (despite randomization and stratification). Please elaborate on the appropriateness of, and biases in both the baseline risks and the relative effectiveness derived from APPEAR-C3G (e.g. as presented in CS Tables 34 and 

   - 35) given these imbalances. 

For details on the potential impact of baseline imbalances on clinical trial results, please refer to the response to question A8. 


Clarification questions 



<!-- page 220 -->

When it comes to use of APPEAR-C3G data in the economic model, it is important to note that only the eGFR slopes in option 1 of CS Table 34 (comparison iptacopan vs placebo based on 6- month double-blind period) would potentially be impacted by imbalances in baseline characteristics between groups. Patients in the iptacopan arm had notably higher proteinuria at baseline and exhibited a steeper pre-trial eGFR decline than the placebo arm, suggesting a more severe disease phenotype.[4, 9] UK clinicians participating in an advisory board suggested that comparisons between the iptacopan and placebo groups may therefore underestimate the efficacy of iptacopan,[4] and results of a post-hoc sensitivity analyses of the change from baseline in eGFR endpoint showed a larger treatment effect for iptacopan after adjusting for baseline UPCR (see response to question A8, Table 7).[9] As such, cost-effectiveness analyses using eGFR slopes as in option 1 of CS Table 34 may bias against iptacopan and should be interpreted with caution. 

eGFR slope options 2 (base-case) and 3 of CS Table 34 would not be impacted by imbalances in baseline characteristics between groups, since both the pre-iptacopan slope and the oniptacopan slope were derived using data from _all_ patients enrolled in APPEAR-C3G. The preiptacopan eGFR slope included historical and screening/run-in data from all APPEAR-C3G participants, and placebo data from the placebo arm patients. The on-iptacopan eGFR slope included data from the iptacopan arm of APPEAR-C3G, as well as data from the placebo arm after patients switched to iptacopan at the start of the open-label period. Therefore, baseline imbalances between the iptacopan and placebo arms of APPEAR-C3G do not affect the basecase economic analysis. 

## _**Model structure**_ 

## **B 2.  Priority question. The model consists of 9 mutually exclusive health states: CKD stages 1-5 (separating between 3a and 3b), dialysis and post-transplant as well as death.** 

- a) The decision to use eGFR rather than reduction in proteinuria (UPCR) is justified by the lack of a robust surrogacy relationship for complement inhibitors. Please elaborate with supporting evidence on the quantitative surrogacy relationship between UPCR reduction and (long-term) clinical outcomes (such as eGFR decline, CKD progression, dialysis initiation, or mortality). i) specifically for complement inhibitors like iptacopan in C3G and, ii) in general in chronic kidney disease. 

The model structure adopted for this submission follows well-established precedents, with health states in previous NICE TAs in chronic kidney diseases generally defined by CKD stages (unless other, non-kidney features of the respective disease prevailed) and KRT health states for dialysis and transplant (see CS Table 31). These health states were confirmed by UK clinicians to be relevant and key determinants of quality of life and costs in C3G.[4] 

Given that CKD stages are defined by eGFR, use of eGFR trial data was considered the most direct approach to modelling disease progression,[5] which is in alignment with the approach taken in several previous appraisals in other chronic kidney diseases (CS Table 31). Clinicians consulted during preparation of the clarification questions response reconfirmed that where 


Clarification questions 



<!-- page 221 -->

eGFR data is available, it should be used directly rather than predicted using surrogacy relationships.[8] 

While evidence from observational and registry studies is generally aligned that a reduction in proteinuria is associated with a positive impact on longer-term outcomes in C3G, analysis methods and estimates of the quantitative relationship vary.[20-23] For example, an analysis of RaDaR data found that a 50% reduction in UPCR from baseline to 12 months is associated with a reduced risk of kidney failure (compared to no UPCR reduction) with a hazard ratio (HR) of 0.33 (95% CI: 0.17, 0.63).[20] A published analysis of data from the Spanish GLOSEN registry concurred with the conclusion that a ≥50% reduction in UPCR was significantly associated with a lower risk of kidney failure, but estimated a HR of 0.79 (95% CI: 0.56, 0.97; p<0.001).[21] The same study also found that there was an inverse relationship between the slope of eGFR and the change of proteinuria over time, reflected below in Figure 1, which supports that reduction in proteinuria positively impacts kidney function as measured by eGFR.[21] 

**Figure 1. Graphical representation of log change in eGFR as a function of log change in proteinuria** 

**==> picture [275 x 274] intentionally omitted <==**

**Abbreviations:** CI, confidence interval; eGFR, estimated glomerular filtration rate; p, p-value. **Source:** Caravaca-Fontán et al. 2022 (Figure 3).[21] 

Importantly, all currently available published evidence on the association of UPCR with eGFR and other clinical outcomes in C3G is based on UPCR reductions observed with currently used SoC treatments. As highlighted in the CS (see Section 1.3.5), these treatments do not address the underlying pathophysiology of C3G and predominantly constitute supportive care. On the other hand, iptacopan, as a Factor B complement inhibitor, is a targeted treatment for C3G. Clinicians consulted during preparation of the clarification questions response summarised that, for example, ACE inhibitors are considered as treating the consequences of CKD, whereas iptacopan, as a disease-modifying treatment, is considered as treating the cause of C3G.[8] Therefore, clinicians considered it plausible that the long-term benefits of reducing UPCR with iptacopan could be greater than the long-term benefits of reducing UPCR with current SoC.[8] 


Clarification questions 



<!-- page 222 -->

Surrogate endpoint literature also warrants caution when it comes to transferring quantitative surrogacy relationships to other classes of treatments.[24] The NICE manual states that surrogate outcome validation is specific to the population and technology type under consideration (NICE manual section 4.6.8), and that extrapolation to a technology of a different class or with a different mechanism of action must be thoroughly justified (NICE manual section 4.6.9).[25] Given these circumstances, Novartis considers that prediction of eGFR or other clinical outcomes based on iptacopan UPCR data and surrogacy relationships from other classes of treatments would introduce undue uncertainty into the appraisal, especially since eGFR data are available from the iptacopan clinical trials in C3G and can be used in the economic model directly. This conclusion was supported by the consulted clinical experts.[8] 

b) Given that UPCR is the primary endpoint of APPEAR-C3G, please provide exploratory analyses assessing the potential correlation between UPCR reduction and eGFR decline. Similarly. please provide exploratory (survival) analyses illustrating the relationship between UPCR and CKD progression as well as between UPCR and dialysis initiation. Additionally, please provide analyses stratifying patients by UPCR response categories (e.g., ≥30% vs. <30% reduction from baseline) and comparing eGFR trajectories as well as dialysis-free survival. 

An analysis was conducted to explore the potential correlation between change in UPCR and change in eGFR in APPEAR-C3G trial data. Please note that the analysis was only performed for the iptacopan arm, since for the placebo arm only six months of data were available. In participants randomised to the iptacopan arm, the exploratory analysis found a statistically significant correlation (p=******) of change from baseline in eGFR at Month 12 with logtransformed change from baseline in UPCR at Month 6, with the correlation coefficient (–****) indicating a moderate negative correlation.[11] While exploratory and limited by sample size and duration of follow-up, this analysis supports the association of UPCR reduction with benefit on eGFR.[11] 

CKD progression is defined by eGFR decline, therefore the result noted above provides information on the relationship between UPCR and CKD progression. No patients initiated dialysis during the 12-month duration of the APPEAR-C3G study and therefore an analysis of the relationship between UPCR and dialysis initiation was not feasible. 

An analysis of eGFR trajectories stratified by UPCR response is shown in Table 12.[11] In the analysis of the 6-month double-blind treatment period of APPEAR-C3G, iptacopan treatment had a positive impact on eGFR decline compared to the pre-iptacopan eGFR slope both in patients with UPCR reduction ≥30% and patients with UPCR reduction <30%. The effect size was larger (and statistically significant versus the pre-iptacopan eGFR slope) in patients with ≥30% UPCR reduction.[11] The small number of patients in the placebo arm who had a UPCR reduction ≥30% (n=4 of overall 36 patients) did not allow a meaningful analysis of eGFR slope stratified by UPCR reduction in the placebo arm. 

In a further analysis of iptacopan arm patients after 12 months in APPEAR-C3G (double-blind + open-label period), similarly, iptacopan treatment had a positive impact on eGFR decline both in patients with UPCR reduction ≥30% and <30%, but there was a larger magnitude of effect in patients with ≥30% UPCR reduction.[11] In both UPCR responder groups, the change in eGFR slope versus the pre-iptacopan slope was statistically significant.[11] 


Clarification questions 



<!-- page 223 -->

Overall, while exploratory and in a small sample size, these analyses suggest that greater reduction in UPCR with iptacopan may translate into greater eGFR benefit, although also lower reductions in UPCR (<30%) were associated with meaningful improvements in eGFR slope compared to the pre-iptacopan eGFR trajectory. 

As noted above, no patients initiated dialysis and therefore an analysis of dialysis-free survival was not conducted.
