- c) Please provide a model structure and scenario analyses using the primary endpoint of APPEAR-C3G, i.e. UPCR to define health states (pre-KRT). 

As noted in the response to question B2 a), the CKD stage-based model structure adopted for this submission follows precedents established by multiple previous NICE TAs (see CS Table 31). The utilised health states were confirmed by UK clinicians to be relevant and key determinants of quality of life and costs in C3G.[4] 

Defining health states by UPCR levels would deviate from previous models used in various other chronic kidney diseases. In addition to this request requiring a complete restructure or rebuild of the submitted model, parameterisation of the model would be challenging, with various required model inputs (e.g. for mortality) generally published by CKD stage and not by UPCR levels. 

Reduction in UPCR is a meaningful trial endpoint and useful to see treatment effect within a short time frame both in a trial setting and clinical practice,[4] but from a clinical perspective, clinicians confirmed that eGFR is the most important outcome to monitor longer-term, as a measure of kidney function.[8] In addition, since KRT is not started based on UPCR levels but based on low eGFR indicating kidney failure, a model using UPCR-based health states pre-KRT would still need to also track eGFR in order to correctly model the start of KRT. 

Due to these reasons, no alternative model structure and scenario analyses have been provided. In case we should have misunderstood the EAG’s request and this related to modelling eGFR decline based on a UPCR surrogacy relationship, we refer to our response to question B2 a). 

- d) Please justify why a different model structure was used compared with previous NICE TAs, for instance in TA358 (considering tolvaptan): i) CKD stages 3a and 3b were not separated and; ii) KRT could consist of conservative care (management to prolong kidney function and control symptoms of ESRD), haemodialysis (HD; either hospital HD, satellite HD or home HD), peritoneal dialysis (PD; either ambulatory or continuous ambulatory PD) or kidney transplantation (either from a living or deceased donor). The TA358 model allows for different KRT in subsequent cycles (although switching between dialysis modalities was not possible). 

i) While TA358 combined CKD stages 3a and 3b,[26] several other TAs separated these states. As noted in Table 31 of the CS, TA942, TA937, TA775 and TA599 included CKD stages 3a and 3b as distinct states,[27-30] while TA882 grouped stages 1–3a and 3b–4.[31] Separating CKD stages 3a and 3b aligns with KDIGO and NICE guidance on CKD staging,[32, 33] and provides additional granularity to the economic modelling. 

ii) As noted on page 105 of the CS, given the young average age at kidney failure, UK clinicians advised that all patients with C3G would be expected to commence KRT following kidney failure, with no patients receiving conservative management instead.[4] As such, conservative care was not considered an appropriate treatment and not included in the model. 

Within the KRT health state, patients are separated into dialysis and post-transplant. When receiving dialysis, the model accounts for the receipt of different types of dialysis for both utilities 


Clarification questions 



<!-- page 226 -->

and costs. For the dialysis utility in the economic model, a weighted average was calculated according to the proportion of patients receiving each type of dialysis, sourced from a RaDaR analysis in patients with C3G (HD: 85.3%; PD: 14.7% [APD: 11.8%, CAPD: 2.9%]).[12] The cost of dialysis was calculated using NHS reference costs, with HD assumed to be repeated three times per week and continuous ambulatory peritoneal dialysis (CAPD) and automated peritoneal dialysis (APD) assumed to be carried out daily.[34-36] Within the calculation of HD costs, hospital, satellite, and home HD were weighted by total activity for the respective HRG codes in the NHS reference costs. Costs for HD, CAPD and APD were then weighted for calculation of the average dialysis cost, with proportions again based on RaDaR data in patients with C3G.[12] 

The cost of kidney transplant in the model also considers both living or deceased donor transplantations, again as a weighted average based on the proportions in RaDaR (living donor: 34.2%; deceased donor: 65.8%).[12] Details of the cost calculations for dialysis and transplant are provided in Table 50 of the CS. 

As with TA358, the model in this submission allows for different types of KRT in subsequent cycles. Patients on dialysis have a per-cycle probability of receiving a transplant in each cycle, while transplanted patients have a per-cycle probability of experiencing graft failure in each cycle, requiring a return to dialysis (see CS Section 3.3.2.2). The model allows for multiple transplants with multiple instances of graft failure over the time horizon, reflecting a common cycle of transplant and dialysis as experienced by patients with C3G (please also refer to the response to question B4).[4, 12, 37] 

e) In the CS it is stated that: 

- “ _A 3-month cycle length was considered to provide sufficient detail to capture the impact on costs and QALYs as patients progressed through the model_ ” 

- “ _Aligned with prior appraisals in other chronic kidney diseases (Table 31) which included cycle lengths ranging from 4 weeks–1 year_ ” 

Please provide additional justification why a 3-month cycle length is considered sufficiently short (rather than 1 month/4 weeks as used in TA599, TA623, TA775, TA825, TA890 and TA937) to capture the impact on costs and QALYs as patients progressed through the model. 

While several previous appraisals used a shorter cycle length, it should be noted that this may have in some cases been driven by other features of the respective disease (e.g. pruritus in TA890 or hyperkalaemia in TA599 or TA623). Among the 13 appraisals identified in the TLR, five used a cycle length longer than 3 months, up to 1 year (see CS Table 31). 

In the case of C3G, with the modelled eGFR decline, a three-month cycle length was considered sufficiently short to capture the impact on costs and QALYs, ensuring that patients sequentially progress through each CKD stage (without skipping CKD stages). From a clinical perspective, a three-month cycle length aligns with recommendations that the presence or progression of CKD should be confirmed based on eGFR measurements taken across a time period of at least 3 months.[33][38] Therefore, a three-month cycle length was considered appropriate.

## **B 3.  KRT initiation was assumed to be at eGFR ≤7.6 mL/min/1.73 m[2] (as stated in CS** 

## **Table 36), which is lower than the standard CKD Stage 5 threshold of <15 mL/min/1.73 m² (as stated below CS Figure 27).** 

- a) What is the clinical rationale for this specific threshold for KRT initiation (of ≤7.6 mL/min/1.73 m[2] )? 

The threshold for KRT initiation used in the economic model base case was derived as a weighted average of eGFR values at time of dialysis initiation or receipt of a pre-emptive transplant, based on UK Renal Registry data (see Section 3.3.2.2 of the CS). The UK Renal Registry, which collects and reports data annually on approximately 70,000 people receiving KRT in the UK, reports that dialysis was on average started at an eGFR value of approximately 7 mL/min/1.73 m[2] , while pre-emptive (without first receiving dialysis) transplants took place at an eGFR of approximately 10 mL/min/1.73 m[2] .[39] These values were in line with estimates from UK clinicians in the C3G advisory board.[4] For the economic model base case, the threshold to start KRT at an eGFR of 7.6 mL/min/1.73 m[2] was derived as a weighted average of the above values, accounting for 18.4% of UK patients with C3G receiving a pre-emptive transplant as their first KRT modality, based on RaDaR data.[12] The KRT threshold value used in the base case was confirmed to be reasonable by a UK clinical expert.[5] 

A scenario analysis presented in the CS set the KRT threshold value to 10 mL/min/1.73 m[2] , representing the average eGFR value at receipt of a pre-emptive transplant.[39] Further scenario analyses are presented in response to question B3 c) (Table 13), showing a limited impact of variation of the KRT threshold on cost-effectiveness results. 

- b) Please justify why a different threshold was used compared with previous NICE TAs, for instance in TA358 (considering tolvaptan) KRT would start at eGFR <8.5 ml/min/1.73 m[2] . 

TA358 used data specific to the indication under assessment, i.e. autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease, based on a publication from 2014.[26, 40] The threshold used in the CS for iptacopan in C3G was derived as a weighted average based on the latest available UK Renal Registry data from 2022, for patients with CKD overall.[39] The threshold used within the CS is thus based on the most recent available data from the UK, and while not C3G-specific, UK clinicians with experience in treating patients with C3G confirmed that the values used in the calculation and the resulting threshold value were appropriate.[4, 5] Scenario analyses showed a limited impact of variation of the KRT threshold on cost-effectiveness results (see response to question B3 c), Table 13). 

- c) Please provide an updated economic model and scenario analyses assuming eGFR values of 5 mL/min/1.73 m2 and 7 mL/min/1.73 m2 (or the midpoint of 6 mL/min/1.73 m2) as the threshold for KRT initiation, in line with NICE guideline NG107 which recommends starting replacement therapy “ _around 5 to 7 mL/min/1.73 m2_ ”. 

Please note that the recommendation in NICE guideline NG107 relates specifically to starting _dialysis_ , rather than KRT more broadly: “1.1.2 Consider starting dialysis when indicated by the impact of symptoms of uraemia on daily living, or biochemical measures or uncontrollable fluid 


Clarification questions 



<!-- page 228 -->

overload, or at an estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) of around 5 to 7 ml/min/1.73 m[2] if there are no symptoms.”[41] Based on the above, NICE guideline NG107 recommends starting dialysis at an eGFR of around 5 to 7 mL/min/1.73 m[2] if the person has no symptoms, or earlier (at a higher eGFR value) if symptoms require it.[41] 

Pre-emptive transplants, however, regularly take place at a higher eGFR value, as confirmed both by UK Renal Registry data (eGFR of approximately 10 mL/min/1.73 m[2] )[39] and UK clinicians treating patients with C3G.[4] Since the KRT threshold within the economic model is applied to all forms of KRT, the base case threshold value was derived as a weighted average of eGFR values for initiation of dialysis and receipt of a pre-emptive transplant (see response to question B3 a)). Based on the clinical advice received during preparation of the CS, a KRT threshold value of 7.6 mL/min/1.73 m[2] is considered the most appropriate for use within the model base case.[4, 5] 

The impact of changing the KRT threshold value is explored in Table 13, including the additional scenario analyses requested by the EAG, overall demonstrating that variation of the KRT threshold has limited impact on cost-effectiveness results (range of ICER change: *****% to *****%). Please note that all cost-effectiveness results presented in this document are based on a revised company base case which accounts for drug wastage, as further explained in the response to question B15. 

The economic model included with the CS provides functionality to flexibly amend the KRT threshold value, by entering alternative values in cell D62 of the Clinical data tab.

- d) In clinical practice some patients may start KRT at different eGFR values due to 

   - complications or comorbidities. Please explain whether and how this was 

   - implemented/considered in the economic model. 

As noted in response to question B3 a), the KRT threshold was derived from mean eGFR values at initiation of dialysis or receipt of a pre-emptive transplant, respectively, as reported in UK Renal Registry data.[39] Variation between individuals starting KRT is assumed to already be considered within these values. 

Variation of the KRT threshold in scenario analyses was seen to have limited impact on costeffectiveness results (Table 13). Please note that the updated economic model submitted with the clarification questions response now also considers the KRT threshold as a parameter in both the deterministic and probabilistic sensitivity analysis. As shown in Figure 18, the KRT threshold was not within the top 10 most influential parameters on the ICER within the DSA therefore is not considered a key model driver. 

- e) Various assumptions related to KRT were based on data from RaDaR, e.g. the percentage of patients receiving a pre-emptive transplant, the median time from dialysis to transplant and the median time to graft failure. The percentage of patients ineligible for a transplant were informed by Adelphi DSP survey data. Please justify why these assumptions were not informed by data from the clinical trials and provide an updated economic model and scenario analysis doing so. 

Given that most patients enrolled in APPEAR-C3G were in early stages of the disease, no meaningful clinical trial data are available to inform KRT inputs in the economic model. 

Parameters relating to dialysis and transplant are also highly specific to geography, with availability of donor organs, transplant protocols, wait times etc. all likely to vary from country to country. Consequently, use of data from the UK was considered most appropriate for economic modelling. RaDaR provides UK-specific data on KRT and time to graft failure in a C3G population,[12] is thus highly relevant to this submission, and was supported by a UK clinical expert as suitable source for these model inputs.[5] Data on transplant ineligibility was sourced from Adelphi DSP survey data, in the absence of RaDaR data, and varied in a scenario analysis presented in the CS, accounting for feedback received from UK clinicians (see CS, Sections 3.3.2.2 and 3.10.3). 

Since no clinical trial data are available for these parameters, no additional scenario analysis is provided. 

- f) Please elaborate on the implications of the responses to the preceding subquestions. 

The implications of the responses to the preceding sub-questions have been noted as part of the relevant responses themselves; please see above. 

- g) According to the CS : “ _people in the SoC arm receiving on average 1.9 transplants_ 

   - _over their lifetime, which a UK clinical expert considered plausible_ ”. Please provide 


Clarification questions 



<!-- page 231 -->

evidence (in addition to expert opinion) supporting the plausibility of this estimate. Moreover, please provide the average number of transplants for iptacopan and elaborate on the plausibility of this estimate. 

C3G commonly recurs following kidney transplantation, with recurrence rates reported in the literature to be between 55–85%, with a median time to recurrence of 14–28 months.[42-48] It is therefore expected that many patients experience graft failure (the median time from transplant to graft failure based on RaDaR data was 6.5 years),[12] and so may receive multiple transplants (please also note the response to question B4 further below). 

Amongst C3G prevalent RaDaR patients (n=240), 61 patients had received one transplant, 12 patients had received two transplants, and 2 patients had  received three or more transplants, at latest follow up.[12] However, this is a cross-sectional study, and given the young average age of the prevalent population (age at latest follow-up: mean [SD] 44.7 [21.3]; median [IQR] 42.8 [25.7, 63.8]) and short median time to graft failure as observed in RaDaR data,[12] it is therefore expected that some patients may receive further transplants during their lifetime. The average number of 1.9 transplants per patient over a lifetime in the SoC arm of the economic model was confirmed as a plausible prediction by clinical experts.[5, 8] 

The average number of transplants per patient over a lifetime in the iptacopan arm of the model (base case) is predicted as 1.46 transplants. A reduction in the mean number of transplants in the iptacopan arm compared with the SoC arm of the model was considered clinically plausible by experts, given that eGFR data from the APPEAR-C3G trial and its extension study suggested that iptacopan is able to slow the progression of C3G in a meaningful way.[4, 8, 10] By slowing the progression of C3G, iptacopan is expected to reduce the number of patients experiencing kidney failure, thereby reducing the number of patients requiring a transplant or dialysis.[8] However, clinical experts found it difficult to comment on the specific value of 1.46 transplants over a lifetime, also considering that the iptacopan arm in the model contains patients on iptacopan as well as patients who discontinued iptacopan during the model time horizon and subsequently receive SoC alone.[8] To further test the model’s sensitivity to variation of transplant model parameters, additional scenario analyses were conducted, which are presented in the response to clarification question B4 a). 

h) CS Table 36 provides KRT input parameters used in the CS base-case: 

- eGFR threshold for starting KRT: 7.6 mL/min/1.73 m2 

- Patients ineligible for a kidney transplant: 16.8% 

- Assumed maximum age for receipt of transplant: 80 years 

- Patients receiving a pre-emptive transplant as their first KRT modality: 18.4% 

- Median time from start of dialysis to transplant (excluding patients receiving a pre-emptive transplant): 1.9 years (8.7% probability per 3-month cycle of receiving a transplant)

<!-- page 232 -->

- Median time from transplant to graft failure: 6.5 years (2.6% probability per 3- month cycle of having graft failure) 

Please justify per input parameter whether it is clinically plausible according to expert opinion and provide supporting evidence. 

- The source and derivation of the KRT threshold are outlined in response to question B3 a). The eGFR threshold for KRT was first discussed as part of a UK clinical advisory board.[4] As kidney failure is defined as eGFR <15 mL/min/1.73 m[2] , an early draft of the economic model initially assumed that KRT would be started at that point, but clinical advisors stated that in practice KRT would only be started at a lower eGFR value.[4] In response to these discussions, the model was amended accordingly and a value of 7.6 mL/min/1.73 m[2] was derived from Renal Registry data as KRT threshold (see response to question B3 a)). This value was confirmed as plausible in further discussions with a clinical experts, who also highlighted the strength of the Renal Registry as a source[5, 8] 

- The value for transplant ineligibility is derived from C3G-specific Adelphi DSP survey data from the EU4 and the UK, which indicated that among 107 people with C3G in need of a transplant, 18 (16.8%) were considered ineligible to receive a transplant.[49] The proposed value of 16.8% of people being ineligible for a transplant was discussed during the aforementioned clinical advisory board.[4] Clinical experts commented that this value seemed high when considering ineligibility for a first transplant, however that the ineligible proportion of patients would increase for subsequent transplants.[4] This was further confirmed by a subsequent expert discussion, who explained that with increasing age, patients may develop more comorbidities and become more sensitised and thus ineligible for a transplant.[5] Therefore, a scenario analysis was included in the CS, assuming that 6.8% were ineligible for a first and 26.8% for a subsequent transplant (reflecting base case value +/- 10%, respectively), with minor impact on the ICER (****** using the updated model; see Table 51) 

- The maximum age for receipt of a transplant was assumed as 80 years in line with NICE TA942 in CKD;[27] while this value was not specifically discussed with clinical experts due to time constraints, this precedent supports the clinical plausibility of this assumption. In order to examine the effect of this limit, a scenario analysis explored having no age limit, which had a negligible effect on the ICER (******; see Table 51) 

- The number of patients receiving a pre-emptive transplant, median time from dialysis to transplant, and median time from transplant to graft failure were based on the C3G cohort in RaDaR,[12] and are therefore both UK- and C3G-specific, making these values highly plausible as model inputs. Clinical experts expressed support for the use of RaDaR inputs to inform modelling during conversations,[4, 8] and advisors further confirmed that the values used in the model were clinically plausible[5, 8] 

## **B 4.  The economic model allows for multiple transplants with graft failure leading** 

## **back to dialysis** 

- a) Please justify the assumption of repeated transplant, and whether this is consistent with clinical practice? Please also elaborate whether it would be more appropriate to cap the maximum number of graft failures and transplants? 


Clarification questions 



<!-- page 233 -->

The assumption that some people with C3G will require multiple transplants over their lifetime is consistent with clinical practice, as kidney transplantation does not address the underlying pathophysiology of C3G. C3G recurrence rates post-transplantation have been reported as 55– 85%, with a median time to recurrence of 14–28 months following transplantation.[42-48] As a consequence of C3G recurrence, the risk of graft failure in C3G is high, with reported graft failure rates of 50% among patients with disease recurrence, and a median time from transplant to graft failure of 77 months.[48] Similarly, RaDaR data from patients with C3G indicates a median time from first transplant to graft failure of 6.5 years (95% CI: 3.0, 8.1).[12] Following graft failure, patients are required to either return to dialysis or receive another kidney transplant. In RaDaR data, among 75 prevalent kidney transplant recipients with C3G, 14 (18.7%) had received two or more kidney transplants at the time of analysis;[12] given the young median age of the prevalent cohort (36.4 years) and short median time to graft failure (6.5 years), it is likely that several additional patients will receive more transplants over their lifetime. 

UK clinicians consulted during the preparation of the clarification questions response confirmed that patients with C3G commonly receive multiple transplants, given the young age at diagnosis and rapid progression to kidney failure.[8] They further advised that from a clinical perspective, it is not appropriate to cap the number of transplants a person with C3G may receive.[8] 

While they confirmed that an average of 1.9 transplants in the SoC arm over a patient’s lifetime, as predicted by the model, was plausible (see response to question B3 g) above), they recommended to check model predictions in terms of what proportion of patients received 3 or more transplants, and what was the maximum.[8] However, it was not possible to perform this check given the memoryless nature of a Markov cohort model structure. 

Therefore, two additional scenarios have been included to investigate the impact of a lower number of transplants on cost-effectiveness results (see Table 14). In the model base case, patients in the SoC arm receive on average 1.9 transplants over a lifetime. In one scenario, the percentage of patients eligible for a subsequent transplant was reduced from 83.18% in the base case to a value of 63.89% (cell D55 of the ‘Clinical data’ tab) to yield an average of 1.5 transplants in the SoC arm. (Please note that a calculation of the average number of transplants within the SoC arm has been added to the economic model and can be found in cell AI12 on the ‘SoC’ tab of the model.) This scenario reduced the ICER (******). In another scenario, transplants were effectively capped at 1, by setting the percentage of patients eligible for a subsequent transplant to 0%. This scenario reduced the ICER further (******* vs base case). These scenario analyses demonstrate that if the average number of transplants received by patients on SoC was lower in clinical practice than predicted in the model base case, the model base case overestimates the ICER of iptacopan compared with SoC alone. All scenario analyses relating to transplant inputs are summarised in the response to question B4 d). 

## b) How is the probability of repeated transplant estimated? 

Using RaDaR data from patients with C3G indicating a median time to graft failure posttransplant of 6.5 years,[12] a per cycle probability of graft failure of 2.6% was calculated and included in the model (see calculation in row 59 of the ‘Clinical data’ tab). Following graft failure, it was assumed that a proportion of patients were no longer eligible for transplantation; in the base case, this was assumed to be same as the proportion that were ineligible for a first transplant (16.8%; input as 83.18% eligible for a subsequent transplant in cell D55 of the ‘Clinical data’ tab). Subsequently, the per-cycle transplant probability of 8.7% (derived from RaDaR data from patients with C3G indicating a median time to transplant [excluding pre-emptive transplants] 


Clarification questions 



<!-- page 234 -->

of 1.9 years;[12] see calculation in row 58 of the ‘Clinical data’ tab) was applied to the transplant eligible patients. 

## c) Is there a distinction between early versus late graft failure in terms of transition probabilities? Please justify why (not)? 

While early graft failure is driven by acute rejection, graft failure in C3G also commonly occurs later on, due to the high rate of disease recurrence following transplantation. Details are provided in the CS, Section 1.3.4.5. Given the memoryless nature of a Markov cohort model structure which does not allow tracking time since receipt of a transplant for an individual patient, it was not possible to incorporate time-varying graft failure rates in the economic model. 

The median time to graft failure (point estimate 6.5 years) was varied in the deterministic sensitivity analysis (DSA) in line with the 95% CI values of the RaDaR analysis (3.0–8.1), with the impact on the ICER shown in Figure 31 of the CS. An updated tornado plot, incorporating the revised base case (see response to question B15) and updated DSA inputs, is presented in the response to question B22 (Figure 18).

## _**Intervention technology and comparators**_ 

## **B 5.  The comparator is SoC alone, which may include ACEi (ramipril; 47.3%), ARB (losartan; 52.7%), CS (prednisolone; 32.4%), MMF (36.5%), and SGLT2ni (dapagliflozin; 5.4%). The exact treatment regimens are modelled as components of the SoC basket, along with the proportion of patients receiving each component.** 

- a) Please clarify and justify whether these proportions are fixed over time, or whether they change over time (e.g. are patients allowed to switch between SoC treatments during disease progression)? 

As SoC is modelled as a single comparator comprising a basket of treatments, patients do not switch between individual SoC treatments over the model time horizon. The proportion of patients receiving each component of SoC was sourced from participant characteristics at baseline in APPEAR-C3G, and was assumed equal in the iptacopan and comparator arms.[9] The proportions were considered broadly reflective of UK clinical practice by clinical experts, except for SGLT2is,[4] which were therefore varied in a scenario analysis, resulting in a negligible increase of the ICER (******; see Table 51). 

The proportions of patients on the individual SoC components were fixed in the model over time (until start of KRT, see below). This is in line with the APPEAR-C3G protocol requiring patients to remain on a stable dose of their SoC background medications throughout the trial. Therefore, the modelling of SoC aligns with the trial data which informed model inputs for disease progression. 

When patients start KRT, all components of the SoC basket were assumed to be discontinued except for ACEi/ARB, since UK clinicians were aligned that these treatments would usually be continued while on KRT, due to their blood pressure-lowering effects.[4, 50] 

- b) Please clarify and justify whether patients can receive multiple SoC treatments simultaneously? Or monotherapy? For example, can a patient be on both an ACEi 

   - (e.g. ramipril) and an ARB (e.g. losartan)? 

Patients can receive multiple SoC treatments simultaneously, aligning with the current treatment pathway for C3G in the UK, presented in the CS (Figure 3) and reproduced below in Figure 2. 

Regarding ACEi and ARB use, guidelines generally recommend the use of one or the other.[33, 51] KDIGO guidelines note that these treatments have been used in combination in diabetic patients, however with uncertainty surrounding the efficacy and potential for increased risk of adverse events.[51] In APPEAR-C3G, two patients (2.7%) received both an ACEi and an ARB simultaneously.[9] 

Given that the proportion of patients on each component of SoC background medication was assumed equal in the iptacopan and comparator arms of the model – reflecting the comparison of ‘iptacopan + SoC’ vs ‘SoC alone’ –  adjustments to the proportion of treatments are expected to have a minimal effect on cost-effectiveness results. Overall, the SoC arm of the model is considered to provide a good representation of the use of the components of SoC in UK clinical practice (also see response to question B5 a) above).

## **Option 1. eGFR slope change analysis APPEAR-C3G by treatment group: historical data + APPEAR-C3G double-blind period** 

Data from the historical period and the 6-month double-blind period of APPEAR-C3G were used for this analysis. The analysis was carried out using a linear mixed effects model including treatment as a factor and time (analysis day from randomisation)/time after change point as a continuous covariate. The treatment by time interaction was fitted as fixed effect. Participant-level intercept and slope (time) was included in the model as random effects allowing the intercept and the slope to vary for each participant. The mean (95% CI) pre- and post-treatment slopes and the slope change (95% CI) were provided by treatment group, as well as for the difference between iptacopan and placebo groups. - b) Please provide step-by-step details of how the rates and probabilities of progression to the next state reported in Table 35 of the CS were calculated. 

The rates and probabilities of progression to the next state are based on the annual rate of eGFR progression for both the iptacopan and SoC arms, taken from Table 35 of the CS (in the base case: annual eGFR slope of −7.224 mL/min/1.73 m[2] /year for SoC and −0.289 mL/min/1.73 m[2] /year for iptacopan). 

As noted on page 103 of the CS, the time to move between states was defined as the time taken for eGFR to decline from the midpoint of the current CKD stage to the midpoint of the following stage. This approach assumes a uniform distribution of patients across a CKD stage and was used in the base case following validation with clinical and health economics experts.[5] The difference between midpoints was divided by the annual rate of eGFR progression to give the time to next state. The rate of progression was then calculated as the reciprocal of the time to next state. 

The probability of progression in each 3-month cycle was calculated as per the following formula:

Where rate of eGFR decline is the reciprocal of the time to next state, as above, 𝑝𝑝𝑖𝑖→1+1 is the probability of progressing from CKD stage 𝑖𝑖 to CKD stage 𝑖𝑖+ 1 and 𝑀𝑀𝑖𝑖 is the eGFR value at the midpoint of stage 𝑖𝑖 . Since CKD stage 1 is defined as eGFR ≥90 mL/min/1.73m[2] and thus has no upper bound, the mean eGFR value of patients in CKD stage 1 at baseline in APPEAR-C3G was used as the midpoint instead (116.9 mL/min/1.73m[2] ). 

To further facilitate the EAG’s understanding, please find a worked example for calculation of the probability of CKD stage 2 patients transitioning to CKD stage 3a with SoC in a 3-month cycle: 

- a) CKD stage 2 is defined as eGFR ≥60 to <90 mL/min/1.73m[2] . The CKD stage 2 midpoint is calculated as 75 mL/min/1.73m[2] (=60+(90-60)/2) 

- b) CKD stage 3a is defined as eGFR ≥45 to <60 mL/min/1.73m[2] . The CKD stage 3a midpoint is 52.5 mL/min/1.73m[2] (=45+(60-45)/2) 

- c) The difference between CKD stage 2 and CKD stage 3a midpoints is 22.5 mL/min/1.73m[2] (=75-52.5) 

- d) With an annual eGFR decline of −7.224 mL/min/1.73m[2] in the SoC arm, it takes 3.11 years to progress from the CKD stage 2 midpoint to the CKD stage 3a midpoint (=22.5/7.224)

- e) This gives an annual rate of progression from CKD stage 2 to CKD stage 3a of 0.32 (=1/3.11) 

- f) This results in a probability of 7.71% for progressing from CKD stage 2 to CKD stage 3a in a 3-month model cycle (=1-EXP(-0.32/4)) 

- c) Please provide an updated economic model and scenario analysis: 

   - I. Using RaDaR data to inform treatment effectiveness of SoC. 

   - II. Apply the iptacopan treatment effect that was observed in the double-blind period (i.e. option 1 of CS Table 34) to SoC as modelled in I. to inform treatment effectiveness of iptacopan. 

The scenario analysis has been conducted as requested by the EAG, with eGFR slope inputs shown in Table 15 and cost-effectiveness results shown in Table 16. From RaDaR data, an eGFR slope of –4.0 mL/min/1.73 m[2] /year (all C3G patients, n=139) was available to inform disease progression in the SoC arm.[12] Application of an iptacopan treatment effect of 3.053 mL/min/1.73 m[2] /year (based on the 6-month double-blind period of APPEAR-C3G) to the RaDaR slope results in an iptacopan slope of −0.947 mL/min/1.73 m[2] /year. 

When reviewing the eGFR slope inputs and resulting model outputs with regards to clinical plausibility, two UK clinicians consulted by Novartis during preparation of the clarification questions response expressed concerns regarding combining data from two different sources and differences in the included populations.[8] While APPEAR-C3G enrolled patients with UPCR ≥1 g/g (despite treatment with a maximally tolerated ACEi/ARB), the RaDaR eGFR slope was generated based on all C3G patients in the registry, including patients who had milder disease (UPCR <1 g/g). Given that high UPCR indicates an increased risk of rapid eGFR decline, clinicians highlighted that for the subgroup of patients reflecting the APPEAR-C3G inclusion criteria (UPCR ≥1 g/g), they would expect a steeper eGFR slope with SoC than informed by the RaDaR analysis in all C3G patients.[8] As this represents an important limitation of the requested scenario analysis,[8] results should be interpreted with caution. 

Please note that based on clinical advice,[8] this scenario analysis uses patient characteristics from RaDaR (as reflected in CS Table 33), in alignment with the source of the SoC eGFR slope.

- d) Please provide an updated economic model and scenario analysis: 

   - I. Using the pre-iptacopan data (i.e. option 2 of CS Table 34), including up to 2.5 years of following (N=74) to inform treatment effectiveness of SoC. 

   - II. Apply the iptacopan treatment effect that was observed in the double-blind period (i.e. option 1 of CS Table 34) to SoC as modelled in I. to inform treatment effectiveness of iptacopan. 

The scenario analysis has been conducted as requested by the EAG, with eGFR slope inputs shown in Table 15 and cost-effectiveness results shown in Table 16. Combining the SoC eGFR slope of –7.224 mL/min/1.73 m[2] /year (pre-iptacopan, APPEAR-C3G population) with the iptacopan treatment effect of 3.053 mL/min/1.73 m[2] /year (based on the 6-month double-blind period of APPEAR-C3G) results in an iptacopan slope of –4.171 mL/min/1.73 m[2] /year. 

Two UK clinicians consulted by Novartis during preparation of the clarification questions response cautioned against combining SoC and iptacopan eGFR slopes from different analyses.[8] The clinicians flagged that a predicted iptacopan slope of –4.171 mL/min/1.73 m[2] /year was inconsistent with the trial data, which suggested stabilisation of eGFR decline with iptacopan (e.g. on-iptacopan slope for APPEAR-C3G patients including extension study data: −0.289 mL/min/1.73 m[2] /year; see Table 15).[8] They further highlighted that a predicted slope of –4.171 mL/min/1.73 m[2] /year indicated steeper eGFR decline with iptacopan than with placebo based on the 6-month double-blind period (−3.079 mL/min/1.73 m[2] /year; see Table 15).[8] In addition, it was noted that this would also result in modelling steeper eGFR decline with iptacopan than with SoC based on RaDaR data (−4.0 mL/min/1.73 m[2] /year; see Table 15).[12] 

On that basis, clinicians considered the iptacopan eGFR slope used in this scenario analysis implausible and not supported by the available trial data,[8] and results of this scenario analysis should be interpreted in that context.

Clarification questions 



<!-- page 245 -->

- e) In the CS, it was stated that “While the rate of eGFR decline may vary over the course of disease, the sample size of the iptacopan trials in C3G did not permit estimation of CKD stage-dependent eGFR decline rates. As such, a simplifying assumption that speed of progression is independent of CKD stage and constant over the course of disease was applied”. Please elaborate on the clinical plausibility of this assumption and the implications on the modelled outcomes (i.e. health state costs, particularly for dialysis and transplants, and health state utilities). 

The clinical plausibility of the assumed constant speed of eGFR progression was discussed with clinical experts as part of a UK clinical advisory board. Clinicians noted that while eGFR slope would be expected to fluctuate, the overall path of disease in C3G is a progressive decline and therefore a linear slope was a reasonable simplification. Advisors also noted that in C3G, eGFR decline does not tend to get steeper as patients get closer to kidney failure, unlike other kidney diseases.[4] Two UK clinicians consulted during preparation of the clarification questions response reconfirmed that an assumption of a linear slope was reasonable and in line with how eGFR data was generally considered in research in nephrology.[8] 

- f) Despite the sample size issue (combining CKD stages, i.e. stages 3A and B and stage 4 and 5, could be considered), please provide an updated economic model and scenario analyses exploring 

   - I. CKD stage-dependent eGFR decline rates from the iptacopan trials in C3G. If not deemed feasible based on the data currently available, please use other literature or evidence (e.g. external data and/or expert opinion).

Please note that an analysis breaking down the data into further CKD stages was not considered feasible due to very small patient numbers in higher CKD stages (also see response to question B7 g) below).

Both the analysis of iptacopan trial data and the RaDaR analysis have the limitation that eGFR decline rates are stratified by a patient’s CKD stage at baseline, rather than providing the rate of decline while in a specific CKD stage (as would be required as a model input). Such an analysis was deemed infeasible for iptacopan trial data due to sample size and the small number of patients in higher CKD stages (see also response to question B7 g) below). With regards to the data available from RaDaR, clinicians did not consider it plausible that eGFR slope would be less steep for patients with baseline CKD stage 3b (eGFR 30–45 mL/min/1.73 m[2] ) compared to patients diagnosed in other CKD stages, and highlighted the small sample size of the individual CKD stage subgroups.[8] Since the available data were not considered suitable for use in the economic model, and clinicians had further confirmed that an assumption of linear eGFR decline over the disease course was reasonable (see response to question B7 e) above), no scenario analysis was implemented in the model.

- II. Time-dependent eGFR decline rates from the iptacopan trials in C3G. If not deemed feasible based on the data currently available, please use other 

   - literature or evidence (e.g. external data and/or expert opinion). 

eGFR decline rates for the double-blind and open-label periods of APPEAR-C3G are presented in the response to question A7 (Table 5). However, as highlighted, UK clinicians advised that a time frame of 6 months may be too short to robustly estimate changes in eGFR,[4] therefore, these estimates by treatment period (each based on 6 months of data) should be interpreted with caution, with eGFR slope analyses based on longer follow-up considered more robust and meaningful by clinical advisors.[4, 8] Therefore, no scenario analysis was implemented in the model. 

- g) Generating transition probabilities from observed transitions between CKD stages was not considered due to the small sample size and low patient numbers in more advanced CKD stages at baseline. Despite the small sample size and low patient numbers, please provide an updated economic model and explore this approach in a scenario analysis. 

Based on the EAG’s request, generation of transition probabilities based on observed transitions between CKD stages in APPEAR-C3G has been attempted, with outputs provided in the following tables. Table 19 and Table 20 present the transition probabilities per 3-month model cycle based on observed CKD stage transitions in APPEAR-C3G for the SoC arm (based on placebo data) and the iptacopan arm, respectively. Due to placebo arm patients switching to iptacopan after the completion of the 6-month double-blind period, SoC transitions could only be informed by 6 months of data (two cycles). Data from patients allocated to the placebo arm following switch to iptacopan at the start of the open-label period were combined with the iptacopan arm data for months 0 to 3 and months 3 to 6, in order to use all available oniptacopan data. 

As visible in the tables below, the patient counts are very low, especially in more advanced CKD stages, resulting in non-meaningful transition probabilities. In the SoC arm (Table 19), based on transition probabilities generated from observed transitions in 36 patients over 6 months, patients in CKD stage 1 or 2 at baseline never progress beyond CKD stage 2, while patients in CKD stage 3a at baseline  remain in 3a indefinitely and patients in CKD stage 3b at baseline remain in 3b indefinitely. If used in the economic model, patients on SoC would therefore never progress to kidney failure, which is implausible and inconsistent with available real-world data from multiple sources indicating a median time to kidney failure of 10 years with current SoC. Data for iptacopan (Table 20) is available from APPEAR-C3G for overall 4 model cycles, with the full trial population (N=74) contributing data for transitions for the first 6 months (due to the placebo arm cross-over); however, transitions from CKD stage 3a or higher are still only informed by singledigit patient numbers and thus not considered robust. Therefore, this approach was not considered suitable to provide valid transition probabilities for economic modelling, due to sample size limitations inherent to evidence generation in ultra-rare diseases, and thus not implemented as a scenario analysis. 

Previous appraisals in CKD which utilised the above approach benefitted from substantially larger sample sizes in their respective clinical trials; for example, the pivotal trial for finerenone in adults with CKD and type 2 diabetes included 5,674 patients (TA877)[53] and the pivotal trial for 


Clarification questions 



<!-- page 248 -->

dapagliflozin in adults with CKD included 4,304 patients (TA775),[29] compared to 74 patients in the APPEAR-C3G trial informing this submission. 

However, it should be highlighted that even though the approach to generating transition probabilities in this submission differs, it equally relies on observed eGFR data. While deriving transition probabilities based on observed CKD stage transitions utilises eGFR as categorical data, eGFR slope – as used in this submission – utilises eGFR as continuous data. Therefore, the selected eGFR slope approach incorporates all observed changes in eGFR, rather than only observed changes in eGFR which resulted in a patient crossing the threshold to another CKD stage. 

Overall, the selected eGFR slope approach can be considered to use data more efficiently, which is especially important with a small sample size, as in this submission.

## **B 8.  Priority question. The iptacopan discontinuation rate (0.063 per year, with a per cycle probability of discontinuation of 1.57%.) among patients who have not reached kidney failure was based on all-cause treatment discontinuation of iptacopan in the pooled APPEAR-C3G, Phase 2 and extension studies (broad safety set).** 

- a) Please comment on the (clinical) plausibility of the iptacopan discontinuation rate in the company’s base-case. 

The iptacopan discontinuation rate was based on all-cause treatment discontinuation data from the broad safety set, including APPEAR-C3G, the Phase 2 study and the open-label extension study, with overall 189.8 patient-years of exposure.[17] One discontinuation due to death (among overall 13 discontinuations) was excluded from the calculation of the discontinuation rate for the economic model, since mortality was modelled separately. Given that the discontinuation rate was derived from all available iptacopan trial evidence in C3G, it represents the best source of data. Clinical experts considered the discontinuation rate plausible and supported its use for the economic model base case.[8] 

- b) Please justify and provide evidence for the assumption of modelling the iptacopan discontinuation rate to be constant over time. 

Discontinuations were observed throughout the clinical trials, with no marked accumulation of either early or late discontinuations. Therefore, a constant discontinuation rate was considered a reasonable assumption for the company base case. However, time-varied discontinuation rates are explored in the response to question B8 e).

## **B 9.  Priority question. In the company’s base-case, a constant iptacopan treatment effect was assumed over the model time horizon while patients remained on treatment.** 

- a) Please justify the assumption of no treatment waning, i.e. that there is a constant lifetime iptacopan treatment effect. 

In C3G, overactivation of the complement alternative pathway leads to deposition of C3 within the glomeruli of the kidneys, triggering inflammation and glomerular injury.[7] Iptacopan is a proximal complement inhibitor that specifically binds Factor B. This selectively blocks alternative pathway overactivation by inhibiting alternative pathway-related C3 convertase activity, leading to decreased cleavage of C3 and reduced C3 deposition in the kidney.[2] 

The ability of iptacopan to inhibit the alternative pathway was assessed with APPEAR-C3G through the examination of circulating biomarker levels, including serum C3 and alternative pathway activity, presented on pages 65 and 66 of the CS. Iptacopan demonstrated rapid and sustained effects on multiple biomarkers for complement alternative pathway dysregulation.[9] This confirms the disease-modifying effect of iptacopan which translated into effects on proteinuria and eGFR, which were sustained throughout APPEAR-C3G and the open-label extension study.[9, 10] 

In the model validation call conducted prior to the CS, the clinical advisor explained that the pharmacological effect of iptacopan will not change over time and therefore, the treatment effect is not expected to wane.[5] This was again confirmed in a call with two clinicians during preparation of the clarification questions response.[8] The clinicians explained that the pathophysiology of C3G (complement alternative pathway overactivation leading to C3 deposition in the glomeruli) is well understood and does not change over time. Similarly, the mechanism of action of iptacopan (blocking complement alternative pathway overactivation and reducing C3 deposition in the glomeruli) and how it targets C3G is also well understood, therefore, the experts concluded that there was no plausible scientific rationale to expect the pharmacological effect of iptacopan to wane over time.[8] 

Treatment effect waning was not considered to apply in the appraisal of iptacopan in paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria (PNH; TA1000).[19] This was consistent with previous NICE appraisals of other complement inhibitors in PNH (TA698 and TA778),[55, 56] as well as in atypical haemolytic uraemic syndrome (aHUS).[57, 58] Complement inhibitors in aHUS were also cited as an example by the consulted clinicians, where they had not observed evidence of treatment effect waning in their extensive personal clinical experience.[8] 

Clinicians further highlighted the strength of the pooled iptacopan C3G trial analyses, with up to 4.7 years of data available from Phase 2 trial patients who continued iptacopan treatment in the open-label extension study, suggesting stabilisation of eGFR;[8] these data are summarised in Section 2.8 of the CS and utilised in a scenario analysis in the economic model (see CS Table 34, option 3; scenario results reported in CS Table 60). They further emphasised that disease progression in C3G patients treated with iptacopan does not necessarily equate to treatment effect waning.[8] While the trial data suggest stabilisation of eGFR with iptacopan, this represents an average and outcomes of individual patients will vary. For example, in patients who already have established fibrosis when starting iptacopan, eGFR is expected to decline since irreversible 


Clarification questions 



<!-- page 258 -->

kidney damage and chronic kidney disease are already present, but iptacopan is still expected to lead to better outcomes for these patients compared to current SoC.[8] 

Based on their understanding of the disease and the mode of action of iptacopan, available trial data, and their clinical experience with iptacopan and other complement inhibitors, the consulted clinicians considered it inappropriate to incorporate non-evidence-based waning assumptions into the economic modelling.[8] 

- b) Please provide time-to-event data on CKD progression (i.e., CKD progression-free survival) for iptacopan + SoC versus SoC alone. Specifically, please analyse time-toevent data separately for progression to CKD stages 2, 3, 4, and 5, as well as for time to dialysis, death, or transplant:

In addition, the number of participants in later CKD stages at baseline was very small. Since the analysis of CKD stage transition probabilities conducted for question B7 g) did not yield meaningful results, it was considered that the same limitations would apply to timeto-event analyses on the same set of data. Therefore, the requested analyses were not considered feasible.

## _**Adverse events**_ 

## **B 10. In the CS, data from the pooled safety set informed serious AEs (SAEs)** 

## **suspected to be related to iptacopan which were included in the analyses.** 

- a) Please explain the rationale and thresholds (severity grade 3 or 4) of including SAEs “suspected to be related to iptacopan”, with severity grades likewise requested by the health economics advisor from the CS “Clinical and Model Validation for Iptacopan in C3G”. 

Severity grade ≥3 corresponds to an AE classification as “severe” in the iptacopan C3G clinical trial reporting. In the double-blind, placebo-controlled period of APPEAR-C3G, 2 severe AEs occurred in the iptacopan arm and one severe AE in the placebo arm, with none of the reported severe AEs occurring in more than one patient.[9] 

To ensure the impact of AEs associated with iptacopan which would be likely to affect QALYs and costs was captured in the model, _serious AEs (SAEs)_ suspected to be related to iptacopan were included. SAEs were defined in the trial protocol as any AEs that are fatal, life-threatening, result in persistent or significant disability/incapacity, constitute a congenital anomaly/birth defect, require inpatient hospitalisation (or prolongation of existing hospitalisation), or are medically significant in the sense that they jeopardise the participant or may require medical intervention to prevent one of the outcomes listed above.[59] On that basis, SAEs were selected because they were expected to have meaningful disutility and cost implications; this approach aligns with how AEs were modelled in the NICE appraisal of iptacopan for its first indication, PNH (TA1000).[19] 

The rationale for only modelling SAEs _suspected to be related to iptacopan_ followed the decision to use data from the broad safety set, rather than the controlled safety set (see response to question B10 b) below). In controlled data with a sufficiently large sample size, AEs that are not associated with the intervention or comparator but occur by chance would be expected to occur at equal rates in both arms of the trial, with effects of these AEs on QALYs and costs ultimately cancelling out in the economic model. Since the broad safety set only reports on iptacopan AEs and does not contain a control arm, it only provided data for modelling AEs for iptacopan (with no AEs modelled for the SoC comparator arm). Use of _all_ SAEs from the broad safety set in the model would have attributed also AEs that occurred by chance to iptacopan. The list of SAEs which occurred in the broad safety set was reviewed with two UK clinicians, who considered it unjustified to assign events which were classified as unrelated to iptacopan (such as [cocaine] 


Clarification questions 



<!-- page 260 -->

overdose, appendicitis or tendon rupture) to iptacopan in the economic model.[8] Given the available evidence, the decision to model only SAEs suspected to be related to iptacopan – while not modelling any AEs for the comparator arm – was supported by clinicians and is thus considered appropriate.[8] 

A new scenario analysis explores the impact of modelling _severe_ AEs (i.e. grade ≥3) suspected to be related to iptacopan; please see below in the response to question B10 d). 

## b) Please explain why data from the broad safety set, having pooled trial populations was used instead of the controlled safety set. 

The controlled safety set provides only six months of data as the duration of the double-blind, placebo-controlled period of APPEAR-C3G was limited to six months.[9] On the other hand, the broad safety set includes all available iptacopan safety data from all iptacopan trials in C3G, with overall 189.8 patient-years of exposure.[17] 

Using the controlled safety set would have excluded all iptacopan AEs which occurred after Month 6 of APPEAR-C3G, and all AEs which occurred in the Phase 2 study and the open-label extension study, from the analysis. Therefore, using the broad safety set as the more comprehensive set of data with substantially longer follow-up (up to 4.7 years iptacopan treatment duration) is a more conservative approach to fully capture the safety profile of iptacopan in the economic model. 

## c) Please explain the simplifying approach of standardising all SAEs to pneumonia/sepsis (CS, Clinical and Model Validation for Iptacopan in C3G). 

As noted on page 107 of the CS and presented in Table 23 (CS Table 38), almost all SAEs suspected to be related to iptacopan were infections with encapsulated bacteria (an AE of special interest for iptacopan) leading to pneumonia or consequences thereof such as sepsis.[17] Therefore pneumonia/sepsis was considered accordingly in the economic analysis for AE disutilities and costs, calculating a weighted average across all severity scores of relevant NHS reference cost categories. While acknowledged as a simplification, it is expected that this approach appropriately captures AE disutilities and costs associated with iptacopan treatment. In addition, sensitivity analysis (DSA and scenario analysis) presented in the CS demonstrated very limited impact of AEs on cost-effectiveness results (see CS Section 3.10).

## _**Health-related quality of life**_ 

## **B 11. Priority question. EQ-5D-5L data in the APPEAR-C3G study were mapped to EQ-** 

## **5D-3L and health state utility values were estimated using a mixed effects linear model with repeated measures.** 

- a) Please argue why a mixed effects linear model with repeated measures is appropriate in this context. 

When analysing longitudinal data, where there are repeated measures for each subject, observations of EQ-5D within each subject will be correlated, as a patient with a higher EQ-5D score at one time point it likely to have a higher EQ-5D score at later time points. This correlation violates the independence assumption of traditional fixed-effects models. Mixed effects models account for this correlation using random effects that quantify variation among subjects and serve to describe cluster-specific trends over time.[60, 61] 

For deriving utility values from EQ-5D data collected across multiple time points in APPEARC3G, a model allowing for a random intercept for each subject was used to account for intrasubject correlations. Mixed effects models have been widely used to analyse utility data for HTA submissions, including in the previous NICE appraisal of iptacopan for paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria (PNH; TA1000).[19] 

- b) Please clarify to which extent repeated measurements were captured in the model, as CS Table 41 does not report a time variable. 

The mixed effects model was used to account for repeated measurements for each subject, via the inclusion of subject-level random effects. A time variable was not included in the model. Table 26 presents the outputs of a model that accounts for time-effects by including fixed-effects covariates for each visit compared to baseline. The impact of including time-effects on other covariates is minimal.

## iii. Please explain the covariate selection process. 

Covariates considered in the regression model included CKD stage, age, sex and baseline EQ5D. CKD stage was included as this is used to define the economic model health states; however, in the regression model that treated CKD stages 1 and 2 as separate, the predicted utility value for CKD stage 2 was higher than for CKD stage 1, which was not deemed clinically plausible. As such, CKD stages 1 and 2 were combined, as outlined in the CS (see Section 3.4.1). 

Age and sex were included to account for any imbalances across health states, as they are known predictors of HRQoL. Similarly, baseline EQ-5D was included in the model to address any imbalances in EQ-5D at baseline. While age was not significant in the model (see CS Table 41), as it is a known predictor of HRQoL it was retained in the final model, as patients in CKD stage 1 were younger than those in other stages. 

Treatment allocation was also considered as a covariate in the model; however this was not associated with a significant impact on HRQoL (p=*****) and so was not incorporated into the final model. No further covariates were considered for the model, as the sample size from APPEAR-C3G was small, and CKD stage, age and sex were considered the most relevant determinants of HRQoL for the model. 

Table 28 presents the outputs of two models that only include CKD stage as covariates. Model 1 includes CKD stages 1 to 4 separately; Model 2 combines CKD stages 1 and 2.

## **B 12. Priority question. For CKD stages 1 to 4, utility values were informed by EQ-5D-** 

## **5L data from the APPEAR-C3G study.** 

- a) Please discuss the representativeness of the utility values derived from the APPEAR- 

   - C3G study for the adult C3G patient population, considering available literature and other evidence. 

UK clinicians participating in an advisory board confirmed that the APPEAR-C3G trial population was reflective of C3G patients who would be anticipated to receive iptacopan in UK clinical practice.[4] Therefore, utility values derived from EQ-5D-5L collected in the APPEAR-C3G trial can generally be considered representative for the modelled population. 

To confirm the most suitable utility values for parameterising the economic model, Novartis discussed several options  (all derived from EQ-5D) with a UK clinician and a UK health economist during a validation call:[5] 

- Option 1: APPEAR-C3G trial data, based on regression model 1 (with separate CKD stages 1 and 2; see CS Table 41) 

- Option 2: APPEAR-C3G trial data, based on regression model 2 (with CKD stages 1+2 pooled; see CS Table 41) 

- Option 3: Adelphi DSP C3G (Lafayette et al. 2024)[62] 

- Option 4: Jesky et al. 2016[63] 

Details on these options are presented below in Table 30.

In the discussion with advisors,[5] it was noted that utility values generated from APPEAR-C3G using regression model 1 resulted in CKD stage 2 having a slightly higher utility value (0.92) than CKD stage 1 (0.91). Combining CKD stages 1 and 2 in regression model 2 resolved this implausibility. Utility values generated from the Adelphi DSP(as reported by Lafayette et al. 2024) also reflected data from patients with C3G;[64] however, the number of observations was substantially smaller than the number of observations in APPEAR-C3G, and utility values were considered implausible (for example,  the CKD stage 3A utility value was higher than CKD stages 1 and 2; see Table 30). In addition, utilities were generated using a US tariff. Jesky et al. 2016 was not specific to patients in C3G but a study in general CKD, with a substantially older population.[63] 

Advisors agreed that APPEAR-C3G option 2 was appropriate to inform utility values for CKD stages 1–4. In the absence of data from APPEAR-C3G for people in CKD stage 5, advisors suggested using data from Jesky et al. 2016 to inform the utility value for CKD stage 5 (preKRT).[5] 

Based on these discussions, data from APPEAR-C3G are considered an appropriate and representative source for utility data used within the model base case. A scenario analysis (presented in the CS) used utility values for CKD stages 1-5 from Jesky et al. 2016. 

b) Please justify pooling CKD stage 1 and 2 instead of keeping them separate, especially since they represent the stages with the highest number of measurements. Please discuss the possibility that later stage measurements are implausibly high. 

In the APPEAR-C3G data, the observed mean utility value for CKD stage 1 (0.883) was deemed implausible, since it was lower than the mean utility value for CKD stage 2 (0.926) (see CS Table 40). A mixed effects linear model for repeated measures fit to the data also resulted in a slightly higher utility value for CKD stage 2 (0.92) than for CKD stage 1 (0.91), though the difference was not statistically significant (see CS Table 41). Pooling utility values for CKD stages 1 and 2 in the utility regression model led to a plausible pattern of utility values by CKD stage (see CS Table 41 and Table 43). 

Several precedents for pooling utility values across CKD stages 1 and 2 exist; in fact, all previous NICE appraisals in CKD which required utility values for CKD stages 1 and 2 used the same utility values for both health states, as outlined below 

- TA942[27] , TA937[28] and TA623[67] used utility values as reported by Jesky et al. 2016, which pooled CKD stages 1 and 2 when deriving utility values (refer to Table 3 in the publication, ‘Stage G1/G2’)[63] 

- TA358[26] used utility values as reported by Gorodetskaya et al. 2005, which pooled CKD stages 1 and 2 when deriving utility values (refer to Table 2 in the publication, ‘GFR ≥60’)[68] 

- TA877[53] and T775[29] derived utility values for use in the appraisal from the respective trial data, pooling CKD stage 1 and 2 values in the utilised regression model 

Details on the utilities used in these appraisals, along with other previous NICE appraisals in CKD as identified in a targeted literature review (TLR), are presented in Table 11 of Appendix F of the CS. 


Clarification questions 



<!-- page 276 -->

With regards to a possibility that utility values for later CKD stages are implausibly high, this was not a concern raised during validation of the utility values with experts.[5] After adjusting utility values reported by Jesky et al. 2016[63] to the age and gender distribution of the APPEAR-C3G population (as described in CS Section 3.4.4.1 ), utility values were similar to the utility values generated from APPEAR-C3G data (see Table 31 below). A scenario analysis included in the CS used the Jesky et al. 2016 utility values for CKD stages 1–5 and was associated with a small improvement of the ICER (****** with updated model; see Table 51).

- c) Please discuss the plausibility of the reported, relatively high utility values for the study population, especially in earlier CKD stages when compared to the UK age- and sexmatched general population utility for the study population (CS Table 43). 

Early stages of CKD tend to be associated with a limited impact on HRQoL. As noted in the response to question B12 b), the utility values derived from APPEAR-C3G were similar to those reported in Jesky et al. 2016,[63] after adjusting for age differences between the populations; therefore supporting the plausibility of the APPEAR-C3G utility values used in the economic model base case. 

## **B 13. The CS used age adjustments in the economic model to address “differences between the source population’s age for literature-based utility values and the baseline of the modelled population”. This is particularly relevant since the CS population is substantially younger (baseline mean age in economic model: 27.9 years) than those in the studies identified in the HRQoL literature review.** 

- a) The study by Lee et al. (2005) informed dialysis and post-transplant health state utilities in the base case, with patients aged between 51.6 years and 64.3 years at time of survey completion, causing relatively low dialysis and post-transplant utilities when compared to prior CKD stages. Please discuss the validity of the utility values from Lee et al. (2005), especially in terms of comorbidities apparent in later ages and the remark by the clinical advisor, considering the post-transplant health state “relatively low” and supporting alternatively the use of Liem et al.’s value (2008) (CS, Clinical and Model Validation for Iptacopan in C3G). 


Clarification questions 



<!-- page 277 -->

KRT is associated with a considerable impact on HRQoL, including from significant potential complications. Dialysis is associated with fatigue, hypotension (low blood pressure), itchy skin and muscle cramps.[69] Kidney transplantation is associated with multiple short-term risks including surgical complications, bleeding, post-transplant infection, and acute rejection of the transplanted kidney.[70] The longer-term risks of transplants similarly include infections, organ rejection, and recurrent disease,[70, 71] which is particularly apparent in C3G. Kidney transplant recipients may also experience significant side effects and risks associated with long-term use of immunosuppressive regimens to prevent graft rejection, such as increased risk of cancer.[70-73] As well as the negative HRQoL impacts of these complications, the independence of people with C3G is limited with dialysis a very time-consuming treatment which puts a burden on the daily life for patients, their families and carers.[37, 74, 75] 

The utility values from Lee et al. 2005 are considered appropriate, as they reflect the impact of KRT on HRQoL in a UK population (N=416) using EQ-5D-3L and a UK tariff.[76] Lee et al. 2005 utilities for dialysis and post-transplant health states were used in seven previous NICE appraisals in various chronic kidney diseases (see Table 34), including a recent appraisal in IgA nephropathy (TA937), which also affects a younger population.[28] 

To account for the differences between the population’s age in the Lee et al. 2005 study and the baseline age of the modelled population, the utilities used in the model were age-adjusted (see CS Section 3.4.4.1 for further details). Therefore, it is expected that the impact of the different population ages in Lee et al. 2005 versus the population in the CS would be limited, with ageadjustments accounting for differences in age-related comorbidities.[76] The approach for age adjustments was also validated with a UK health economist.[5] 

While the clinical advisor stated that the post-transplant utility value from Lee et al. 2005 was relatively low, they also highlighted expected variation in HRQoL between patients, since not all patients have good outcomes following a transplant; for example, some patients experience surgical complications.[5] 

As requested by the EAG, a scenario analysis is provided using the post-transplant utility value from Liem at al. 2008,[77] with results in Table 32 showing an increase in the ICER by ******. Liem et al. 2008 was considered as potential source for utilities during development of the CS, but validation with clinical and health economic experts highlighted that its methodology (a metaanalysis of EQ-5D-based utility values reported across multiple international studies which did not consistently provide information on the value sets used) introduced significant uncertainty.[5, 77] Experts therefore preferred using utility values from Lee et al. 2005, as it was a UK study.[5]

This is the same study as that referred to in B13 b). Lafayette et al. 2024 was a congress abstract;[62] Sinha et al. is a submitted manuscript (Novartis data on file).[78] The submitted manuscript only reports EQ-5D utility values for eGFR <30 mL/min/1.73m[2 ] and >30 mL/min/1.73m[2] , but not by CKD stage. In addition, the limitation that a US tariff was used remains. Therefore, the submitted manuscript was not considered to provide suitable data for cross-validation of utility values.

NICE technology appraisals (TAs) in chronic kidney diseases with final guidance published in the last 10 years were reviewed in a TLR conducted in December 2024 and summarised in the CS and its appendices (see response to B26 for further details). The utility results of the TLR have been reproduced here for convenience. Overall, 13 TAs met the eligibility criteria and were included in the TLR. Clarification questions 



<!-- page 291 -->

- e) Please cross validate the utility values in the current company base-case with the utility values sourced in b), c) and d). 

Utility values generated from APPEAR-C3G trial data or identified in the TLR of previous NICE TAs (see Appendix F of the CS) were reviewed with UK clinical and health economic experts with regards to their suitability for use in the economic model.[5] For CKD stages 1–4, utility values based on EQ-5D-5L collected in patients with C3G in the APPEAR-C3G trial (baseline mean age 27.9 years) were preferred for the base-case analysis, utilising values estimated with the regression model pooling CKD stages 1 and 2.[5] Jesky et al. 2016,[63] a UK study which collected EQ-5D-3L data from 745 patients with CKD of any aetiology and a median age of 64 years, was considered appropriate to inform the utility value for CKD stage 5 (pre-KRT), for which no data were available from APPEAR-C3G.[5] A scenario analysis explored the impact of using utility values from Jesky et al. 2016 for CKD stages 1–5 (pre-KRT).[63] Utility values from the Adelphi DSP, as reported by Lafayette et al. 2024,[62] were not deemed clinically plausible (see response to question B13 b)) and therefore not used in the analysis. 

To inform dialysis and post-transplant utilities in the economic model, experts considered the values published by Lee et al. 2005,[76] which were used in 7 previous NICE appraisals, as most appropriate.[5] Lee et al. 2005, a UK study, estimated utility values for different KRT modalities from EQ-5D-3L collected in 416 patients (mean age 55.5 years in women, 58.2 years in men),[76] using a UK tariff;[91] utility values for haemodialysis (HD), peritoneal dialysis (PD), and posttransplant were reported as 0.44, 0.53, and 0.71, respectively.[76] For the dialysis utility in the economic model, a weighted average was calculated according to the proportion of patients receiving each type of dialysis, sourced from a RaDaR analysis in patients with C3G (HD: 85.3%; PD: 14.7% [APD: 11.8%, CAPD: 2.9%]).[12] 

Utility values from Liem et al. 2008[77] and Li et al. 2017[92] were also discussed with clinical and health economics experts but not considered suitable for use in the model.[5] The methodology of Liem et al. 2008[77] was considered to introduce uncertainty, since it is a meta-analysis of EQ-5Dbased utility values reported across multiple international studies which did not consistently provide information on the value sets used; experts therefore preferred using Lee et al. 2005, given that it was a UK study.[5] In addition, the small difference in the utility values of HD (0.56) and PD (0.58) reported by Liem et al. 2008[77] may underestimate the negative HRQoL impact of 3x weekly in-centre HD compared to at-home PD.[5] 

Utility values from Li et al. 2017[92] were not considered suitable for use in the economic model by the experts for several reasons.[5] The publication reported a utility value for people on the transplant waiting list (0.77), rather than people on dialysis, and the clinical expert highlighted that people on the transplant waiting list tend to be healthier than people on long-term dialysis.[5] This value was therefore not seen as representative of the HRQoL of people receiving chronic dialysis. Furthermore, the study used the preliminary value set for England to generate utility values from EQ-5D-5L,[93] which NICE advises against utilising.[94] Therefore, based on expert advice,[5] utility values from Li et al. 2017 were not used in the analysis. 

- f) Based on the cross-validation assessment, please provide an updated economic model and scenario analyses exploring utility values sourced in b), c) and d). 

As described in the response to question B13 e), the utilities used within the model were selected following a TLR to gather potentially relevant sources from similar appraisals and discussions 


Clarification questions 



<!-- page 292 -->

with UK clinical experts, to ensure the utilities selected were relevant for C3G. No other utility values were considered appropriate for inclusion in the model. Results of the scenario analysis requested by the EAG (Liem et al. 2008 utility value for post-transplant health state) have been provided in the response to question B13 a). 

## **B 14.  The CS included SAE disutilities when related to iptacopan.** 

- a) Please provide evidence on the safety profile for the chosen comparators, and address whether safety profiles might differ when the comparator treatments are given respectively when iptacopan is added, implying an inclusion of comparator adverse events. 

SoC is associated with various side effects, as discussed in Section 1.3.5 of the CS. Immunosuppressants including corticosteroids (CS) and mycophenolate mofetil (MMF) are associated with gastrointestinal side effects and increased risk of infections.[50, 95] CS are also associated with various other side effects including musculoskeletal effects (osteoporosis and myopathy), weight gain, hypertension and insomnia which can be worsened by increased doses and continued administration.[96] Angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors (ACEis) and angiotensin-receptor blockers (ARBs) were generally considered to have a favourable safety profile by UK clinicians participating in an advisory board.[50] 

In the APPEAR-C3G trial, iptacopan was administered in addition to optimised background therapy, including ACEis/ARBs at a maximally tolerated dose, with some patients also on concomitant CS and/or mycophenolic acids (MPA [including MMF]) or SLGT2is (continuation of stable dose during the trial).[97] Therefore, the safety data from the trial appropriately reflect the safety profile of iptacopan being administered in addition to SoC. 

Furthermore, by not modelling AEs in the SoC arm of the economic model, while SAEs suspected to be related to iptacopan are modelled in the iptacopan arm, the economic model adopts a conservative approach, as all AE-related impacts are attributed to iptacopan rather than SoC. 

- b) This approach resulted in infections being included with a disutility of 0.156, derived as the EQ-5D-3L score difference between acute presentation in cough and lower respiratory tract infections and recovery in week 4. Please report additional literature to verify this estimate for the UK setting. 

The disutility was taken from a study by Oppong et al. 2013,[98] which was identified through a published SLR on the impact of acute pneumococcal disease on health state utility values.[99] Oppong et al. 2013 collected EQ-5D-3L from patients in England with cough and lower 

respiratory tract infections with a longitudinal study design. As Oppong et al. 2013 collected data in England and generated utility values using a UK tariff, it is therefore an accurate source for the UK setting. Utility values at acute presentation (baseline) and following recovery (Week 4) were presented,[98] allowing for the calculation of a disutility that was independent of the included population’s general utility, and was therefore less impacted by differences in population characteristics such as age and comorbidities. On that basis, Oppong et al. 2013 is considered an appropriate source for the disutility and given the minimal impact of the AE disutility on the ICER, no additional literature has been searched for. 


Clarification questions

- c) Please provide an updated economic model and scenario analyses exploring 

   - alternative disutility values sourced in b). 

In line with the response above to clarification question B14 b), the AE disutility used in the economic model was deemed suitable and therefore no additional values from the literature have been provided. 

The disutility value of 0.156 from Oppong et al. was varied by 20% of the mean within the DSA and was not among the 10 most influential parameters within the economic model. 

To test the impact of alternative disutility values further, two scenario analyses were run using disutility values of 0.1 and 0.2, respectively. Results are shown in Table 35 below, further confirming a minimal impact of the AE disutility on the ICER (range of ****** to ****** impact on the ICER across both scenarios).
