## _**Cost and healthcare resource use identification, measurement and valuation**_ 

**B 15.  Priority question. Table 45 of the CS presents acquisition costs for iptacopan with a cost per day and per year derived from the cost per pack. This approach implicitly assumes that a daily dosage can be acquired. Please provide an updated economic model and scenario analysis taking a per-pack costing approach rather than utilising acquisition costs per day to derive annual costs.** 

Within the economic model, the iptacopan price per year is calculated via a daily iptacopan price (for dosing 200 mg twice daily). This is then divided by the number of cycles per year and applied to the number of patients on iptacopan per cycle throughout the time horizon to calculate the total acquisition cost of iptacopan. 

We agree that this approach implies that individual iptacopan capsules can be acquired and therefore neglects to account for the cost of pack wastage when a patient discontinues iptacopan. In the economic model submitted with the clarification questions response, the approach to calculating the acquisition cost of iptacopan has been adjusted to account for wastage, as described below. 

With each pack containing 56 capsules of iptacopan 200 mg and twice daily dosing, approximately 3.26 packs are required per 3-month model cycle. Therefore, the maximum number of iptacopan packs that a patient opens per model cycle is 4. To conservatively reflect the maximum wastage possible when a patient discontinues iptacopan, the cost of an additional ~0.74 packs is added to the total acquisition cost of iptacopan, thereby accounting for the cost of 4 packs in a patient’s final model cycle on iptacopan. This change in costing has been implemented in cell EK2 of the ‘Iptacopan’ tab in the economic model. 

The cost of iptacopan pack wastage has been incorporated in a revised company base case, which is presented in Table 36 below; the impact on cost-effectiveness results is small (change in ICER from the original company base case is ******).

- b) Please provide justification for the chosen approach, rather than deriving a unit cost from the National Mean for each given HRG Code. 

The adopted approach is considered the most appropriate as it adjusts the costs associated with lobar, atypical or viral pneumonia (DZ11), bronchopneumonia (DZ23), and sepsis (WJ06) and their respective CC Scores based on their relative frequency as recorded in the NHS Reference Costs.[36] A simple average of the costs of grouped HRG codes DZ11, DZ23 and WJ06 would assume that these occur at equal frequency, which would be incorrect. 


Clarification questions 



<!-- page 303 -->

- c) Please provide a scenario analysis utilising an average unit cost derived from the national means for the HRG codes presented in CS Table 52. 

As requested by the EAG, a scenario analysis has been conducted calculating the weighted average of each grouped HRG code (across all CC scores) and subsequently taking a simple average of these: 

SAE scenario cost = (Weighted average across code DZ11 + Weighted average across code DZ23 + Weighted average across code WJ06) / 3 

This results in an average cost of £2,951.90. A scenario analysis shows limited impact on the cost-effectiveness results (see Table 44). However, as explained in the response to b), the SAE cost as used in the CS is considered more appropriate.

## **B 18.  The CS states that all costs were inflated to the 2022/2023 fiscal year. Please clarify why 2022/23 was selected, rather than 2023/2024. Further, please specify how costs derived from NHS National Cost Collection 2023/24 were handled and where inflation calculation can be found in the economic model.** 

Costs were inflated to the 2022/23 fiscal year as relevant, using the NHSCII Pay and Price Index.[101] At the time of the company submission, the latest PSSRU Unit Cost of Health and Social Care Manual was the 2023 edition, which did not include inflation indices up to the 2023/24 fiscal year. This created a small misalignment in cost year between the inflated costs and costs informed by the National Schedule of NHS Costs 2023/24, but in all cases used the most recent available information.[36] 

In the economic model, inflation calculations can be found within each inputs cell calculation where applicable (e.g., cell D47 within the ‘Cost data’ tab for the inflation of costs sourced from Liu et al. 2015).[102] Each inflation calculation references cells R13:R27 of the ‘Cell links’ tab which shows the cumulative inflation factor sourced from the PSSRU Unit Cost of Health and Social Care Manual 2023.[101] 

## _**Results**_ 

## **B 19.  Tables 1, 2 and 3 of Appendix H in the CS present disaggregated costs,** 

## **outcomes, and kidney survival outcomes, respectively.** 

- a) In Table 1, dialysis and (post-)transplant costs are significantly higher for the SoC 

   - arm versus the iptacopan +SoC arm. Please justify and discuss the plausibility of the presented results. 

The available clinical trial data on eGFR stabilisation with iptacopan treatment, as summarised in Section 2 of the CS, suggest that iptacopan is able to slow the progression of C3G in a meaningful way.[4, 10] By slowing the progression of C3G, iptacopan is expected to maintain patients in earlier CKD stages for longer, and thus prolong kidney survival and delay the need for KRT. For example, in the economic model base case, kidney survival at 10 years is estimated as 90.22% for the iptacopan arm compared with  51.84% for the SoC arm. Fewer patients in the iptacopan arm experiencing kidney failure and requiring KRT early in the disease course results in a reduction of dialysis and transplant costs compared with the SoC arm. 

Dialysis and transplant are the health states associated with the highest healthcare resource utilisation in chronic kidney diseases.[103] A reduction in the need for dialysis or transplants is meaningful not only in terms of direct NHS cost, but also beneficial from an NHS capacity perspective and leads to important improvements for patients, given the risks and quality of life impacts of dialysis and transplantation. 

- b) Table 2 shows that total QALYs in CKD stage 1 for the iptacopan +SoC arm are 110.06% higher than in the SoC arm with the % absolute QALY increments falling in 


Clarification questions 



<!-- page 306 -->

## later stages. Please justify and discuss the plausibility of the results presented in table 2. 

As noted in response to question B19 a), the available clinical trial data suggest that iptacopan is able to slow C3G progression, thereby maintaining patients in earlier CKD stages for longer, while reducing the number of patients reaching kidney failure, compared to SoC alone. By slowing progression, patients receiving iptacopan stay in earlier CKD stages for longer and therefore accrue more QALYs in early CKD stages than patients in the SoC arm, who progress to kidney failure more quickly and consequently accrue more QALYs in the dialysis and transplant health states.

## **B 21.  Priority question. When running the PSA, the EAG noticed that this has implications on the deterministic results in the model (including errors and implausible cost results). In addition, the PSA does not vary trial HSUVs, the proportion of CAPD/APD/HD patients, resource use parameters, and eGFR midpoint values.** 

- a) Please provide an updated economic model with this implication fixed and include an overview of all changes made within the economic model. 

Novartis has not observed any implications on the deterministic results or other unintended consequences when running the PSA. 

It is possible that what the EAG has observed occurs if a user changes a model input and subsequently runs the PSA without making further necessary changes on the ‘Control’ tab. If edits are being made to the model prior to running the PSA, it is necessary to run the ‘CopyFormulas’ macro by pressing the button in cell C2 of the ‘Control’ tab. 


Clarification questions 



<!-- page 308 -->

## b) For PSA reproducibility, please ensure that a fixed seed is included. 

A fixed seed has now been included within the economic model and within the updated PSA results presented below in response to question B21 d). This can be found in cell C49 of the ‘Settings’ tab. 

## c) Please provide justification for the decisions to exclude these parameters from the PSA. 

Trial health state utility values (HSUVs) are already varied within the PSA in the originally submitted economic model. Trial HSUVs, found within cells E15:E19 of the ‘Utility data’ tab, are derived from the coefficients of a linear regression model. The parameters from the regression model are varied within the PSA using a Cholesky decomposition distribution, which can be found in rows 570:574 of the ‘Control’ tab. Details of the variance-covariance matrix used within the Cholesky decomposition can be seen in cells BE21:BQ26 on the ‘Control’ tab. Please note that the parameters within rows 22:26 of the ‘Control’ tab need not be varied given the individual components are varied within rows 570:574. 

The economic model submitted with the clarification questions response has been updated to vary the proportion of CAPD/APD/HD patients (rows 42:44, ‘Control’ tab) and the proportion receiving each healthcare resource use (rows 108:234, ‘Control’ tab) in the PSA. 

eGFR midpoint values are not varied within the PSA, as they are part of the model structure and represent structural uncertainty rather than an input associated with parameter uncertainty. If these values were to be varied within the PSA, variable progression through CKD stages would be modelled i.e., each probabilistic run would result in a different midpoint for each CKD stage which in turn would cause progression throughout the modelled health states to be based on inconsistent distances between CKD stages (in other words, progression would no longer be uniform). Therefore, eGFR midpoint values have not been included within the PSA. 

Novartis acknowledges that using the midpoint of each CKD stage (midpoint between upper and lower bound defining the CKD stage) for CKD stage transitions is a simplification, but one that was considered necessary in a Markov cohort approach. A scenario was provided in the CS where transition probabilities are calculated based on the difference between the upper bounds of CKD stages rather than midpoints, with a limited change (+****%; see Table 51) compared to the base case ICER. 

d) Please provide an updated economic model and results for the PSA that includes the aforementioned parameters: trial HSUVs, proportions of CAPD/APD/HD patients, resource use parameters, and eGFR midpoint values. 

In line with the responses above, an updated economic model has been provided which additionally varies the proportions of CAPD/APD/HD patients and resource use parameters. Whilst updating these parameter inclusions within the PSA, the model has also been amended to additionally vary the KRT threshold, maximum age for transplant, and vaccination and antibiotic annual frequencies and proportion of patients within the PSA in the updated economic model. 

Please note that when adding inputs to the PSA which correspond to proportions equal to 100% e.g., the proportion receiving antibiotics, a beta distribution is used. For a beta distribution to 


Clarification questions 



<!-- page 309 -->

sample values between 0 and 1 correctly, the mean value used within the formula to calculate the beta distribution cannot be a value of 1 (which would correspond to the modelled base case value of 100%). As a result, a simplification has been made to use a mean value of 99% (0.99) within the beta distribution instead of the modelled base case value of 100%. Within the economic model this is applied to the proportion receiving each resource use (rows 108:114, 124:130, 140:146, 156:162, 172:178, 188:194, 204:210, 220:226, 494, 497, 499 and 502 of the ‘Control’ tab). 

Updated probabilistic results (using 1,000 simulations) are presented in Table 48 and Table 49. An updated probabilistic ICER convergence plot, cost-effectiveness scatter plot and costeffectiveness acceptability curve are shown in Figure 15, Figure 16 and Figure 17.

## **B 24. The (results of the) technical validity assessments are not described in detail nor are detailed validation exercises (i.e. specific black-box tests) described in CS. The CS mentioned that “two checklists, based on the published TECH-VER checklist” were used for technical validation.** 

- a) Please provide a detailed description of the validity assessments performed as well as the results. 

The model was validated by an independent team of health economists who were not involved in the original model development through two approaches. First, the internal validation checklist was completed to set up different scenarios ensuring the model responds appropriately; for instance, setting all utility values to 1 should make LYs equal QALYs. This process tests the model's reaction to extreme values. The internal validation checklist (adapted from the TECHVER checklist to be more comprehensive) was completed twice – once upon review of the draft model developed by the global Novartis team (prior to adapting for the NICE submission) and once upon completion of the model adaptation for the NICE submission.[107] The initial checklist identified errors which were subsequently amended, while the final checklist identified no further errors. 

Next, a detailed quality control was completed. This involved thoroughly reviewing every cell in the model to verify the correctness of all formulae, proper coding of macros, accurate referencing, absence of spelling or grammar errors, and consistent formatting. 

- b) Please provide the filled-out TECH-VER checklist as well as any other checklist used for technical validation.

## **B 25. Further external validation of modelled effectiveness would be desirable.** 

- a) Please report on the face validity of the model structure, modelling assumptions, model inputs, intermediate outcomes as well as final outcomes in more detail (including what aspects were assessed and what were the considerations as well as conclusions). 

- b) Please assess the external validity of model inputs, intermediate outcomes as well as final outcomes using 

   - I. evidence used to develop the economic model. 

   - II. evidence not used to develop the economic model. 

As noted in Section 3.13 of the CS, Novartis UK held two advisory boards with nine (April 2022) and ten (November 2024) UK clinicians with experience in treating patients with C3G in NHS clinical practice; insights from both advisory boards informed this submission.[4, 50] Advisors provided their views on the current SoC and treatment landscape for C3G, level of unmet need, and iptacopan trial data, as well as clinical input for modelling disease progression and disease management before and after kidney failure. 

Additionally, calls with two individual UK clinicians were conducted to clarify specific points of uncertainty relating to the submission, and model validation was undertaken in a joint call with one clinical and one external health economics expert from the UK.[5] Model validation covered selection of the base case for modelling disease progression and treatment effect, health state utility values, health state costs, and AEs, as well as validation of clinical outputs of the draft economic model. Further input from two UK clinicians was obtained on a call conducted during the preparation of the clarification questions response.[8] 

The modelling approach, inputs and assumptions presented in this submission considered the feedback received by clinical and health economics experts, as detailed throughout Section 3 of the CS. These calls confirmed the overall face validity of the modelling approach. Further discussion of the face validity of the model has been included throughout the responses within this document, with the responses to question B1–B20 providing further detail on the clinical plausibility and validity of the choices of model structure, assumptions, inputs, intermediate and final outcomes, in light of the evidence available, including the considerations and conclusions.

## **B 26.  Please provide cross validations, i.e. comparisons with other relevant NICE TAs focussed on similar, potentially relevant, diseases (e.g. related NICE recommendations and NICE Pathways listed in the final scope) and elaborate on the identified differences regarding:** 

- a) Model structure and assumptions 

- b) Input parameters related to:

- c) Estimated (disaggregated) outcomes per comparator/ intervention 

   - I. Life years 

   - II. QALYs

As noted in Section 3.1 of the CS, given the lack of published cost-effectiveness studies in C3G, an additional targeted literature review (TLR) was undertaken of NICE technology appraisals (TAs) in chronic kidney diseases with final guidance published in the last 10 years, in order to support economic model development and inform potential sources for input values. The TLR methodology was described in full in Appendix E (Section E.2); briefly, a search of the NICE website was conducted on 13[th] December 2024, using an existing filter available on the website for NICE products on chronic kidney disease, for published TA guidance. The search identified 16 TAs. Among these, 3 TAs were excluded; TA482 was excluded since it focused on children and young people, while TA165 and TA117 were excluded since final guidance was published more than 10 years ago. None of the identified appraisals were for treatments for C3G.

While none of the identified TAs covered interventions for C3G, information was considered as relevant during the development and parameterisation of the economic model for iptacopan in C3G. The iptacopan model uses a CKD stage structure, with CKD stage 5 denoted as pre-KRT and separate KRT states for dialysis and post-transplant. The overall 9 model health states are consistent with two previous recent appraisals in IgA nephropathy (TA937)[28 ] and CKD (TA775),[29] providing precedent for this model structure. Further appraisals have used CKD staging and/or separated KRT into dialysis and post-transplant health-states in different structures,[26, 31, 53] further supporting the overall approach as a valid representation of a chronic kidney disease. 

The base case economic analysis used APPEAR-C3G-derived efficacy and utility values for CKD stages 1–4, in line with the NICE preference for EQ-5D,[25] therefore supporting the validity of the approach. Efficacy was modelled using trial eGFR data, consistent with six of the appraisals identified in the TLR, although methods for generating transition probabilities varied.[26-29, 53, 86] Only two of the prior appraisals used trial data to inform utility values;[29, 53] while this is therefore an uncommon approach, the use of utility values generated from EQ-5D in the pivotal trial is considered is a strength of this submission, since it reflects NICE’s preference.[25] 

Utilities for CKD stage 5 (pre-KRT), dialysis, and transplant were sourced from published literature as no data were available from APPEAR-C3G. For CKD stage 5 (pre-KRT), a utility value from Jesky et al. 2016, a UK study which collected EQ-5D-3L data from 745 patients with CKD of any aetiology,[63] was used. This study was used as a source of utility data for CKD stage 5 in two previous appraisals,[27, 28] and was used a source of CKD stages 1–4, transplant and dialysis utilities in a third.[67] Due to its clinical relevance and precedent in other appraisals, Jesky et al. 2016 is therefore considered a valid source of utilities for the economic model. A scenario analysis used utility values from Jesky et al. also for CKD stages 1–4, with a limited effect on the ICER (*****%). 

Dialysis and transplant utilities were sourced from Lee et al. 2005, a UK study estimating utility values for different KRT modalities from EQ-5D-3L collected in 416 patients.[76] Again this is a highly relevant source, and as such has been used in seven previous appraisals as a source of transplant and/or dialysis utilities.[26, 27 , 28, 29 , 79 , 85 , 86 ] 

Costs were sourced from NHS reference costs for dialysis and transplant (which account for the majority of healthcare resource use costs) in line with previous appraisals, and following the calculation methods as initially used in TA775 and subsequently adopted in TA942.[27, 29] Additionally, post-transplant costs were based on an NHS Blood and Transplant fact sheet used in multiple previous appraisals (TA775, TA890, TA942).[27, 29, 85] Transport costs for HD were estimated from Liu et al. 2015, as used in previous appraisals (TA937, TA809).[28, 87] 

Overall, due to the alignment to the NICE reference case and the use of UK-specific data from literature with precedent of use in multiple prior appraisals, the approach taken for these inputs is considered valid for decision making. 

The deterministic base case results in this submission gave total LYs of 21.59 for iptacopan + SoC and 21.11 for SoC alone, and QALYs of 16.88 for iptacopan + SoC and 15.13 for SoC. The LYs and QALYs for both iptacopan + SoC and SoC were higher than both the intervention and comparator LYs and QALYs in previous appraisals, although a full comparison was not possible due to values in several published appraisals having been redacted (Table 52). However, due to the differences in disease, intervention, comparator, and time horizon, differences between these values were to be expected, with results of previous appraisals of limited relevance to the current submission. 


Clarification questions 



<!-- page 326 -->

The total costs for iptacopan + SoC were £********* (updated company base case) and the total costs for SoC alone were £355,162, which were also greater than the total costs of interventions and comparators in the previous appraisals; however, it must be noted that nine of the 13 prior appraisals redacted total costs for the intervention, limiting the ability to conduct such a comparison. In addition, it should be highlighted again that previous appraisals covered different diseases, interventions, comparators, and time horizons, and as such a comparison of outcomes with previous appraisals is not considered meaningful.

What**<br>**do carers experience**<br>**when caring for someone**<br>**with the condition?**|Because C3GN is an ultra-rare condition, patients and carers reported difficulties with getting a diagnosis in<br>the first place.<br>It took one patient some two years to achieve a diagnosis of C3GN.  Currently in her fifties, she explained:<br>“There were no treatments at that time, so even hearing that there’s a potential treatment is just so exciting.<br>We so rarely hear about anything for us.”<br>She described being put on steroids in her early twenties and being told not to eat anything with protein, salt or<br>sugar, which meant ‘basically anything’. She started dialysis at 26 years old and received a kidney from her<br>mother three years later.  “I’ve been very lucky.  I’m now 22 years post-transplant and I’ve not had the disease<br>back.<br>“I’ve never had children because there wasn’t enough information about whether I could pass it on.”<br>Another patient currently in her 40s was diagnosed at age 14 years. Because she had been diagnosed<br>relatively quickly and put on blood pressure medication, her native kidneys lasted well. About 10 years ago,<br>whilst working in a senior role in London, she was suddenly told that she needed a kidney transplant. She<br>underwent a successful transplant (with a kidney donated by her husband) which lasted for about 10 years.|

<!-- page 336 -->

**==> picture [268 x 48] intentionally omitted <==**

She had a second transplant in June last year from a deceased donor and is currently enjoying ‘excellent’ health: “I need to keep my mind strong and have brilliant people around me. I was encouraged not to let my disease stop me and was very lucky with my medical team. “When my first kidney failed, I was told to just go on holiday because they thought I would be restricted.” The mother of teenage patient with C3GN described the difficulties of getting a diagnosis. Her son first developed symptoms – puffiness around his eyes – at age 10. Then he developed a lump in his neck which would not go away.  Finally, he got an appointment with a paediatrician who ran blood and urine tests. The next day, they got a call from the hospital saying they thought her son had nephritis but needed further tests. Her son was tired and grumpy and had lost interest in life; it was hard to know whether this was due to illness or being a pre-teen. She said: ”He is currently on the maximum dose of blood pressure tablets and mycophenolate as well. He still has proteinuria but is not classed a priority for any other treatments. “We don't want him to need dialysis or a transplant in the near future, but he will be quite low on the list of priorities for new treatments. That's a challenge for us.” Patients and carers stress that living with C3GN is frightening; they face a lot of uncertainty in their lives. One commented: “If and when you get to end stage [kidney disease], you are always thinking ‘please God, let this kidney work’. It’s very frightening.” They also feel alone; the condition is so rare there is ‘no-one else to talk to about this exact thing’. One commented: “We get diagnosed at a very young age.  When most of my friends were going out and having fun, I had to stay in and do 24-hour urine samples.” Having C3GN can be an embarrassment, particularly for teenagers.  The mum remarked: “It’s hard handling the uncertainty and dealing with the sheer number of tests required all the time. We don't know if it’s getting worse. Plus, all the other things around adolescence. Is it affecting his height etc.? There should be better reassurance and guidance.” One patient commented: “This disease affects you at a young age and will affect you for the rest of your life. Whether you have a good transplant or not, it will still affect you. It impacts your schooling, career choice and 

Patient organisation submission Iptacopan for treating complement 3 glomerulopathy [ID6283] 

4 of 14 



<!-- page 337 -->

**==> picture [268 x 48] intentionally omitted <==**

where you live. I had to change careers and move house to be near a hospital. It puts you at an economic disadvantage and really contributes to health inequalities.” Another said: “Because it is rapid and aggressive, you can quickly get to end stage. This impacts your relationships. In the ‘90s, my friends were out raving; I was doing peritoneal dialysis. I saw my friends settle down with partners and have babies. At the same time, I was thinking can I survive another month?” Patients and carers recognised the impact of C3GN on black and minority groups, as well as those from lower socio-economic backgrounds who do not have good support networks around them. For the mum, her son’s diagnosis came as a big shock. She is constantly chasing: “Hospitals are not always great at communication, so I chase for test results, prescriptions and constantly have to follow up in case something gets missed. “Before diagnosis, there’s the early uncertainty. Because you haven't got a ‘thing’, any single symptom could be serious.” School life can be challenging for children with C3GN: ”I had to go to a parents’ evening with a piece of paper to ask every teacher to let him go to toilet and drink water. He’s on a low salt diet – so are school dinners suitable? I have to check up on what he’s eating. “Different levels of understanding can make it challenging. I need to be on first name terms with school nurse in case anything is going around, such as chicken pox.” Carers also experience an impact on their ability to work: “I’ve turned down job opportunities, because I might need to pivot. So, this also limits my career path.” For those patients who have reached kidney failure and have had a kidney transplant, there are other challenges: "We are dependent on medications generally available to transplant patients. Immunosuppression can make you vulnerable to things like COVID. You also need to be aware of longerterm conditions like kidney associated dementia, osteoporosis and other kidney-associated disease.”

## **9. What do patients or carers think are the advantages of the technology?** 

## Patient 1 comments: 

“I think this is a super exciting development in such a rare kidney disease which I had for nearly three decades. The big advantage is that it’s the first time ever there has been a drug available that actually treats the specific condition. I was 14 when I was first diagnosed, it was scary, things were uncertain and there was no treatment - no child or carer should have to hear that.  They need hope of actual treatment that tackles the disease directly. 

To quote Carla Nester - “As a clinician treating young people living with C3G, I see firsthand the challenges with therapies used to treat this condition today, underscoring the vital need for dedicated treatment for these patients,” said Carla Nester, M.D., M.S.A., F.A.S.N., Professor of Pediatrics-Nephrology at the University of Iowa and APPEAR-C3G Co-Investigator. “I am encouraged to see these data, which reinforce the clinically meaningful impact on kidney health measures we saw at 6 months. As the only oral complement inhibitor intended to treat C3G, Fabhalta could provide new hope for people living with this condition.” 

## Patient 2 comments: 

- The first advantage and one of the most important is: this gives patients hope……that may not seem a practical advantage but for me being told there was no cure or treatment was devastating. Knowing there is a treatment that may help gives you a fighting chance, hope! 

- Reading the information, we have on this drug so far – this looks to be groundbreaking for patients in this group.  In particular it helps with proteinuria within the first two weeks and over a year this becomes sustained and meaningful reductions. This is major news and an incredible improvement for these patients. The disease is rapid and progressive and this is a drug that can change this for patients. 

- • This patient group are mainly children and young adults. The disease can mean needing dialysis and transplant within 5-10 years. This medication has the potential to change this. 

- Young transplant patients may need several transplants over the course of a lifetime, each transplant exposing them to more antigens and reducing the likelihood of finding a right match the next time – so anything that means it takes longer to get to a transplant stage may mean less dialysis and less transplants are needed over a lifetime. 

- Being young patients and being poorly with kidney disease and living with stage 4 or 5, dialysis and transplant means you lose time off school or reduced training opportunities, leading to inequalities when it comes to employment, salaries over a lifetime etc.  - this medication not only slows the progression but improves the health of patients and I hope this means young people have opportunities to finish schooling and training, find better jobs. Maybe less dependence on being close to hospital.

- With the improvement in proteinuria this could mean patients may need less frequent routine visits and certainly reduced renal replacement therapies over their lifetime. 

- It is important to remember these patients will live their whole life with this disease.

## **Living with the condition** 

|**6. What is it like to live**<br>**with the condition? What**<br>**do carers experience**<br>**when caring for someone**<br>**with the condition?**|Living with the condition varies from patient to patient, depending on the severity of the disease and its rate of<br>progression to end stage renal failure. For someone with a slow rate of disease progression there might be very<br>little impact on daily life for many years. Whereas for someone who has had rapid disease progression, and is at<br>end stage renal failure, a life on dialysis has a huge impact on daily life. For patients with slow progression, and<br>those who receive transplants, there is a severe anxiety associated with this diagnosis. The disease often recurs<br>in transplants so patients must deal with not knowing when the disease may strike. This anxiety is made that<br>much worse by the current lack of an effective treatment. Patients can feel like “a ticking time bomb.” If the C3G<br>patient is a child, then the parent caring for that child has a huge impact on their life and their ability to remain in<br>work. Children need a lot of extra care, can spend extended periods in hospital, and need to be accompanied to<br>in centre dialysis treatment. Carers may also administer dialysis treatment at home, whether PD or Home HD, as<br>the child will not be able to do this on their own. Caring for a patient with C3G is also mentally taxing. Carers will<br>see the patient deteriorate over the course of many admissions, appointments and often procedures. Due to the<br>current lack of effective treatments, patients do not tend to ever improve. The best-case scenario is usually<br>stabilisation, for a time, before further deterioration.|
|---|---|

## **Current treatment of the condition in the NHS** 

|**7. What do patients or**<br>**carers think of current**<br>**treatments and care**<br>**available on the NHS?**|At present C3G progresses to end stage renal failure. There is currently no treatment to prevent this happening.<br>At best current options delay this inevitability. Treatment for end stage renal failure is either dialysis or a<br>transplant. The disease currently recurs in half of transplanted kidneys at the five year mark, which results in<br>patients needing dialysis treatment or another transplant. Each time a C3G patient is transplanted, antibody<br>sensitivity increases, which results in a smaller pool of potential donors for that patient. This means waiting<br>longer for a suitable donor to be found and spending more time on dialysis. Long periods of dialysis are<br>detrimental to overall health and lowers life expectancy for patients.|
|---|---|
|**8. Is there an unmet need**<br>**for patients with this**<br>**condition?**|Yes. Here is currently no cure for this disease. Some medications might slow down progression to end stage<br>renal failure, but none prevent it.|

This technology<br>provides a great deal of hope to patients and carers, where there has previously been none.<br>Patients are optimistic about the advantage of this technology being a single, simple oral tablet. This would be to prevent the loss of the<br>transplanted kidney. Halting the malfunction in the complement system that causes the disease would prevent<br>damage to the kidney.<br>Transplanted patients, who have lost previous transplanted kidneys from C3G, might be another group who would<br>benefit more from the technology than stable patients with the diagnosis. This would be to prevent the loss of the<br>transplanted kidney. Halting the malfunction in the complement system that causes the disease would prevent<br>damage to the kidney.|

## **What is the expected place of the technology in current practice?** 

||**9. How is the condition**<br>**currently treated in the**<br>**NHS?**|Supportive treatments including inhibition of the renin-angiotensin system with angiotensin converting<br>enzyme inhibitors (ACEi) or angiotensin receptor blockers (ARB) for management of chronic kidney<br>disease due to C3G.<br>More recently, some clinicians will add in a sodium glucose co-transporter 2 inhibitors (SGLT1i) for<br>management of chronic kidney disease due to C3G.<br>If significant proteinuria [proteinuria >1g/day] and/or declining kidney function, immunosuppression with<br>mycophenolate mofetil and corticosteroids. Choice of immunosuppression with mycophenolate and<br>steroids is based on observational data only. **8. What is the main aim of treatment for C3** Ultimately the aim of treatment with C3G is to stop end stage kidney failure, **glomerulopathy?** however, it is not feasible to evaluate this in clinical trials as progression to end (For example, to stop progression, to improve mobility, to stage kidney failure occurs over a 10-15 year period in ~50%. cure the condition, or prevent progression or disability) This problem with clinical endpoints was specifically addressed in C3G by the Kidney Health Initiative (KHI), a public–private partnership between the American Society of Nephrology and the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA). For a more detailed summary- Clin J Am Soc Nephrol. 2024 Sep 1;19(9):1201-1208). This expert panel assessed the currently available data supporting the efficacy end points (1) proteinuria, (2) eGFR, and (3) histopathology. In essence, in a disease where the pathophysiology of disease is exquisitely known (i.e. activation of the alternative pathway {AP} of complement), blockade of the AP associated with a favourable effect with lowering of proteinuria, stabilization, in eGFR and improved histologic changes provides convincing evidence of efficacy, They specifically noted that complete alignment of all 3 end points would not be required. **9. What do you consider a clinically significant** The KHI reviewed the evidence for treatment thresholds and concluded that **treatment response?** there was a lack information on the minimum thresholds for change in any of the (For example, a reduction in tumour size by x cm, or a three end points (1) proteinuria, (2) eGFR, and (3) histopathology that would be reduction in disease activity by a certain amount) considered clinically meaningful in C3G.

|•<br>Do you expect the technology to increase length of life<br>more than current care?<br>•<br>Do you expect the technology to increase health-<br>related quality of life more than current care?|The clinical trials of iptacopan in C3G does provide evidence of clinically<br>meaningful benefits compared to current standard of care.<br>The data suggests that iptacopan will delay progression of renal failure (both<br>in native and post-transplant disease) and the need for dialysis.<br>It is an extrapolation to comment on any increase in life expectancy based on<br>short term studies with proteinuria as the primary end point although it is not an<br>unreasonable assumption to make that preventing end stage renal failure will<br>increase length of life.<br>I would expect improved quality of life on iptacopan vs standard of care<br>based on delaying progression of renal failure. In up to 5 sentences, please summarise the key messages of your statement: 

There is a high unmet need for patients with C3G with no treatment known to work 

The reduction in proteinuria is significant and from natural history studies will decrease the risk of kidney failure. 

The stabilisation of eGFR appears significant and from natural history studies will decrease the risk of kidney failure Iptacaopan has a beneficial safety profile in C3G 

The totality of evidence suggests that iptacopan should be used with blockade of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone as first line treatment in both native and transplant recurrent C3G

## **Part 2: Key messages** 

In up to 5 sentences, please summarise the key messages of your statement: 

The use of technology that blocks C3 activation in C3G is a step change in management as it targets the underlying 

pathophysiology (abnormal complement activation in glomeruli). 

C3G is associated with a high risk of kidney failure in both native and transplant kidneys despite the use of immunosuppression and supportive care; there is a significant unmet clinical need. 

The iptacopan trial phase 3 data demonstrated a reduction in proteinuria and reduction in glomerular C3 staining and these results imply that the treatment will result in reduced rates of kidney failure. 

The treatment is a twice daily tablet and appears well-tolerated. 

The risk of infection common to all complement inhibition can be mitigated by pre-treatment vaccination and fever plan. 

Thank you for your time.

|**6. What is your experience of living with C3**<br>**glomerulopathy?**<br>**If you are a carer (for someone with C3**<br>**glomerulopathy) please share your experience of**<br>**caring for them**|I first became unwell with C3G in 2010, at age nine, in the absence of any<br>comorbidities or other past medical history. This is, unfortunately, a common age at<br>first presentation. The disease took only two months to damage the kidneys enough<br>for me to require dialysis. At this time, it took a considerable amount of time to<br>receive a correct diagnosis due to knowledge of the disease being minimal, even<br>among nephrologists. After a period of haemodialysis, I commenced peritoneal<br>dialysis and returned home after three months in hospital, while my Mother began<br>the work-up to donate her kidney. My clearance was not good on dialysis and I was<br>chronically nauseated and fatigued, causing me to miss most of the remainder of<br>primary school. After 18 months on dialysis, I received my transplant, and despite<br>significant post-operative complications whilst still an inpatient, I returned home<br>after four months in hospital with a healthy kidney.<br>I was aware that the disease was recurrent, and would eventually return, however I<br>did not expect this to happen a mere 18 months after my transplant, when my<br>bloods were deranged at a routine follow-up appointment, and the resulting<br>diagnostic biopsy showed some crescents on the sample. Although I was<br>asymptomatic, it was at this point that it became clear that due to the disease and<br>the lack of drug treatments at the time, that the clock had begun ticking, and it<br>would only be a matter of time until I would be back on dialysis. This process took<br>five years, during which time I was closely monitored, and was briefly treated with<br>Eculizumab, which had some positive effects, albeit temporarily. I began taking<br>ACE-inhibitors, and later diuretics to slow the process and manage symptoms.<br>The process of slowly deteriorating is mentally, as well as physically, taxing. The<br>bad memories of my previous period of dialysis were still fresh in my mind, and the<br>inevitability of this was clear. unwell to attend school. I recommenced dialysis a few months later, just after my 18[th] birthday. I was not able to sit my A levels, due to missing so much of my final year, so I left education at 18, on dialysis, and without the qualifications I’d worked so hard to achieve in order to enter medicine. This was extremely difficult for me mentally, as I knew that the competitiveness of medicine meant that that ship had most likely sailed. My second period of dialysis was haemodialysis in hospital, which gave me a better quality of life than peritoneal dialysis due to a better clearance. However, it remained very disruptive to my life, as I could only work four days a week on nondialysis days. Some haemodialysis patients feel their worst just before a session, when the level of toxins in their bodies are highest, and some patients feel worse afterwards, due to the effects of the dialysis itself. I always felt unwell after a session, so most of the remainder of those days were spent at home with malaise, a headache or muscle cramp. During the 18 months that I spent on dialysis, while my Father was worked-up to donate his kidney, I felt extremely stuck in my situation. I could not re-enter education, go abroad, or exceed my fluid limit of 1.5l per day, at a time when I was 18 years old and trying to enjoy myself with my friends. I received my second transplant from my Dad in December 2019, at age 19. For the most part, post-operatively, I was much more straightforward this time, and began taking Iptacopan a couple of months after the surgery, remaining on it ever since. I entered the phase two study and remain on the extension study. Five and a half years on, my bloods, urine and last biopsy look very good and I hope that the treatment will continue to work for as long as the kidney does. After some time spent working in the NHS, while completing a level three qualification as a substitute for A levels, I am now two thirds through my paramedic science honours degree, and have not written off medical school yet. I know that another period of dialysis, and hopefully a transplant, is inevitable. I was extremely lucky to have two parents who were willing, and able to donate to me. However my kidney is 53 years old, so will not live forever. I hope that C3G is not the reason for this, but it is the reason that I have spent the last 15 years in and out of hospital. I have been told that another transplant may not be possible due to the

## **Part 2: Key messages** 

In up to 5 sentences, please summarise the key messages of your statement: 

- C3G currently has no cure or effective treatments, except dialysis and transplant, which merely delay end-stage renal failure and do not target the specific mechanism of the disease. 

- C3G is extremely disruptive to patient’s lives, as not only will it lead to the requirement of dialysis, but the gradual deterioration is physically, mentally and emotionally difficult for patients and their families. 

- Iptacopan is the first in kind treatment for C3G and has been shown to be effective. 

- Iptacopan has the potential to prevent other patients from requiring dialysis, an expensive treatment that holds a low quality of life, whether they have their native kidneys or have been transplanted. 

- Iptacopan is easy to administer, and causes little to no side effects. 

Thank you for your time.

## **1. Executive summary** 

This summary provides a brief overview of the key issues identified by the External Assessment Group (EAG) as being potentially important for decision making. If possible, it also includes the EAG’s preferred assumptions and the resulting incremental cost-effectiveness ratios (ICERs). 

Section 1.1 provides an overview of the key issues. Section 1.2 presents the key model outcomes. Section 1.3 discusses the decision problem (DP), Section 1.4 issues relate to the clinical effectiveness, and Section 1.5 issues related to the cost effectiveness. A summary in presented in Section 1.6. 

Background information on the condition, technology and evidence and information on key as well as non-key issues are in the main EAG report, see Sections 2 (DP), 3 (clinical effectiveness) and 4 (cost effectiveness) for more details. 

All issues identified represent the EAG’s view, not the opinion of the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE).

## **1.2 Overview of key model outcomes** 

NICE Technology Appraisals (TAs) compare how much a new technology improves length (overall survival) and quality of life in a quality-adjusted life year (QALY). An ICER is the ratio of the extra cost for every QALY gained. 

11 



<!-- page 428 -->

CONFIDENTIAL UNTIL PUBLISHED 

Overall, the technology is modelled to affect QALYs by: 

- Increased time to disease progression with incremental QALYs in chronic kidney disease (CKD) stage 1-4 of 4.93 (283% of total deterministic incremental QALYs). 

Overall, the technology is modelled to affect costs by: 

- Increased acquisition costs (with Patient Access Scheme [PAS]) in iptacopan + standard of care (SoC) arm (increased costs of XXXXXX, XXX of the total deterministic incremental costs). 

The modelling assumptions that have the greatest effect on the ICER are: 

- The assumption that the iptacopan before-after comparison using APPEAR-C3G including the open-label extension study is reflective of treatment effectiveness in United Kingdom (UK) clinical practice. The upper (10.39) and lower (3.48) parameter values of the (deterministic) one-way sensitivity analysis of iptacopan treatment effectiveness resulted in ICERs of XXXXXX and XXXXXX, respectively.

## **1.6 Summary of the EAG’s view** 

The estimated EAG base-case ICER (probabilistic), based on the EAG preferred assumptions highlighted in Section 5.1, was £ XXXXXX per QALY gained. The probabilistic EAG base-case analyses indicated cost effectiveness probabilities of X% at willingness-to-pay (WTP) thresholds of £20,000 and £30,000 per QALY gained. The most influential adjustment was estimating the estimated glomerular filtration (eGFR) slope for SoC based on National Registry of Rare Kidney Diseases (RaDaR) data and subsequently applying the iptacopan treatment effect from the randomised double-blind period of APPEAR-C3G to inform the iptacopan eGFR slope. The EAG’s ICER increased most in the scenario analysis with alternative assumptions regarding kidney replacement therapy (KRT) utilities. 

In conclusion, there is large remaining uncertainty about the effectiveness and cost effectiveness of iptacopan + SoC, which can be partly resolved by the company. This includes providing CKD stagedependent and time-dependent eGFR decline rates, full details of the time to treatment discontinuation (TTD) model selection process based on the NICE Decision Support Unit (DSU) Technical Support Document (TSD) 14 guidance, analyses to assess the assumption of a constant treatment effect during and beyond the observed period, analyses of additional (patient-level) European Quality of Life-5 Dimensions (EQ-5D) data on CKD stage 5+ patients, explanation and justification of the mechanisms by which the economic model generated a substantial proportion of QALYs and costs beyond the observed data, and providing the full advisory board meeting minutes. Therefore, the EAG believes that the CS nor the EAG report contains an unbiased ICER of iptacopan + SoC compared with SoC.

## **2.1 Population** 

The population in the decision problem (DP) is the same as in the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) scope i.e. adults with complement 3 glomerulopathy (C3G).[1, 2] 

In fact, the proposed positioning of iptacopan is shown in Figure 5 of the company submission (CS) and stated to be: _“…in patients who remain at risk of disease progression.”_ No other description of the population is provided. 

**EAG comment:** There is a lack of clarity in the population eligible for iptacopan. In response to the request for subgroup analysis in the NICE scope, the company state: _“While the Phase 2 trial included a cohort of patients with post-transplant recurrence of C3G, the trial was single-arm and the sample size was considered too small (N=11) to robustly inform economic modelling in a post-transplant subgroup. Therefore, the economic analyses presented are based on data in native kidney patients. Given that the underlying disease mechanism is the same in native kidney and post-transplant recurrent C3G, UK clinicians advised that iptacopan data in native kidney patients are considered transferable to transplanted patients.”_ (see Table 2.1). This would imply that the C3G recurrence post-transplant subgroup is included in the DP population even if there is no subgroup analysis. 

In conclusion, it appears that the DP population includes both native and post-transplant C3G recurrence, although this is unclear and therefore can be regarded as a key issue. It also raises the questions as to the appropriate comparator for this subgroup. 

## **2.2 Intervention** 

The intervention in the DP is the same as in the NICE scope i.e. iptacopan, given as 200 mg twice daily (b.i.d.) in combination with established clinical management (ECM), comprising of angiotensinconverting enzyme inhibitors/angiotensin II receptor blockers (ACEis/ARBs) (unless not tolerated or contraindicated), with some patients also being on corticosteroids (CoS), mycophenolate mofetil (MMF) and/or sodium-glucose co-transporter-2 inhibitor (SGLT2is).[1, 2] This aligns with the design of the iptacopan clinical trials, in which patients were administered iptacopan on top of these background therapies. 

## **2.3 Comparators** 

The comparators in the NICE scope are: 

- ECM without iptacopan, which may include: 

   - ACEis 

   - ARBs 

   - CoS 

   - MMF 

   - SGLT2is 

- In people who have previously had a kidney transplant and who have highly aggressive C3G recurrence as specified in the NHS England clinical commissioning policy for eculizumab: 

   - Eculizumab 

However, DP excludes eculizumab on the basis that it is considered of limited relevance as a comparator because in United Kingdom (UK) clinical practice its use is uncommon, with the National Health 

28 



<!-- page 445 -->

CONFIDENTIAL UNTIL PUBLISHED 

Service (NHS) England commissioning policy restricting use to a small subgroup among patients with post-transplant recurrence, and its use is limited to patients with highly aggressive recurrent disease. 

**EAG comment:** Therefore, in the clarification letter the company were asked to include eculizumab as a comparator in clinical effectiveness analyses and a cost-effectiveness analysis (CEA) for the appropriate subgroup as used in UK clinical practice, or exclude this subgroup from the DP.[3] The company responded:[4] _“There is no head-to-head data for iptacopan versus eculizumab in C3G, and, as further explained in the response to clarification question A11, an indirect treatment comparison is deemed infeasible. It was therefore not possible to include eculizumab as a comparator within the costeffectiveness model.”_ 

They went on to argue that eculizumab use is extremely limited in UK clinical practice (~1 patient per year on average) and is of reduced relevance in light of the fact that iptacopan would be delivered at an earlier point in the care pathway given that NHS England criteria require evidence of a significant decline of transplant function (>20% decline in estimated glomerular filtration rate [eGFR]) within the previous 3 months before eculizumab can be initiated, in contrast with iptacopan, which: _“…can be started as soon as recurrence is diagnosed via biopsy of the transplanted kidney, and before the onset of clinical signs such as eGFR decline.  this is in line with the available clinical trial evidence from the iptacopan Phase 2 study (see CS Section 2.5.1) and the draft SmPC (section 4.2).”_ This might indicate that, if recurrent C3G post-transplant patients were treated with iptacopan then they would never become eligible for eculizumab, which would rule it out as a comparator. However, this can only be the case if iptacopan is found to be cost effective and recommended at this earlier point in the care pathway. This uncertainty implies a key issue, notwithstanding the uncertainty in the DP population described above. 

## **2.4 Outcomes** 

The outcomes in the DP are in line with those in the NICE scope. 

## **2.5 Subgroup analyses** 

The company did not perform any of the subgroup analyses specified in the NICE scope. In particular, they stated that the only trial data to inform those patients with C3G recurrence post-transplant was from the very small single arm Phase 2 trial, and that the mechanism of action of iptacopan would imply the generalisability from the APPEAR trial, which was in the native population.[1] However, an indirect treatment comparison (ITC) could have been performed, albeit with much uncertainty given the small sample size. Therefore, the lack of subgroup analysis for this population is a key issue.

## **3. Clinical effectiveness** 

## **3.1 Critique of the methods of review(s)** 

The company performed a systematic literature review (SLR) to identify and summarise the available randomised controlled trial (RCT) and other relevant evidence relating to the efficacy and safety of iptacopan and other interventions for the treatment of adults with C3G. 

## _**3.1.1 Searches**_ 

The following paragraphs contain summaries and critiques of the searches related to clinical effectiveness presented in the CS.[1] Canada's Drug Agency (formerly the Canadian Agency for Drugs and Technologies in Health [CADTH]) evidence-based checklist for the Peer Review of Electronic Search Strategies (PRESS) was used to inform this critique.[5] The EAG has presented only the major limitations of each search strategy in the report. 

Appendix B of the CS details the SLR conducted to identify published evidence on the clinical efficacy and safety of iptacopan and any potentially relevant comparators in the treatment of C3G.[6] 

## **EAG comment:** 

- Searches were undertaken to identify published evidence on the clinical efficacy and safety of iptacopan and any potentially relevant comparators in the treatment of C3G. The CS, Appendix B and the company’s response to clarification provided sufficient details for the EAG to appraise the literature searches.[1, 4, 6] 

- The following databases were searched from inception on 3 October 2021 and updated on 14 October 2024: Embase, MEDLINE, the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews (CDSR) and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL). 

- Three key conference proceedings (European Renal Association - European Dialysis and Transplant Association [ERA-EDTA], the American Society of Nephrology [ASN] and the World Congress of Nephrology [WCN]) were searched on 16 December 2021 and updated on 18-22 October 2024. 

- The following trials registries were searched on 16 November 2021 and updated on 22 October 2024: www.ClinicalTrials.gov, the World Health Organisation International Clinical Trials Registry Platform (WHO ICTRP) and the European Union Clinical Trials Register (EUCTR). 

- Ten regulatory and Health Technology Assessment (HTA) bodies' websites, the Database of Abstracts of Reviews of Effects (DARE), the NHS Economic Evaluation Database (NHS EED) and the HTA database were searched in October 2024. Bibliographies of systematic reviews and metaanalyses and other selected studies were reference checked. Supplementary searches were conducted on Google and Google Scholar. 

- No date or language limits were applied to the searches. 

- The database searches for the clinical effectiveness SLR consisted of a single search facet for C3G. In the MEDLINE and Embase searches this was then combined with study design filters designed to limit results to controlled trials and non-randomised clinical trials. This broader approach to the search strategy design ensured that no relevant records were likely to be missed, as no intervention/comparator search facet was included to potentially limit the results. 

- All searches were transparent and reproducible, and contained a good range of search terms, synonyms and subject headings.

## _**3.1.2 Inclusion criteria**_ 

The company provided details on their eligibility criteria in Appendix B of the CS.[1] It is apparent that this represents a broad criteria going so far as to being vague. The Table includes the same entry for intervention and comparator and describes outcomes as ‘ _including but not limited to’_ . This Table should be clear, should be specific and should eliminate or minimise ambiguity as to be able to determine precisely what the company are looking to include but this is not the case here.

|---|---|---|
|**Population**|Patients diagnosed with C3G<br>Studies including patients classified<br>as MPGN type II (now referred to<br>as DDD)were also included.|Any other patient population.<br>Studies conducted in mixed patient<br>population without reporting C3G-<br>specific data.|

## _**3.1.3 Critique of data screening and extraction**_ 

The CS states that study selection occurred  in two stages: titles and abstracts were reviewed then full texts of potentially relevant articles were screened in order to obtain the final list of included studies. 

31 



<!-- page 448 -->

CONFIDENTIAL UNTIL PUBLISHED 

Each record was screened by two independent reviewers, with any discrepancies between reviewers reconciled with the help of a third independent reviewer, at both abstract and full-text searching stage. 

The EAG acknowledges that this method of screening is optimal to minimise risks of bias and error. However, the CS states that for data extraction, one reviewer performed the task, with a second reviewer being involved to conduct checks. This is a well-used method, however, it increases the likelihood of errors and bias and so the preferred method would have been used for screening, with two independent reviewers. The EAG asked the company to confirm how disagreements between the reviewer and the checker were resolved. In their response to clarification the company stated that ‘ _any discrepancies in data extraction were discussed between the two reviewers. If consensus could not be reached, a third independent reviewer was consulted to make a final decision_ ’.[4] 

**EAG comment:** The EAG is satisfied that screening and data extraction was conducted with an appropriate method to minimise bias and error. We do of course highlight that this was not the optimal method and always recommend that such tasks are competed in duplicate independently. 

## _**3.1.4 Quality assessment**_ 

The APPEAR-C3G trial was assessed using the Cochrane Risk of Bias 2 tool (see Table 3.2), while the single-arm Phase 2 trial was assessed using the Cochrane Risk Of Bias In Non-randomised Studies – Intervention (ROBINS-I) tool (see Table 3.3). APPEAR-C3G was determined to be at low risk of bias, while the Phase 2 trial was considered to be associated with a moderate risk of bias. 

Quality appraisals were conducted by one reviewer and then checked by another. As with screening and data extraction, this represents a widely used method but one that has an increased risk of bias and error compared to appraisals conducted independently by two reviewers. We asked the company to clarify how disagreements between reviewers were resolved. In their response to clarification the company stated that ‘ _any discrepancies in data extraction were discussed between the two reviewers. If consensus could not be reached, a third independent reviewer was consulted to make a final decision_ ’.[4]

## **3.2 Critique of trials of the technology of interest, their analysis and interpretation (and any standard meta-analyses of these)** 

## _**3.2.1 Study retrieval**_ 

The CS reports that a SLR was conducted in October–December 2021 and updated in October 2024. The company acknowledges the SLR scope was broad, including randomised and non-randomised clinical trials in patients diagnosed with C3G, in receipt of any intervention for C3G.[1] 

One thousand, four hundred and eighty-one citations were identified in the database searches resulting in 1,461 citations for title and abstract screening after the removal of duplicates. Forty-nine citations were identified for the full-text review. Of these, 10 records were included. Grey literature searches identified five relevant records. Of these 15 included records, four were each linked to another publication resulting in 11 unique studies (see Figure 3.1). Seven hundred and thirty-four citations were identified in the SLR update. Seven hundred and five citations were title and abstract screened after duplicate removal. Of these, 34 citations were identified for the full-text review. Seven records were included. Grey literature searches identified 11 relevant records. Therefore, a total of 18 records were included from the SLR update (see Figure 3.2). Thirteen of these 18 records were linked to studies included in the original SLR, while five records described four unique studies not previously identified. 

By completion of the update, 33 publications reporting on 15 unique studies were included. Two studies included patients with C3G who were treated with iptacopan (APPEAR-C3G and the Phase 2 trial, with open-label extension study results for patients originating from the Phase 2 trial included as linked publications for the Phase 2 trial).

## _**3.2.2 Summary of details for the trials**_ 

This Section will provide a summary and description of the relevant trials as they are presented and described in the CS.[1] 

## _**3.2.2.1 APPEAR-C3G**_ 

APPEAR-C3G (NCT04817618) is an international, multicentre, randomised, double-blind, parallel group, placebo-controlled Phase 3 study to evaluate the efficacy and safety of iptacopan in patients with native kidney C3G.[1] It is comprised of a screening/run-in period (see Figure 3.3) lasting up to 90 days; a 6-month double-blind treatment period, during which patients received blinded treatment with 200 mg iptacopan or placebo orally b.i.d. (randomisation 1:1); and a 6-month open-label treatment period, during which all patients received open-label iptacopan 200 mg orally b.i.d.[1] 

Following completion of study treatment at 12 months, patients were given the option to discontinue iptacopan treatment and enter a 30-day safety follow-up period or continue iptacopan treatment by transitioning to a roll-over open-label extension.[1] This submission only considers the adult cohort of the trial, in line with the patient population described in the decision problem.[1]

Seventy-four patients were enrolled in the adult cohort, with 38 patients randomised to the iptacopan arm and 36 randomised to the placebo arm. All 74 patients completed the 6-month double-blind period.[1] Two patients in the iptacopan arm discontinued double-blind treatment. Both of these patients continued double-blind study visits (without treatment) until the end of the double-blind period, and then transitioned to the open-label period where they attended study visits and received open-label Iptacopan.[1] Seventy-three patients completed the full 12 months of the study (6 months double-blind period plus 6 months open-label period). One patient originally randomised to the placebo arm discontinued treatment during the open-label period, with the reason recorded as patient decision, was lost to follow-up and discontinued from the study.[1] 

## _**3.2.2.2 Supportive evidence**_ 

Two studies were identified that provide supportive evidence of the clinical efficacy of iptacopan for the treatment of patients with C3G. This is the Phase 2 study and the open label extension study. The open label extension study provide data on the long-term clinical efficacy and safety of iptacopan in C3G, as it represents the longest follow-up period in the clinical trial programme for iptacopan in C3G.[1] These trials are briefly summarised below. 

## _3.2.2.2.1 Phase 2 Study_ 

The Phase 2 study (NCT03832114) was an international, multicentre, open-label, single-arm, nonrandomised study in adults with biopsy-confirmed C3G. Two cohorts of patients were included, one with native kidney C3G (native kidney cohort; Cohort A) and one with C3G recurrence following kidney transplantation (post-transplant recurrent cohort; Cohort B). All patients received iptacopan b.i.d. for 12 weeks. A total of 27 patients were enrolled and completed the study: 16 in the native kidney cohort and 11 in the post-transplant recurrent cohort.[1] Figure 3.4 and Table 3.3 provide details.

The trial included a screening period comprised of run-in (≤60 days) and a 30-day baseline period. Patients then entered treatment period 1 (12 weeks), with dose escalation of iptacopan up to 200 mg b.i.d. At Week 12, kidney biopsies were collected; which were optional for the native kidney cohort but mandatory for the post-transplant recurrent cohort.[1] Following 12 weeks of treatment in the Phase 2 study, patients could roll over to the extension study if treatment continuation was found to be beneficial. If continuation of treatment was not deemed beneficial by the investigator, study medication was titrated down to 25 mg once daily for 7 days, followed by 10 mg once daily for a further 7 days. The patient then continued in the follow-up period (12 weeks) until the end-of-study (EOS) visit.[1]

## _**3.2.4 Baseline characteristics**_ 

Baseline characteristics were provided in the CS[1] to describe the relevant populations. In the APPEARC3G trial 74 patients enrolled in the study, 47 were male (63.5%) and 27 were female (36.5%). The majority of patients were of White race (68.9%) and from study sites in Europe (55.4%). The mean (SD) age of all patients was 27.9 (10.7) years. 

The CS states that ‘ _The treatment arms were generally balanced; however, there were imbalances between groups in some baseline disease characteristics_ ’.[1] The EAG considers any differences between groups of 5% to be relevant and noteworthy. We do not necessarily make the claim that such differences will reflect clinical or statistically meaningful difference, but we emphasise this to ensure that this is taken into consideration when interpreting the results. The iptacopan group had more males than the placebo group (71.1% versus 55.6%), as well as differences in baseline urine protein-to-creatinine ratio (UPCR) (24-hours) ≥339 g/mol [3 g/g] (55.3% versus 30.6%). The iptacopan arm had notably lower eGFR at baseline, compared with those from the placebo arm (89.30 versus 99.22) with more patients having an eGFR at baseline of <60 ml/min/1.73 m[2  ] (26.3% versus 11.1%), and less at ≥60 ml/min/1.73 m[2  ] (73.7% versus 88.9%) (see Table 3.8). The EAG considers such imbalances to be significant and impactful.

The EAG asked the company to provide information on how these differences between the characteristics of the two arms would impact the results.[3] In their response to the request for clarification, the company stated that ‘… _The baseline imbalances suggest a more severe disease phenotype in the participants in the iptacopan arm. This was also noted by UK clinicians participating in an advisory board, and they suggested that due to this, comparisons between iptacopan and placebo groups may therefore underestimate the iptacopan treatment effect_ ’.[4] 

As a consequence of these acknowledged imbalances, the company provided details on post hoc analyses which were described within the CS but also replicated in the clarification response.[4] The company stated that ‘ _The results of these post-hoc sensitivity analyses were consistent with the results_ ’[4] _of the primary analysis, suggesting that these baseline imbalances did not impact the UPCR endpoint_ . 

The company also stated that ‘ _The pre-specified analysis of CfB in eGFR included the background immunosuppression stratification factor (corticosteroids and/or mycophenolic acid treatment at randomisation) and baseline eGFR as covariates. Additional post-hoc sensitivity analyses were carried out to assess the impact of adjusting for other baseline covariates where imbalances had been observed_ . _…The adjustments for age at C3G diagnosis or subtype of C3G yielded results consistent with the prespecified analysis ._ ’ The company emphasize that ‘ _the CfB in eGFR analysis adjusted for baseline UPCR resulted in a larger numerical improvement for iptacopan versus placebo when compared to the pre-_

It is clear from the table above that there were minimal UK based participates involved in this trial with only nine in total. Minor imbalances beyond 5% were present across some characteristics including but not limited to those in the iptacopan group being younger and having more patients with lower 

53 



<!-- page 470 -->

CONFIDENTIAL UNTIL PUBLISHED 

eGFR (<60 ml/min/1.73 m[2] ). However, given the small sample of nine, differences by proportion will obviously be larger and appear more pronounced, when in reality these differences reflect only a few patients. The EAG therefore, does not consider these to be remarkable, however the presentation of data that has so few UK based participants does not allow for consideration of meaningful generalisability. 

A particular interest to the EAG was how the data in this submission could be generalised to the population of England and Wales. The EAG requested information on this and in the company’s response stated that ‘ _in a UK advisory board, clinical experts were aligned that the inclusion criteria of the APPEAR-C3G and Phase 2 trials were valid, and that the trial populations were reflective of patients with C3G seen in UK clinical practice. For example, the advisors agreed that the concomitant medications (including ACEi/ARBs) in APPEAR-C3G were appropriate and representative of management of C3G patients within UK clinical practice, and that C3G patients generally present with UPCR levels well above 1 g/g (≥113 mg/mmol). The trial generalisability to the C3G population in England and Wales was further supported by the fact that several UK study sites had participated in the_ trials’[4] . 

The company go on to provide tabulated data showing a comparison of patient characteristics in APPEAR-C3G and the C3G population of National Registry of Rare Kidney Diseases (RaDaR) data from patients with C3G in the UK which reflects the clinical characteristics of relevant UK based patients. The EAG noted that the RaDaR study indicated that the baseline patient characteristics in the APPEAR-C3G potentially do not accurately reflect UK clinical practice as the proportion of females in APPEAR-C3G is lower and the clinical characteristics (e.g. mean eGFR and chronic kidney disease [CKD] stage) do seem to reflect a healthier population in APPEAR-C3G.  However, the company reiterated that ‘ _Median age at diagnosis was similar in APPEAR-C3G and the RaDaR cohort. Age at latest follow-up was higher in the prevalent RaDaR cohort than in APPEAR-C3G patients at baseline. The lower percentage of females in APPEAR-C3G (36.5%) compared to RaDaR (47%) was noted by UK clinicians as a common finding in clinical trials, especially in young age groups where pregnancy is a concern._ ’[4]

**EAG comment:** The EAG noted that there were imbalances in relevant baseline characteristics between the intervention arm and control arm of the APPEAR-C3G trial. The EAG asked the company to discuss the impact of these imbalances in relevant baseline characteristics between the two arms on the results being derived from the APPEAR-C3G trial. In responding to the EAG’s request, the company provided 

56 



<!-- page 473 -->

CONFIDENTIAL UNTIL PUBLISHED 

a response, and the company also performed post-hoc sensitivity analyses due to these imbalances. The EAG considered that the results of these post-hoc sensitivity analyses where these imbalanced baseline characteristics were adjusted for were generally consistent with the results of the primary analysis. 

The EAG did not consider the inclusion of nine patients derived from three sites across the UK as constituting a meaningful representation of ‘ _several UK study sites’_ or of a meaningful number of patients to justify supportive of generalisability. The EAG also notes that there are differences in characteristics between trial patients and those in _RaDaR_ cohort, and while clinical opinion and advice is important and valid and has suggested the trial populations can be generalised, little evidence was presented to support such a generalisation. 

## _**3.2.5 External validity**_ 

The EAG has some concerns about the applicability and generalisability of the included trials to the relevant population in England and Wales. Primarily we do not think it clear as to whether the DP population includes both native and post-transplant C3G recurrence and the relevance and generalisability of the trial population to the clinical population of England and Wales is of limited evidence, with some differences in characteristics with the RaDAR cohort, and with minimal involvement of UK based sites (three) and participants (nine). Additionally, the EAG highlights that the DP excludes eculizumab on the basis that it is considered of minimal relevance as a comparator, however if recurrent C3G post-transplant patients were treated with current ECM then they might receive it. This uncertainty is obviously a concern. The EAG is of the position an ITC could have been performed to generate data relevant to this subpopulation. 

**EAG comment:** Concerns exist around the relevance and generalisability of the included data to the clinical population in England and Wales, and particularly C3G post-transplant patients.

The EAG noted that there was a big increase in CfB of eGFR at Day 14 for the iptacopan arm of the APPEAR-C3G trial. The EAG asked the company to provide an explanation for this big increase in CfB of eGFR at Day 14 for the iptacopan arm of the APPEAR-C3G. In responding to the EAG’s request, the company provided the following response: 

- _“C3G patients experience overactivation of the complement alternative pathway which leads to deposition of complement component 3 (C3) within the glomeruli, triggering inflammation. Two UK clinicians consulted on a call to obtain clinical expert input for Novartis’ response to the EAG’s clarification questions assumed that the numerical increase in eGFR at Day 14 following iptacopan initiation is due to the rapid resolution of the intense inflammation in the kidney of C3G patients through alternative pathway inhibition._ 

- _The increase in eGFR on Day 14 of iptacopan treatment was transient and short-term, with the Day 30 mean eGFR value on a similar level as subsequent measurements.”_ 

The company further provided a sensitivity analysis on eGFR slope which excluded the data of Day 14 measurements (see Table 3.20 below).

## _**3.2.6.7 Exploratory efficacy results: effect of iptacopan on complement biomarkers**_ 

The company reported that “ _With iptacopan treatment, there was a rapid rise in serum C3 levels, which was sustained throughout the study, while the C3 concentration in the placebo arm remained unchanged. In addition, decreases were observed with iptacopan in alternative pathway activity, plasma Bb, plasma sC5b-9 and urinary sC5b-9. Circulating biomarker levels were measured up to Month 12, to demonstrate the change in inhibition of the complement pathway following initiation of iptacopan treatment in the placebo-iptacopan switch arm. A sustained increase of serum C3 in the iptacopan arm was observed for the entire 12 months treatment period, as well as a rapid rise in placebo arm patients after switching to iptacopan at Day 180, mirroring the effect seen in the iptacopan arm in the double-blind period._ ”[1] Further details can be found in Table 3.26.

## _**3.2.7 Adverse events**_ 

The safety sets presented in this Section are shown below:[1] 

- The controlled safety set (N=74) includes data from the 6-month double-blind placebo-controlled period of APPEAR-C3G from all adult patients who received at least one dose of iptacopan 200 mg b.i.d. (N=38) or placebo (N=36) 

- The broad safety set (N=101) includes data from all adult patients who received at least one dose of iptacopan 200 mg b.i.d. in the treatment period of any of the three iptacopan studies in C3G (Phase 2, APPEAR-C3G, and the ongoing open-label extension study), up to the data cut-off date of 6 May 2024.
