## _**3.2.7.4 Deaths**_ 

The company reported that “ _One death occurred across the three C3G studies, during the open-label extension study. The cause of death was presumed to be cardiac arrhythmia that the investigator did not consider to be related to iptacopan._ ”[1] 

**EAG comment:** The company was asked to clarify the details of the one death and clarify any cardiovascular (CV) events reported, given the potential link between complement inhibition (or lack of it) and thrombosis. The company detailed that “ _A 24-year-old patient, originally in the Phase 2 Study, was found unresponsive and declared dead on Day 501. Post-mortem examination revealed no obvious_ 

76 



<!-- page 493 -->

CONFIDENTIAL UNTIL PUBLISHED 

_cause of death. The evidence pointing to cardiac arrhythmia included arteriolar-nephrosclerosis, a clinical history of C3G, hypertension, focal myocardial scar, and a clinical history of hypocalcaemia. The patient had pre-existing conditions including anxiety, palpitations, and hyperparathyroidism. Possible confounders for the event included concomitant medications of methylphenidate (potential adverse drug reactions [ADRs] of tachycardia and arrhythmia), venlafaxine (potential ADRs of tachycardia and arrhythmia) as well as trazodone (warning for QT prolongation)_ .” 

The company also provided the details of the CV events in the broad safety set in the iptacopan clinical trials in C3G, in Table 3.33 below. The company further stated that “ _across the clinical studies included in the marketing authorisation application for iptacopan in its first indication (paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria [PNH]), no clinically meaningful abnormalities in cardiac safety-related assessments were observed._ ”[4]

## _**3.2.7.5 Treatment discontinuations due to AEs**_ 

The company reported that “ _No treatment discontinuations due to TEAEs were reported in the controlled safety set. In the broad safety set, three patients discontinued iptacopan treatment due to TEAEs during the ongoing open-label extension study. All three cases were due to SAEs not related to iptacopan treatment, as determined by the investigator._ ”[1] 

The company also reported that “ _In the controlled safety set, TEAEs leading to study treatment interruption were reported in 10.5% and 11.1% of patients in the iptacopan and placebo groups, respectively. The most frequently reported TEAE leading to interruption of iptacopan treatment was COVID-19 (reported in four patients, 10.5%). In the broad safety set, TEAEs leading to study treatment interruption were reported in 10.9% of patients. In addition, one patient had a temporary dose reduction due to non-serious tonsillar hypertrophy._ ”[1] 

**EAG comment:** The company was asked to clarify the nature of these SAEs and the rationale for concluding that they were unrelated to iptacopan, as the CS stated that three patients discontinued iptacopan due to AEs (all in the open-label extension study), with SAEs determined not to be related to iptacopan. The company provided the details regarding the three patients who discontinued iptacopan due to SAEs in the open-label extension study, 

- _“One patient discontinued iptacopan due to an SAE of renal impairment_ 

77 



<!-- page 494 -->

CONFIDENTIAL UNTIL PUBLISHED 

- _One patient discontinued iptacopan due to an SAE of C3G (post-transplant recurrent patient with C3G progression confirmed in kidney biopsy)_ 

- _One patient discontinued iptacopan due to an SAE of acute kidney injury from immune complex glomerulonephritis (post-transplant recurrent patient with several confounding events leading to eGFR decline, none of which were suspected to be related to iptacopan by the investigator; the investigator suspected postinfectious, crescentic glomerulonephritis on top of not yet remitted C3G as the cause of the acute kidney injury)”_[4] 

## _**3.2.7.6 Adverse events of special interest**_ 

The company reported that “ _The AEs of special interest for iptacopan were determined based on its mechanism of action, pre-clinical safety studies and clinical studies, and include infections caused by encapsulated bacteria, testicular effects, thyroid changes, malignancy, hypersensitivity, and decreased platelets._ ”[1] 

The company further reported that “ _In the controlled safety set, three patients in the iptacopan group and one patient in the placebo group were reported to have infections caused by encapsulated bacteria. Additionally, one patient in the placebo group experienced a non-serious TEAE of blood thyroid stimulating hormone increased. In the broad safety set, 10 patients (including the three described above in the controlled safety set) were reported to have infections caused by encapsulated bacteria. Most patients had infections that were non-serious and not considered to be related to iptacopan treatment. All infections resolved and patients either continued iptacopan treatment or resumed after resolution of the infection. Additionally, eight patients reported AEs recorded as hypersensitivity, but these were not considered related to iptacopan treatment. No AEs of special interest related to testicular effect, malignancy or decreased platelet count were reported in either safety population._ ”[1] Further details can be found in Table 3.34.

## **3.5 Conclusions of the clinical effectiveness Section** 

The CS, Appendix B and response to clarification[1, 4, 6] provided sufficient details for the EAG to appraise the literature searches conducted to identify relevant clinical evidence on the clinical efficacy and safety of iptacopan and any potentially relevant comparators in the treatment of C3G. Searches were conducted in October-December 2021 and updated in October 2024. Searches were transparent and reproducible, and a good range of bibliographic databases, conference proceedings, trials registers and grey literature resources were searched. Overall, the EAG has no concerns about the literature searches conducted. 

The study selection criteria for participants, interventions, comparators and outcomes in the SLR of clinical effectiveness generally encompassed those specified by the NICE final scope. The data extraction process was satisfactory and in line with recommended good practice in SLRs. The process for the assessment of risk of bias in the included studies was satisfactory. The process of assessing risk of bias and the number of reviewers involved were described. The number of studies retrieved, screened 

81 



<!-- page 498 -->

CONFIDENTIAL UNTIL PUBLISHED 

and included was clear based on the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic reviews and MetaAnalyses (PRISMA) flow chart. 

One pivotal RCT was identified as being relevant to the SLR: one RCT (APPEAR-C3G) provided the main source of evidence. APPEAR-C3G (NCT04817618) is an international, multicentre, randomised, double-blind, parallel group, placebo-controlled Phase 3 study to evaluate the efficacy and safety of iptacopan in patients with native kidney C3G. Phase 2 study [NCT03832114] and an open label extension study were identified that provided supportive evidence of the clinical efficacy of iptacopan for the treatment of patients with C3G. The Phase 2 study (NCT03832114) was an international, multicentre, open-label, single-arm, non-randomised study in adults with biopsy-confirmed C3G. The open label extension study provided data on the long-term clinical efficacy and safety of iptacopan for the treatment of patients with C3G. 

The results of APPEAR-C3G trial showed that, at 6-month follow-up (double-blind period), iptacopan treatment was associated with a statistically significant reduction in 24-hour UPCR by 35.1% (95% confidence interval [CI]: 13.8%, 51.1%) following 6 months of treatment compared with placebo (both arms as add-on to background therapy). The results from the open-label period of APPEAR-C3G showed that among patients initially randomised to iptacopan, the observed reduction in 24-hour UPCR was sustained up to Month 12 (40% geometric mean reduction from baseline; geometric mean ratio 0.60 (95% CI: 0.45, 0.80). At 6-month follow-up (double-blind period), the adjusted mean difference (MD) of eGFR for iptacopan treatment versus placebo was 2.16 ml/min/1.73 m[2] (95% CI: −2.75, 7.06). The results from the open-label period of APPEAR-C3G showed that at 12-month followup, the mean changes from baseline in eGFR in the iptacopan arm and the placebo-iptacopan switch arm were 0.44 ml/min/1.73 m[2] (95% CI: −3.76, 4.64) and 1.15 ml/min/1.73 m[2] (95% CI: −3.22, 5.53), respectively. 

In terms of the ITC analysis, the company stated in the evidence submission that ITC analysis for the comparison of iptacopan versus eculizumab was not feasible because the outcome (eGFR) used in the economic model was not reported in the eculizumab trials. Therefore, the EAG asked the company to conduct ITC analyses based on other outcomes (e.g. proteinuria) that were reported in the eculizumab trials for the subgroup of patients who have previously had a kidney transplant and who have highly aggressive C3G recurrence, with the use of the post-transplant recurrent cohort of the Phase 2 trial of iptacopan. 

In responding to the EAG’s request, the company stated that an ITC of proteinuria outcomes was not considered meaningful due to marked differences in the eculizumab trial populations and the patients included in the post-transplant recurrent cohort of the iptacopan Phase 2 trial. The three eculizumab trials enrolled patients with proteinuria >3.5 g/day, proteinuria ≥3 g/day, and proteinuria >1 g/day, respectively. However, elevated proteinuria was not an inclusion criterion for the post-transplant cohort in the iptacopan Phase 2 trial; the enrolled patients’ proteinuria levels were predominantly normal at baseline, with a geo-mean of 0.28 g/day. 

The EAG agreed that given the substantial differences of proteinuria levels at baseline between the included patients from the included eculizumab trials and the patients included in the post-transplant recurrent cohort of the iptacopan Phase 2 trial, it would be less meaningful to conduct an ITC based on proteinuria outcomes from these trials. 

Given that an ITC analysis for the comparison of iptacopan versus eculizumab was not conducted for the subgroup of patients who have previously had a kidney transplant and who have highly aggressive

## _**4.2.2 Model structure**_ 

A de novo health-state transition model was developed using a state-transition (Markov) approach to simulate the progression of CKD through to kidney failure and kidney replacement therapy (KRT). The model comprises nine mutually exclusive health states (HSs) (CS, Figure 27): 

1. CKD stage 1 (eGFR ≥90 ml/min/1.73 m²) 

2. CKD stage 2 (eGFR 60–89 ml/min/1.73 m²) 

3. CKD stage 3a (eGFR 45–59 ml/min/1.73 m²) 

4. CKD stage 3b (eGFR 30–44 ml/min/1.73 m²) 

5. CKD stage 4 (eGFR 15–29 ml/min/1.73 m²) 

6. CKD stage 5 (eGFR 8–15 ml/min/1.73 m²) 

7. Dialysis (KRT initiated at eGFR ≤7.6 ml/min/1.73 m²) 

8. Post-transplant (KRT initiated at eGFR ≤7.6 ml/min/1.73 m²) 

9. Death 

Key model assumptions: 

- Disease progression assumptions 

   - eGFR was assumed to decline at a constant rate, regardless of CKD stage. 

   - Transitions to less severe CKD stages were not allowed (i.e., no backward transitions). 

   - Death was modelled as an absorbing state and could be reached from any other HS. 

- Treatment-related assumptions 

   - A constant treatment effect was assumed over time, conditional on patients remaining on treatment. 

   - Patients discontinuing iptacopan were assumed to receive SoC alone after which no residual iptacopan treatment effect was assumed 

   - Patients on iptacopan were assumed to stop treatment at the point of commencing KRT. 

   - Patients on SoC were also assumed to stop treatment at the point of commencing KRT, except for ACEis/ARBs which were continued during KRT. 

- Initiation of KRT 

   - The threshold for initiating KRT was set at eGFR ≤7.6 ml/min/1.73 m² (see CS Section 3.3.2.2). At this point, patients either received a pre-emptive transplant (moving to the ‘Post-transplant’ state) or initiated chronic dialysis (‘Dialysis’ state). 

   - All patients with C3G were assumed to commence KRT following kidney failure; conservative management was not considered. 

- Dialysis and transplant assumptions 

   - While in the ‘Dialysis’ state, patients had a (time independent) probability of receiving a transplant each cycle until age 80 years. 

87 



<!-- page 504 -->

CONFIDENTIAL UNTIL PUBLISHED 

- Patients in the ‘Post-transplant’ state could experience graft failure each cycle, transitioning back to ‘Dialysis’ (time independent probability). 

- The model allowed for multiple transplant-graft failure cycles over the model time horizon. 

- The model accounts for different dialysis modalities (haemodialysis [HD], continuous ambulatory peritoneal dialysis [CAPD] and automated peritoneal dialysis [APD]) in estimating costs and utilities: 

   - Modality proportions: the distribution of dialysis types was based on RaDaR registry data in patients with C3G: HD: 85.3%, APD: 11.8%, CAPD: 2.9%. 

   - Utility valuation: a weighted average utility for dialysis was calculated using the above modality proportions. 

   - Cost valuation: dialysis costs were derived from NHS reference costs. HD was assumed to occur three times per week, and APD and CAPD daily. HD costs were further weighted by setting (hospital, satellite, home) based on HRG-coded activity. A weighted average dialysis cost was then calculated using the modality proportions. 

**EAG comment:** The main concerns of the EAG relate to: a) the use of eGFR-based HSs rather than proteinuria reduction (UPCR); b) the eGFR threshold used to initiate KRT; and c) assumptions surrounding repeated kidney transplants. 

- a) The company modelled CKD progression using eGFR-based HSs rather than UPCR, despite UPCR being the primary endpoint of APPEAR-C3G. In clarification response B2, the company concluded (while acknowledging the exploratory nature and small sample size of the analyses) that greater UPCR reductions with iptacopan may translate into greater eGFR benefit, while also lower reductions (<30%) were associated with meaningful improvements in eGFR slope compared to pretreatment trajectories. The company further justified the eGFR-based model structure by citing precedents in previous NICE Technology Appraisals (TAs) (see CS, Table 31) and confirmation from UK clinicians that CKD stage (based on eGFR) is more relevant for estimating quality of life (QoL) and costs in C3G. They also noted that KRT initiation is based on eGFR, not UPCR, and that UPCR-based HSs would still require tracking eGFR to model KRT initiation. Given these points, the EAG considers the use of an eGFR-based structure reasonable. 

- b) The use of an eGFR threshold of 7.6 ml/min/1.73 m² to initiate KRT in the model is considered reasonable and justified (based on clarification response B3), as it reflects a weighted average of typical initiation points for both dialysis (around 5–7 ml/min/1.73 m[2] , per NICE guideline NG107) and pre-emptive transplantation (typically at higher eGFR, ~10 ml/min/1.73 m[2] , based on UK registry data and clinical input). While NG107[16] specifically addresses dialysis initiation, the model applies a unified threshold across all KRT modalities. Scenario and sensitivity analyses varying the threshold showed limited impact on cost effectiveness outcomes, indicating that the eGFR threshold to initiate KRT was not a key model driver. 

- c) The assumption of multiple kidney transplants in the economic model is consistent with clinical practice for C3G, given high post-transplant recurrence rates (55–85%) and a median graft survival of 6.5 years, as observed in RaDaR data. While the average of 1.9 lifetime transplants in the SoC arm is supported by clinical expert opinion, RaDaR data also show that 19% of transplant recipients had already received two or more transplants, despite the relatively young cohort age. For the iptacopan arm, the model predicts a lower average of 1.46 transplants, which, according to the company, experts deemed plausible due to iptacopan’s potential to slow disease progression, though they found it difficult to validate the precise number. Experts advised against capping the maximum number of transplants, as this would not reflect clinical reality. Scenario analyses that reduced or 

88 



<!-- page 505 -->

CONFIDENTIAL UNTIL PUBLISHED 

capped transplant frequency led to lower incremental cost-effectiveness ratios (ICERs), suggesting that the base-case may conservatively overestimate the ICER of iptacopan + SoC compared to SoC. The probabilities of graft failure and repeated transplantation were derived from RaDaR data, incorporating cycle-based probabilities and transplant eligibility assumptions. 

## _**4.2.3 Population**_ 

Consistent with the NICE scope as well as the pivotal randomised trial (APPEAR-C3G; NCT04817618), the population considered in the CS (CS, Table 1) was adults with C3G. Specifically, native kidney C3G patients with continued risk of disease progression on a maximally tolerated licensed dose of an ACEi or ARB. The anticipated indication of iptacopan in C3G is as follows: “ _Iptacopan is indicated for the treatment of adult patients with complement 3 glomerulopathy (C3G) in combination with a renin-angiotensin system (RAS) inhibitor, or in patients who are RAS-inhibitor intolerant, or for whom a RAS inhibitor is contraindicated_ ” (CS Table 2). ## _**4.2.4 Interventions and comparators**_ 

The intervention is modelled as iptacopan + SoC, in line with the APPEAR-C3G trial and the proposed positioning of iptacopan in the C3G treatment pathway (CS, Figure 5). Iptacopan is modelled as 200 mg oral capsules which are taken b.i.d. 

In line with the final scope of this appraisal, the comparator is SoC alone (see CS, Section 1.3.5) consisting of: 

- ACEi (ramipril; 47.3%) 

- ARB (losartan; 52.7%) 

- CoS (prednisolone; 32.4%) 

- MMF (36.5%) 

- SGLT2in (dapagliflozin; 5.4%) 

Patients can receive multiple SoC treatments simultaneously (aligning with CS, Figure 3). However, regarding ACEi and ARB use, guidelines generally recommend the use of one or the other. 

Eculizumab was included in the final scope for people who have previously had a kidney transplant and who have highly aggressive C3G recurrence as specified in the NHS England clinical commissioning policy for eculizumab. However, the company did not include eculizumab as a comparator. 

**EAG comment:** The main concerns of the EAG relate to: a) representativeness of SoC as observed in the APPEAR-C3G trial for UK clinical practice; and b) the exclusion of eculizumab as comparator. 

- a) It is unclear to the EAG to what degree the SoC as observed in the APPEAR-C3G trial is consistent with the RaDaR registry data and UK clinical practice. According to the company (response to clarification question A10), their advisors agreed that the concomitant medications (including ACEi/ARBs) in APPEAR-C3G were appropriate and representative of management of C3G patients within UK clinical practice. Nevertheless, the EAG believes a scenario analysis including SoC treatment distribution based on RaDaR would be informative. Notably this only affects the SoC costs (SoC effectiveness is based on SoC as observed in the APPEAR-C3G trial). 

- b) Inconsistent with the scope and the NHS England clinical commissioning policy for eculizumab, eculizumab was not included as a comparator in the economic model. In response to clarification question A3 (referred to in B6), the company highlighted three main reasons for not including eculizumab: a) limited evidence (no head-to-head data and an ITC was deemed infeasible by the company); b) limited relevance as a comparator iptacopan; and c) limited use of eculizumab in UK clinical practice for the population of interest (see Section 2 for further details). 

## _**4.2.5 Perspective, time horizon and discounting**_ 

The analysis was performed from the NHS and Personal Social Services (PSS) perspective. Discount rates of 3.5% were applied to both costs and benefits. The model cycle length was 3 months with a lifetime time horizon (72.1 years, i.e., up to age 100 years) and a half-cycle correction was applied. 

**EAG comment:** The approach is in concordance with the NICE reference case. 

## _**4.2.6 Treatment effectiveness and extrapolation**_ 

The main source of evidence on treatment effectiveness used for iptacopan + SoC and SoC alone is the APPEAR-C3G trial.

## _**4.2.6.1 Modelling of disease progression**_ 

The company modelled transitions through CKD stages using eGFR slopes (the rate of eGFR decline, defined as the average change in eGFR in a 1-year period). The time to move between CKD stages 1 to 5 was defined as the time taken for eGFR to decline from the midpoint of the current CKD stage to the midpoint of the following stage, assuming a uniform distribution of patients across a CKD stage. Transitions to KRT were modelled to take place at the KRT threshold (7.6 ml/min/1.73 m2) instead of the midpoint value. Although the company acknowledged that the rate of eGFR decline may vary over the course of disease, it assumed that the speed of progression in the economic model was independent of CKD stage and constant over the model time horizon. 

The company considered three options for estimating the eGFR slope for both treatment strategies (see Table 4.4): 

- 1) Randomised comparison using APPEAR-C3G (CS scenario analysis). 

- 2) Iptacopan before-after comparison using APPEAR-C3G including the open-label extension study (CS base-case). 

- 3) Iptacopan before-after comparison using APPEAR-C3G and Phase 2 native kidney cohort A including the open-label extension study (CS scenario analysis). 

The company selected the iptacopan before-after comparison using APPEAR-C3G including the openlabel extension study (option 2) for their base-case whereas the other two options were explored in scenarios. The selected eGFR slopes were used to calculate the 3-month per cycle probability of disease progression (see Table 4.4).

## _**4.2.6.2 Modelling of KRT**_ 

Once patients reached an eGFR value of 7.6 ml/min/1.73 m2 in the company’s base-case, they were assumed to start KRT (dialysis or a transplant). Out of these, 18.4% were modelled to receive a preemptive transplant (based on RaDaR data), while the remaining 81.6% of patients started dialysis. For patients in the dialysis HS, a per-cycle probability of 8.7% receiving a transplant was modelled (based on RaDaR data). Based on Adelphi Disease Specific Programme (DSP) survey data, 16.8% of patients in need of a transplant were assumed ineligible and remained in the dialysis HS until death. Additionally, patients aged ≥80 years were assumed not to receive a transplant. For patients that received a transplant, a 2.6% probability of graft failure was modelled per cycle, after which patients returned to the dialysis HS. The company modelled repeated transplantation following graft failure, however, it was assumed that a proportion of patients was no longer eligible for another transplant (16.8%, i.e., the same as ineligibility for first transplant). All input values related to KRT are summarised in the CS, Table 36. 

## _**4.2.6.3 Modelling of treatment discontinuation**_ 

The discontinuation rate among patients on iptacopan before reaching kidney failure was based on allcause treatment discontinuation of iptacopan in the pooled APPEAR-C3G, Phase 2 and extension studies (broad safety set), resulting in a per cycle (3 months) discontinuation probability of 1.57%. SoC treatments were assumed not to be discontinued prior to kidney failure. For both iptacopan and SoC it was assumed that patients would discontinue treatment at the point of commencing KRT, except for 

92 



<!-- page 509 -->

CONFIDENTIAL UNTIL PUBLISHED 

ACEi/ARB as these would usually be continued according to UK clinicians. Patients who discontinued iptacopan, either before or upon reaching kidney failure, were assumed to subsequently receive SoC alone with the SoC eGFR slope applied from the point of discontinuation onwards. 

## **4.2.6.4** _**Modelling of mortality**_ 

The company informed mortality in its economic model using mortality ratios, standardised to the general population of England and Wales for patients in RaDaR with and without kidney failure, from a study by Wong 2024[17] (CS, Table 39). In this study, a total of 27,285 people from the UK with rare kidney diseases were analysed, including 1,089 people with either C3G or MPGN. 

**EAG comment:** The main concerns of the EAG relate to: a) the data used for generating eGFR slopes, b) the assumption that the speed of progression in the economic model was independent of CKD stage and constant over the model time horizon, c) the modelling of treatment discontinuation, d) the assumption of a constant iptacopan treatment effect over the model time horizon while patients remained on treatment, and e) the approach for modelling disease progression. 

- a) The company estimated eGFR slopes using a before-after comparison (i.e., pre-iptacopan data for SoC and on-iptacopan data for iptacopan) based on APPEAR-C3G including the open-label extension study. This approach is considered suboptimal by the EAG as the resulting iptacopan treatment effect was based on an observational comparison rather than a randomised comparison (based on APPEAR-C3G trial, i.e., CS, option 1) and is therefore prone to bias. The company, however, considered the SoC eGFR slope based on the randomised double-blind period of APPEAR-C3G to be implausible based on clinical advisors input and inconsistency with published literature, their clinical experience and real-world RaDaR data on the median time from diagnosis to kidney failure. Therefore, the EAG requested additional scenario analyses in clarification question B7 using 1) RaDaR data (all C3G patients, n=139) and 2) pre-iptacopan data (i.e., CS option 2) to inform the eGFR slope of SoC, and subsequently apply the iptacopan treatment effect as observed in the randomised double-blind period of APPEAR-C3G to inform the iptacopan eGFR slope. Both scenario analyses resulted in substantially increased ICERs. All alternatives considered, the EAG regards the approach of estimating the eGFR slope for SoC based on RaDaR and subsequently applying the iptacopan treatment effect from the randomised double-blind period of APPEAR-C3G to inform the iptacopan eGFR slope to be the most reasonable for (relative) treatment effectiveness in the economic model and adopted this in its EAG base-case. This approach preserves randomisation for the estimated treatment effect and uses the SoC eGFR slope based on real-world RaDaR data. Additionally, an EAG scenario analysis was explored informing the eGFR slope in both arms based on the randomised double-blind period of APPEAR-C3G. 

- b) The EAG questions the company’s assumption that the speed of progression in the economic model was independent of CKD stage and constant over the modelled time horizon. In response to clarification question B7e, the company stated based on clinical expert inputs that a linear slope was a reasonable simplification as the overall path of disease in C3G is a progressive decline. In addition, it was stated that unlike other kidney diseases, in C3G eGFR decline does not tend to get steeper as patients get closer to kidney failure. The company provided CKD-specific eGFR slopes which the EAG did not consider informative, as these were limited to the patient’s CKD stage at baseline rather than providing the rate of decline while moving through CKD stages. Additionally, time-dependent eGFR decline rates were provided in Table 5 of the clarification response, indicating that eGFR slopes varied over time over the pre-randomisation, double-blind and openlabel treatment periods. The EAG therefore considers the company’s assumption of a constant, CKD-independent decline rate over time to be potentially implausible and insufficiently justified. 

93 



<!-- page 510 -->

CONFIDENTIAL UNTIL PUBLISHED 

Over- or underestimation of the speed at which patients progress in the economic model is likely to have significant implications for the long-term modelling of costs and effects, particularly those associated with KRT such as dialysis and kidney transplantation. The EAG therefore considers this to be a key issue. 

c) The company modelled a constant treatment discontinuation rate of 0.063 per year for patients on iptacopan who have not reached kidney failure based on all-cause treatment discontinuation of iptacopan in the pooled APPEAR-C3G, Phase 2 and extension studies (broad safety set). The EAG questioned the plausibility of assuming a constant discontinuation rate over time and therefore requested additional analyses including time-varying discontinuation rates. The company provided time to treatment discontinuation (TTD) analyses for both the pooled data and for the APPEARC3G trial only. Scenario analyses were presented for the exponential and log-normal curves as these had the best statistical fit (AIC/BIC), which had a minor impact on the cost effectiveness results. However, the impact of these TTD analyses may be more pronounced when waning of the iptacopan treatment effect is additionally incorporated in the economic model (comment d) below). It was further stated that clinical experts agreed on the exponential curve resulting in the most plausible extrapolation of TTD, whereas the Weibull and Gompertz extrapolations were considered implausible. The EAG noted, however, that the company did not provide further details on these clinical expert inputs, and that various other criteria from the NICE Decision Support Unit (DSU) Technical Support Document (TSD) 14 guidance to assess the most suitable parametric model were lacking (e.g. evidence to assess the clinical plausibility of the long-term TTD estimates resulting from the parametric survival curves). Considering the currently available evidence, the EAG considers the statistical fit of all curves to be within an acceptable range except for the generalised gamma (specifically the Bayesian information criterion [BIC]).. However, the company should provide full details of the TTD model selection process based on the NICE DSU TSD 14 guidance for the EAG to assess the most appropriate curve to inform treatment discontinuation in the economic model. 

- d) The company assumed a constant iptacopan treatment effect over the model time horizon while patients remained on treatment. The EAG considers that this strong assumption required further exploration. Consequently, the EAG requested further justification and evidence that supports the company’s assumption, as well as scenario analyses exploring waning of the iptacopan treatment effect at different time points. The company argued that the disease-modifying effect of iptacopan was sustained throughout the APPEAR-C3G trial and that clinical experts agreed that the treatment effect is not expected to wane. Also, the EAG’s clinical expert agreed that “ _the on-target effect on complement inhibition will remain comparable throughout_ ”. However, the company did not provide the evidence requested by the EAG in clarification question B9b to assess potential treatment waning, stating that this was not deemed feasible due to the limited number of CKD stage transitions were observed during APPEAR-C3G. Although acknowledging the clinical expert inputs, the EAG considers the assumption of a constant iptacopan treatment effect over the model time horizon while patients remained on treatment to be insufficiently assessed. Therefore, the EAG would like to see further evidence of a constant treatment effect during the observed period, as requested in clarification question B9b, as well as scenario analyses exploring treatment waning beyond the observed period. 

- e) Contrary to several previous TAs where transition probabilities from observed transitions between CKD stages were used to model disease progression, the company used eGFR slopes to transition through CKD stages in the current appraisal. This was justified by the small sample size and the low number of patients in more advanced CKD stages at baseline. Nevertheless, upon request the company explored generating transition probabilities from observed transitions between CKD stages in response to clarification question B7g. Based on the provided results of this analysis, the

EAG agrees that the company’s approach of using eGFR slopes is more appropriate to model disease progression in the economic model. 

## _**4.2.7 Adverse events**_ 

The company’s economic model captured SAEs suspected to be related to iptacopan. These were sourced from the broad safety set (pooled trial populations), resulting in four patients experiencing a total of nine SAEs. The company stated that some SAEs were linked and thus merged to a total of five SAEs occurring in 189.9 patient years, giving a SAEs per-cycle probability of 0.66%. The 32.1-day duration of SAEs presentation assumed in the economic model was also sourced from the broad safety set. 

The CS detailed that almost all SAEs suspected to be related to iptacopan were infections with encapsulated bacteria (an AE of special interest for iptacopan) leading to pneumonia or consequences thereof such as sepsis and thus proceeded to standardise them to pneumonia and sepsis in the economic analysis in a simplifying assumption. **EAG comment:** The main concerns of the EAG relate to: a) the definition of AEs relevant for the CS DP, b) evidence used to identify AEs, c) standardisation and merging of SAEs. 

- a) The EAG considers the company’s definition of AEs relevant to the DP, i.e., SAEs suspected to be related to iptacopan, to be unsatisfactory. First, it diverges from Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events (CTCAE) for AEs. Second, it is unclear how “suspected to be related to iptacopan” was assessed and clinically justified. The definition impeded an inclusion of AEs for the comparators, thereby preventing an assessment of differences in consequences on health outcomes and resource use as stipulated by NICE. Upon inquiry, the company explained while CS and MF are associated with side effects, ACEis and ARBs were considered well tolerable by clinical experts.[4] The EAG is concerned that safety profiles might differ when the comparator treatments are given respectively when iptacopan is added, to which the company highlighted that the iptacopan AEs reflect a patient population where it is added to background SoC. Nevertheless, the EAG supports the company’s claim having chosen a conservative approach by disregarding consequences of comparator AEs. The company stressed that the definition of SAEs was also used in an earlier NICE appraisal of iptacopan.[18] The EAG considered the CTCAE definition to be the most appropriate and modelled all severity grade 3+ AEs (incidence >0%) irrespective of a suspected relationship with iptacopan in its base-case. 

- b) Whereas the modelled CS population was native kidney C3G patients with continued risk of disease progression on a maximally tolerated licensed dose of an ACEi or ARB, i.e., in line with the inclusion criteria of APPEAR-C3G (see EAG report Section 4.2.3), the company used the broad safety set (including patients with post-transplant recurrence) to inform SAEs in its base-case. The decision for the broad safety set was supported by two clinical experts consulted by the company[19] upon EAG clarification question B10b as it increases exposure duration (patient-years) substantially. The EAG’s clinical expert agreed with the company’s reasoning.[19] In the iptacopan arm of the controlled safety set (APPEAR-C3G trial), three SAEs and one of them related to iptacopan were identified during 18.3 patient years.[20] (Table 2.1). Although the EAG acknowledges the substantially increased exposure duration with the broad safety set, it is unclear what the impact of differences between the CS population and the broad safety population may be on modelling of AEs. Thus, the EAG decided to rely on the controlled safety set in its EAG base-case analysis. 

- c) The company’s standardisation of all SAEs to pneumonia/sepsis further constraints the health economic assessment, taking into account the few AEs the company considered relevant for the submission. However, as the clinical expert consulted by the EAG agrees with the company’s 

95 



<!-- page 512 -->

CONFIDENTIAL UNTIL PUBLISHED 

rationale based on the chosen definition of relevant AEs,[19] the EAG considers the company’s approach to be reasonable. Next to that, the company merged SAEs in its base-case which it assumed to be linked, stating that these occurred concurrently and concerned pneumonia progressing to sepsis. However, this may underestimate resource use and impact on HRQoL of these events. Whereas it is reassuring that the EAG clinical expert agrees with the company’s rationale,[19] the EAG is concerned that the impact on AE-related costs and health benefits remains unknown. 

## _**4.2.8 HRQoL**_ 

The utility values considered in the CS were based on the APPEAR-C3G clinical trial and literature. 

## _**4.2.8.1 HRQoL data identified in the literature review**_ 

A SLR, updated most currently in November 2024, identified two studies in C3G which provided utility values, but these were considered insufficient. The first study, a randomised clinical trial, reported European Quality of Life-5 Dimensions 5-Level (EQ-5D-5L)-based utility values at baseline and 26 weeks yet not HS-specific ones.[21] The second study reported utility values for CKD stages 1 to 4/5 derived from the EQ-5D-5L, mapped with the United States (US) tariff.[22] It was discarded in the CS because CKD stage 1 patients had the worst HRQoL after patients with CKD stage 4/5. 

Additionally, NICE TAs on general CKD published in the last 10 years were reviewed and 13 TAs identified.[1] (Table 42). The studies by Jesky 2016[23] and Lee 2005[24] were the main sources that informed utilities for CKD stages 1 to 5 and dialysis and transplant, respectively. 

## _**4.2.8.2 Health state utility values**_ 

EQ-5D-5L data was sourced from the APPEAR-C3G trial for CKD stages 1 to 4 and mapped to EQ5D-3L with the Hernandez-Alava 2022[25] algorithm in line with NICE recommendations. A mixed effects linear regression model for repeated measures provided utility values for the economic model. The model included the covariates CKD stage, age, sex, and baseline utility. The company pooled CKD stage 1 and 2 utilities in its base-case since it perceived the lower stage 1 value to be implausible. CKD stage 5 utility was informed by Jesky 2016,[23] providing European Quality of Life-5 Dimensions 3- Levels (EQ-5D-3L) data from a CKD (any aetiology) UK study population of 64 years in median age. Dialysis and post-transplant utilities by Lee 2005,[24] providing EQ-5D-3L data from a UK kidney failure population (N=416) of 58.2 years and 55.5 years in mean age, for males and females respectively. A joint dialysis utility value was derived as a weighted average of 85.3% of C3G patients getting HD and 14.7% getting peritoneal dialysis (PD), based on the RaDaR study.[26] The HS utilities from these different study populations were adjusted for the age- and sex-matched general population utility from Hernandez-Alava,[25] employing a utility multiplier. Likewise, the age-related decline in health over time was captured. In a scenario, all CKD HS utilities were informed by  Jesky 2016[23] instead of APPEARC3G. A summary of utility values used in the company’s base-case is provided in Table 4.5.

## _**4.2.8.3 Disutility values**_ 

Based on the CS reasoning detailed in Section 4.2.7, standardising all SAEs to pneumonia and sepsis, the company included a single disutility for infections for iptacopan in the economic model. It was taken from Oppong 2013,[28] who reported a 0.156 utility difference from acute presentation of cough and lower respiratory tract infections to recovery at week 4 in English patients based on EQ-5D-3L. 

**EAG comment:** The main concerns of the EAG relate to: a) (face) validity of the chosen CKD stage 5+ utilities b) the longitudinal data regression analyses of APPEAR-C3G trial data to inform CKD stages 1-4 in the health economic model, c) issues related to early CKD stages, and d) validity of chosen disutility value 

- a) For CKD stage 5+, the company informed utility values in their economic model by literature. As these studies reported from divergent and substantially older patient populations, the company adjusted for age and gender to match the modelled patient population (baseline mean age: 27.9 years). However, the EAG is apprehensive of the steep decline from CKD stage 4 to 5+, with the 5+ CKD stage utilities potentially capturing general CKD comorbidities apparent in later ages yet not applicable for C3G specifically. The clinical advisor consulted by the company deemed the post-transplant HS utility (0.76) “relatively low” and supported alternatively the use of Liem 2008[2] value (0.81)[29, 30] In the health economic model, patients treated with the comparator treatments spend more time in the dialysis and post-transplant HSs, implying significant consequences of the choice of higher CKD stage utility values for the CEA. In response to clarification question B13, the company stressed the considerable impact of KRT on HRQoL, the use of Lee 2005[24] utility values in prior TAs[4] (Table 34) and shortcomings related to the Liem 2008[29] meta-analysis. However, the Liem 2008[29] was also considered appropriate in prior TAs[4] (Table 34) and increased the ICER by XXXXX in a provided scenario analysis by the company when solely the post- 

97 



<!-- page 514 -->

CONFIDENTIAL UNTIL PUBLISHED 

transplant utility was adjusted, highlighting the immense impact on uncertainty surrounding CKD stage 5+ values derived from the wider CKD literature. The EAG clinical expert highlighted that the data might be confounded as C3G patients are generally younger at kidney failure, and thereby less likely to have comorbidities such as diabetes or hypertension apparent in the general CKD population.[19] However, the expert also stressed that health impacts of kidney failure and dialysis treatment should not be discounted. The EAG hence decided to keep Lee 2005[24] utility values in its base-case and use Liem 2008[29] utility values for dialysis and post-transplant in a scenario analysis. 

- b) The company used a mixed effects linear regression model for repeated measures to estimate CKD stage 1-4 utilities. It included subject-level random effects but no time variable, stating in response to clarification question B11 that the inclusion of fixed time effects on other covariates were minimal.[4] The company further provided evidence supporting the normality assumption, yet demonstrated linearity only for the covariates age[4] (Figure 8) and to a limited extent for baseline EQ-5D[4] (Figure 9). Based on the mean EQ-5D scores over time by CKD stage[4] (Figure 4), assuming a linear trend over time might be inappropriate. The EAG is concerned that time was included neither as a fixed nor random effect yet might be a confounding variable, biasing estimates and standard errors if subject-specific time trends and time-varying correlation were at present. However, the EAG agrees with the company that despite these weaknesses, expected differences seem minor. Further model specification, for instance with regard to slope shapes, interaction terms and variance-covariance structure would require more in-depth analyses and model fit assessments. Missing data of EQ-5D was up to 9% (baseline, Day 14 visit), assumed missing at random and not imputed. This level of missingness was deemed acceptable by the EAG. However, the EAG has no information on missing data of independent variables which would benefit from imputation despite EQ-5D at baseline. 

- c) The EAG noticed the utility values for early CKD stages (Table 4.5) were relatively close to the UK general population one (0.92)[1] (Table 43). Upon inquiry, the company stated that early CKD stages present with little impact on HRQoL, which the EAG clinical expert agreed to for generally symptom-free CKD stages 1 and 2.[19] Moreover, values were deemed similar to the (higher) ones from Jesky 2016[23] after age and sex adjustments, a study on general CKD in a substantially older population. From older and different CKD populations, TAs presented by the company in clarification response, Table 33[4] had mostly lower utilities compared to the CS. The Adelphi DSP C3G study (N=385), which included 32 UK patients,[31] reported EQ-5D-5L based on 100 observations from a cross-sectional survey which was open for 9 months.[22] Utilities were derived using the US tariff and substantially lower. The study also showed unexpectedly increasing values for CKD stages 1-3A.[4] (Table 30) The EAG is concerned about the considerable uncertainty surrounding early CKD stage utilities, and therefore requested a scenario analysis using the Adelphi DSP study which the company did not provide. 

   - Moreover, the company pooled CKD stage 1 and 2 utility values since stage 1 utilities estimated by the mixed effects regression model were lower than stage 2 utilities. The EAG saw some shortcomings in this approach, as these stages report the highest number of measurements, underlying data issues might be masked or disease burden misrepresented. Upon inquiry, the company highlighted implausibility with regard to disease development and statistical nonsignificance of the slightly higher value of CKD stage 2 compared to 1 in the regression analyses (Table 41).[1] It also referred to previous NICE TAs in CKD which all pooled CKD stage 1 and 2.[4] In light of the arguments provided by the company and the support by the independent clinical expert consulted by the EAG,[19] the EAG agrees with the chosen approach. 

- d) To assess the impact of pneumonia and sepsis, the company used a utility value on infections from Oppong 2013.[28] The authors reported a 0.156 utility difference from acute presentation of cough and lower respiratory tract infections to recovery at week 4 in 168 English patients, 50 years of 

98 



<!-- page 515 -->

CONFIDENTIAL UNTIL PUBLISHED 

mean age, based on EQ-5D-3L. However, for the 181 Welsh patients of on average 53 years of age also included in the study, they reported a utility difference of 0.146. The EAG requested the company in clarification question B14[4] to verify the chosen disutility value of 0.156 with additional literature, which the company did not provide. As impact is expected to be small, the EAG regards the uncertainty of this estimate a minor limitation. 

## _**4.2.9 Resources and costs**_ 

The cost categories included in the model were treatment acquisition costs, HS costs (healthcare resource utilisation [HCRU]: disease monitoring, transplant, and dialysis costs), vaccination and antibiotic costs, and event costs including: AE management costs, end of life costs, CV events (scenario analysis only) costs. 

Where available, unit prices were based on the National Schedule of NHS costs (2023-24),[32] the 2023/2024 drugs and pharmaceutical electronic marketing information tool (eMIT)[33] , the 2023 Unit Costs of Health and Social Care,[34] and the British National Formulary (BNF).[35] Where unavailable, unit prices were sourced from literature. 

Costs were inflated to the 2022/23 fiscal year using the NHS Cost Inflation Index (NHSCII) Pay and Price Index.[34] 

## _**4.2.9.1 Resource use and costs data identified in the literature review**_ 

According to the CS, the cost and HCRU SLR identified six studies reporting HCRU in C3G. Out of these, the company did not consider any to provide relevant evidence for use in the submission, with reasons for not utilising each identified study provided in Appendix G, Table 9. As such, an additional targeted literature review (TLR) was conducted on NICE TAs in CKD with final guidance published in the last 10 years. Overall, 13 TAs were identified with HCRU sources for each summarised for CDK stages 1-4; CKD stage 5 (pre-KRT); dialysis; transplant (one-off); and post-transplant (long-term). CS Table 44 provides an overview of the HS cost sources utilised in the identified previous NICE TAs in CKDs. 

## _**4.2.9.2 Treatment acquisition costs (with Patient Access Scheme [PAS])**_ 

For the iptacopan + SoC arm, patients incurred costs of iptacopan in addition to the costs of background SoC therapies. Patients in the SoC comparator arm incurred the costs of SoC background therapies only. Provided all therapies are administered orally, no administration costs were included. 

## _4.2.9.2.1 Iptacopan_ 

In the CS, the cost of iptacopan was set to XXXXX (list price: £26,500) per 28-day pack, XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX 

XXXXX XXXXX. From here, a per annum cost was derived by calculating the average cost per day by dividing the pack price by the number of doses per pack. 

## _4.2.9.2.2 SoC background therapies_ 

For C3G, SoC could include ACEi/ARBs, MMF, CoS, and SGLT2is. Here, the proportion of patients receiving each of the components of SoC was derived from baseline characteristics in APPEAR-C3G and assumed equal for iptacopan + SoC and SoC. As per the CS, the specific ACEi/ARBs used to calculate costs reflect the most used treatments within these classes from the UK cohort of the Adelphi DSP study.[36] For treatments in the other SoC background therapy classes, the cheapest medication

HS costs reflect HCRU for disease monitoring (nephrologist monitoring visits; per visit disease monitoring tests) and, for KRT HSs, transplant and dialysis costs. 

## _4.2.9.3.1 Monitoring costs_ 

Outpatient resource use was derived from a survey of UK clinicians participating in an advisory board.[12] Clinician inputs were averaged to derive economic model inputs. Monitoring visits per HS and per visit disease monitoring tests and unit costs are presented in CS, Table 47 and Table 48, respectively. 

## _4.2.9.3.2 Dialysis and (post-)transplant costs_ 

The one-time cost of kidney transplant was taken as a weighted average for living donor transplant and deceased donor transplant. The proportion of patients receiving a living or deceased donor transplant was derived from RaDaR data in patients with C3G. Transplants were costed using 2023/2024 NHS reference costs.[32] Post-transplant costs comprised annual costs for immunosuppression medication, based on an NHS Blood and Transplant fact sheet.[37]

## _**4.2.9.4 Vaccination and antibiotic costs**_ 

As per the summary of product characteristics (SmPC), patients receiving iptacopan must be vaccinated against N. meningitidis and S. pneumoniae, with vaccination against H. influenzae type B recommended. All patients in the economic model on iptacopan receive vaccinations for N. meningitidis and S. pneumoniae every 5 years (modelled as 0.2 per year), and one vaccination for H. influenzae type B at the start of iptacopan treatment. Vaccination costs were sourced from the BNF. As per UK clinicians, the cost of prophylactic antibiotics (penicillin) was also included for all iptacopan patients (CS, Table 51). 

## _**4.2.9.5 Event costs**_ 

## _4.2.9.5.1 Adverse event costs_ 

The inclusion and distribution of AEs in the economic model are described in Section 4.2.7 of the EAG report. To cost AEs in the economic model, a weighted average unit cost was derived using 2023/24 NHS reference costs for lobar, atypical and viral pneumonia (HRG codes DZ11K-DZ11V), bronchopneumonia (HRG codes DZ23H-DZ23N), and sepsis (HRG codes WJ06A-WJ06J). Costs were weighted based on total activity in the NHS reference costs. The total weighted average unit cost per AE utilised in the economic model was £2,819.03. 

## _4.2.9.5.2 End-of-life costs_ 

End-of-life costs (one-off cost upon entering the death state) were modelled as the hospital costs for terminal care in the 30 days prior to death. These were taken from Kerr 2016,[39] which reported end-oflife care in CKD in England and aligned with the approach taken in TA937.[40] 

## _4.2.9.5.3 Cardiovascular event costs (scenario analysis only)_ 

CV events were included in a scenario analysis only. The costs associated with stroke and myocardial infarction were sourced from 2023/24 NHS reference costs and TA942.[41] An acute cost per event (stroke: £7,172.71; myocardial infarction: £3,522.51) and annual post-event cost (stroke: £1,303.78; myocardial infarction: £893.41) were included as a one-off cost weighted by the proportion of patients experiencing an event in each cycle. 

**EAG comment:** The main concerns of the EAG relate to: a) wastage costs at iptacopan discontinuation; b) misalignment between inflated costs and costs informed by National Schedule for NHS Costs; c) reproducibility of (post-)transplant and dialysis, and SAE costs. 

- a) In the CS, acquisition cost calculations assumed no waste. That is, per pack costs were used to derive an average cost per daily dose. Provided each pack of iptacopan (200 mg) contained 56 capsules to be taken b.i.d. ~3.26 packs are required (and initially modelled) per 3-month model cycle. This is likely to underestimate iptacopan acquisition costs. The NICE process and methods guide states that the costs of oral treatments dispensed in tablet packs should be evaluated on a perpack basis, unless clinical experts or other evidence suggests that prescribing and dispensing is done such that there would be no wastage. Clarification question B15 requested an updated economic model and scenario analysis taking a per-pack costing approach. In response, the company provided the updated their base-case results modelling an additional ~0.74 packs to the total acquisition cost of iptacopan (i.e., modelling four packs in a patient’s last model cycle on treatment), accounting for tablets not used upon treatment discontinuation. This scenario resulted in an increase in incremental costs of XXX and an increased (deterministic) ICER from XXXXXX to XXXXXX (XXX). The

Provided 2023 edition of the Personal Social Services Research Unit (PSSRU) Cost of Health and Social Care Manual was the latest version at the time of submission, the EAG noted a slight misalignment between inflated costs and costs derived from the National Schedule of NHS Costs 2023/2024. ## **5.2 Company’s sensitivity analyses** 

The company performed and presented the results of probabilistic sensitivity analyses (PSA), deterministic sensitivity analyses (DSA) as well as scenario analyses. The probabilistic CS base-case analyses indicated cost effectiveness probabilities of X% at WTP thresholds of £20,000 and £30,000 per QALY gained. DSA showed that the results were most sensitive to changes in analysis approach taken to model iptacopan treatment effect, and the age and constant coefficients utilised in the APPEAR-C3G utility linear regression model. The company conducted several scenario analyses. The results showed ICERs ranging between XXXXXX and XXXXXX per QALY gained. The three most influential scenarios that increased the ICER were 3) eGFR slope data from APPEAR-C3G placebo comparison (based on 6 months of data), 5) CKD stage transitions at upper eGFR bound of CKD stage, and 2) eGFR slope data from pooled population (APPEAR-C3G and Phase 2 native kidney cohort; up to 4.7 years iptacopan treatment duration). 

**EAG comment:** The main concern of the EAG relates to the inclusion of HSUV parameters within the PSA. 

- a) Health state utility values (HSUVs) for CKD stages 1-4 (i.e., trial utilities) were not varied in the PSA. Clarification question B-21 requested justification for the exclusion of HSUV. In response, the company suggest that these were implicitly included as the parameters utilised in the linear regression model to derive utilities were varied using a Cholesky decomposition distribution. However, HSUV calculations in the economic model seem not to be linked to the probabilistically varied parameters but instead to a separate table (model sheet “Control”, cells BF22:BF26) with

linear regression model parameters hard coded to the cells. That is, no result changes were observed by the EAG when setting linear regression model parameters to not be varied in the PSA. Upper and lower parameter values were assumed to be +/- 20% of the deterministic input for trial HSUVs, and calculated using the 95% CI for post-transplant and dialysis HSUVs. ## **5.3 Model validation and face validity check** 

## _**5.3.1 Face validity assessment**_ 

The company held two advisory board meetings with nine (April 2022) and 10 (November 2024) UK clinicians experienced with C3G. Discussion points were the current SoC and the C3G treatment landscape, the level of unmet need, iptacopan trial data, modelling disease progression and disease management before and after kidney failure. 

Additional calls occurred separately with two clinicians on uncertainty within the CS, in particular surrounding the eGFR-based modelling approach. A joint call involving one clinical and external health economic expert addressed model validation, i.e., base-case selection for disease progression and treatment effect, HSUVs and costs, AEs, and clinical outputs of the draft economic model. 

## _**5.3.2 Technical verification**_ 

An independent team of health economic experts not involved in model development assessed the model with a quality control and internal validation checklist, based on the published TECH-VER checklist.[44] An independent analyst performed a full input quality check against original sources. 

## _**5.3.3 Comparisons with other TAs**_ 

Cross-validation with other TAs was not explicitly mentioned in the CS, Section B3.13. 

## _**5.3.4 Comparison with external data used to develop the economic model**_ 

Validation of external data used to develop the economic model was not explicitly mentioned in the CS, Section B3.13. 

## _**5.3.5 Comparison with external data not used to develop the economic model**_ 

Cross-validation with external data not used to develop the economic model was not explicitly mentioned in the CS, Section B3.13.

The EAG noted however, that only summaries rather than full meeting minutes of these were provided, although requested in clarification question B23. The EAG considers this to be a serious transparency issue as it is unable to verify various assumptions made by the company, and the full meeting details should therefore be provided.

## **6. EAG’s additional analyses** 

## **6.1 Exploratory and sensitivity analyses undertaken by the EAG** 

Table 6.1 summarises the key issues related to the cost effectiveness categorised according to the sources of uncertainty as defined by Grimm 2020:[48] 

- Transparency (e.g. lack of clarity in presentation, description, or justification) 

- Methods (e.g. violation of best research practices, existing guidelines, or the reference case) 

- Imprecision (e.g. particularly wide CIs, small sample sizes, or immaturity of data) 

- Bias & indirectness (e.g. there is a mismatch between the DP and evidence used to inform it in terms of population, intervention/comparator and/or outcomes considered) 

- Unavailability (e.g. lack of data or insight) 

Identifying the source of uncertainty can help determine what course of action can be taken (i.e., whether additional clarifications, evidence and/or analyses might help to resolve the key issue). Moreover, Table 6.1 lists suggested alternative approaches, expected effects on the cost effectiveness, whether it is reflected in the EAG base-case as well as additional evidence or analyses that might help to resolve the key issues. 

Based on all considerations in the preceding Sections of this EAG report, the EAG defined a new basecase. This base-case included multiple adjustments to the original base-case presented in the previous Sections. These adjustments made by the EAG form the EAG base-case and were subdivided into three categories (derived from Kaltenthaler 2016): 

- Fixing errors (correcting the model where the company’s submitted model was unequivocally wrong) 

- Fixing violations (correcting the model where the EAG considered that the NICE reference case, scope or best practice had not been adhered to) 

- Matters of judgement (amending the model where the EAG considers that reasonable alternative assumptions are preferred) 

## _**6.1.1 EAG base-case**_

## **6.3 EAG’s preferred assumptions** 

The estimated EAG base-case ICER (probabilistic), based on the EAG preferred assumptions highlighted in Section 5.1, was £ XXXXXX per QALY gained. The probabilistic EAG base-case analyses indicated cost effectiveness probabilities of X% at WTP thresholds of £20,000 and £30,000 per QALY gained. The most influential adjustment was estimating the eGFR slope for SoC based on RaDaR data and subsequently applying the iptacopan treatment effect from the randomised doubleblind period of APPEAR-C3G to inform the iptacopan eGFR slope. The ICER increased most in the scenario analysis with alternative assumptions regarding KRT utilities. 

## **6.4 Conclusions of the cost effectiveness Section** 

The CS, Appendices E F and G, and response to clarification[1, 4, 13, 14] provided sufficient details for the EAG to appraise the literature searches conducted to identify relevant studies on cost effectiveness, HRQoL and cost/health care resource use in C3G. The searches for economic evidence were conducted on 16 September 2020 and updated on 10 October 2024. The searches for healthcare resource use were conducted on 11 February 2021 and updated on 10 October 2024. HRQoL searches were conducted on 22 January 2021 and updated on 12 November 2024. Searches were transparent and reproducible, and comprehensive strategies were used. A good range of databases, HTA websites and other grey literature resources were searched. Overall, the EAG has no concerns about the literature searches conducted. 

114 



<!-- page 531 -->

CONFIDENTIAL UNTIL PUBLISHED 

The company’s cost effectiveness model complied with the NICE reference case. The most prominent issues highlighted by the EAG are reported in the key issue tables in Section 1.5. 

Firstly, the company’s approach of estimating eGFR slopes was suboptimal. Using a before-after comparison (i.e., pre-iptacopan data for SoC and on-iptacopan data for iptacopan) based on APPEARC3G and the open-label extension study rather than using the randomised double-blind period of APPEAR-C3G is prone to biasing the estimated eGFR slopes. The EAG concluded that the approach of estimating the eGFR slope for SoC based on RaDaR  and subsequently applying the iptacopan treatment effect from the randomised double-blind period of APPEAR-C3G to inform the iptacopan eGFR slope to be the most reasonable for (relative) treatment effectiveness in the economic model. Secondly, several assumptions were made regarding the time independence of various parameters over the modelled time horizon. There was substantial uncertainty related to the assumption that the speed of eGFR progression was independent of the CKD stage and constant over time. Such an assumption could lead to either overestimation or underestimation of the progression speed, which in turn would have substantial implications for the long-term modelling of costs and effects, particularly those associated with kidney replacement therapies such as dialysis and kidney transplantation. Next to that, the rate of discontinuation from iptacopan treatment was assumed to be constant over time. This assumption was questioned by the EAG and its clinical expert, who indicated that the discontinuation rate over subsequent years remains uncertain. The EAG preferred using parametric survival modelling based on TTD to inform this aspect of the economic model. The impact of these analyses may be more pronounced when combined with assumptions related to waning of the iptacopan treatment effect. A more detailed explanation of the TTD model selection process, as per NICE DSU TSD 14 guidance, is necessary for a comprehensive assessment. Furthermore, the assumption of a constant iptacopan treatment effect over the model time horizon was also scrutinised. Despite assertions from the company and the EAG clinical expert that the " _on-target effect on complement inhibition will remain comparable throughout_ ", this assumption was deemed insufficiently assessed. Additional evidence demonstrating a constant treatment effect during the observed period, along with scenario analyses exploring potential treatment waning beyond the observed period, would be valuable in addressing this critical issue. Thirdly, CKD stage 5+ utility values were considered relatively low, potentially resulting from agerelated comorbidities in the older, wider CKD population that was used to inform these utility values in the economic model. Analyses of additional (patient-level) EQ-5D data on CKD stage 5+ patients might help to resolve this key issue. Fourthly, the EAG noted that the majority of absolute and incremental QALYs and costs for iptacopan + SoC and SoC were accumulated beyond the observed data period, requiring explanation as to the mechanism by which the model generated these differences and justification as to why these generated differences are plausible provided the available evidence. Finally, the company did not provide the full advisory board report, which was considered a serious transparency issue as it hinders validation of various modelling assumptions informed by clinical experts. 

The estimated EAG base-case ICER (probabilistic), based on the EAG preferred assumptions highlighted in Section 5.1, was £XXXXXX per QALY gained. The probabilistic EAG base-case analyses indicated cost effectiveness probabilities of X% at WTP thresholds of £20,000 and £30,000 per QALY gained. The most influential adjustment was estimating the eGFR slope for SoC based on RaDaR and subsequently applying the iptacopan treatment effect from the randomised double-blind period of APPEAR-C3G to inform the iptacopan eGFR slope. The ICER increased most in the scenario analysis with alternative assumptions regarding KRT utilities. 

In conclusion, there is large remaining uncertainty about the effectiveness and cost effectiveness of iptacopan + SoC, which can be partly resolved by the company. This includes providing CKD stage- 

115 



<!-- page 532 -->

## CONFIDENTIAL UNTIL PUBLISHED 

dependent and time-dependent eGFR decline rates, full details of the TTD model selection process based on the NICE DSU TSD 14 guidance, analyses to assess the assumption of a constant treatment effect during and beyond the observed period, analyses of additional (patient-level) EQ-5D data on CKD stage 5+ patients, explanation and justification of the mechanisms by which the economic model generated a substantial proportion of QALYs and costs beyond the observed data, and providing the full advisory board meeting minutes. Therefore, the EAG believes that the CS nor the EAG report contains an unbiased ICER of iptacopan + SoC compared with SoC.

## **Background to addendum** 

Following the factual inaccuracy check, the company provided an updated economic model including a XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXX. 

Additionally, modelling errors and inaccuracies by both the company and EAG were identified, including: 

- EAG_1 became obsolete following the company’s fix of lacking CKD stage 1-4, post-transplant and dialysis HSUVs in the PSA. CKD stage 1-4 HSUVs are now varied through parameters to the linear regression analyses, rather than directly. 

- The button “Sensitivity analysis!B10:C10” is not working properly, and thus the EAG used “Control!C2” alternatively to perform the identical action of updating parameters before a probabilistic analysis run. Additionally, within the updated economic model, cell G2 in the Control tab used the “COUNT” formula to determine the number of inputs to iterate over within the PSA. This has been updated to “COUNTA” to avoid the exclusion of non-numeric cells (specifically, the constant value in the utility linear regression now included in the PSA). 

- Wastage costs for SoC therapies at discontinuation are now weighted by the proportion patients receiving each treatment (EAG_2). 

- For EAG_6 (scenario analysis), “Analysis 3” (rather than “Analysis 1”) is now selected in cell C7 in the Clinical Data tab. 

This addendum provides updated EAG results including the company’s updated iptacopan price and including fixes for the modelling errors and inaccuracies above.
